Both the neutral cobalt(III) precatalyst and the synthesized π‐allyl‐cobalt(III) complex are catalytically active, and the catalytic system displays broad substrate scope, good functional‐group tolerance, and moderate to high regioselectivity. These results provide key mechanistic insights into cobalt‐mediated nitrene transfer reactions and establish a foundation for the development of selective cobalt‐catalyzed C─H amination reactions.

articles.title: Catalysis by a Metastable Photoswitchable Cage
articles.abstract: The introduction of ortho‐methyl substituents on aryl‐substituted ortho‐tetrafluoroazobenzene photoswitches breaks the π‐conjugation and improves photoswitching selectivity and increases the thermal half‐life of the metastable isomer. Using this approach, a visible‐light‐responsive ligand was assembled with a non‐switchable ligand and palladium(II) ions into a mixture of molecular cages. When irradiated with 530 nm light, the system converges to form a single product, a metastable, mixed‐ligand molecular cage. This cage can be reversibly disassembled using 424 nm light, an example of integrative self‐sorting controlled by light. The metastable assembly can catalyze both Michael addition and nitroaldol reactions. Importantly, visible light accesses a metastable catalytic state inaccessible under thermodynamic control. We demonstrate that the active assembled species can be switched on and off at will using visible irradiation and the metastable species is the most catalytically active assembly.

articles.title: Catalyst‐Controlled Divergent Strain‐Release Amination and Skeletal Remodeling of Bicyclo[1.1.0]Butanes
articles.abstract: Catalyst‐controlled nitrene transfer enables divergent amination reactions of bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes through distinct modes of activation of their highly strained central σ‐bond. Under Rh(II) catalysis, bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes undergo selective strain‐release amination to furnish aminocyclobutenes, which provide efficient access to cyclobutane amino acids through a simple amination–hydrogenation sequence. In contrast, photocatalytic nitrene activation redirects the reaction pathway toward double amination and skeletal remodeling, affording functionalized dihydropyrrolidines that can be readily converted into pyrrole heterocycles under acidic conditions. The synthetic utility of both approaches is further demonstrated, for example, in a telescoped synthesis of cyclobutane amino acids from diazo precursors or downstream diversification reactions. Mechanistic experiments and computational studies reveal distinct catalyst‐dependent nitrene activation pathways that govern the fate of a common reactive intermediate and underpin the observed divergent reactivity.

articles.title: Catalytic Anionic Substituents Effects as Selectivity Mediators in Photocatalytic Hydrogen Atom Transfers
articles.abstract: Photo‐induced hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) catalysis has become a powerful platform for the direct and selective functionalization of ubiquitous C─H bonds. Traditionally, the outcome of these transformations is dictated by the interplay between C─H bond dissociation energies and polar effects, enabling predictable yet inherently substrate‐controlled selectivity. Recently, a fundamentally new strategy has emerged that relies on the catalytic and reversible modulation of substrate electronics to transiently enhance the reactivity of targeted C─H bonds. Notably, catalytic full or partial deprotonation of oxygen‐ and nitrogen‐containing functional groups has proven remarkably effective in selectively activating adjacent C─H bonds toward HAT, a phenomenon known as the anionic substituent effect. Rather than relying solely on the intrinsic properties of a substrate, this concept allows chemists to reprogram C─H bond reactivity in situ, unlocking previously inaccessible levels of selectivity in the direct functionalization of abundant functional groups under mild photocatalytic conditions. In this minireview, we discuss the mechanistic principles underpinning catalytic anionic substituent effects (CASE), the diverse strategies developed to generate them, and their impact on photocatalytic HAT‐mediated C–H functionalization. By highlighting recent advances and emerging opportunities, we illustrate how transient electronic activation is reshaping the design of selective C–H functionalization reactions.

articles.title: Catalytic Enantioselective Remote Transannular Desymmetrization of Calix[4]Arenes to Inherently Chiral Double‐Macrocycles
articles.abstract: There has been a recent surge in research aimed at synthesizing inherently chiral macrocycles that lack point, axial, planar, or helical chirality. To overcome the structural limitations of existing inherently chiral macrocyclic systems, which often suffer from facile racemization due to conformational flexibility, we report herein an asymmetric synthesis of a new class of inherently chiral double‐macrocyclic molecules through an intramolecular macrocyclization strategy, employing calix[4]arenes as the starting platform. Catalyzed by [Pd(allyl)Cl]2 and a chiral phosphoramidite ligand, calix[4]arene derivatives bearing a monoaryl bromide linker at the upper rim underwent a facile enantioselective remote transannular Suzuki–Miyaura coupling with the adjacent upper‐rim position of the neighboring arene unit, furnishing the desired inherently chiral double‐calixarene macrocycles in up to 71% yield and 91% ee. The resulting double macrocycles feature stable conformations and unique semi‐enveloped chiral cavities, and exhibit promising chiral catalytic and chiroptical properties.

articles.title: Chalcogen‐Driven Conformational Control for Room‐Temperature Phosphorescence and Zn2+ Coordination‐Induced Delayed Fluorescence in Phenazine Derivatives
articles.abstract: Purely organic luminescent materials are pivotal for optoelectronics, with chalcogen‐fused phenazines serving as basic building blocks owing to their strong electron donating ability and enhanced spin–orbit coupling effect. However, a systematic understanding of how the chalcogen identity governs intrinsic conformational preference between quasi‐axial (QA) and quasi‐equatorial (QE) forms remains elusive. To address this, we designed a series of derivatives featuring phenoxazine, phenothiazine, and phenoselenazine donors coupled with a terpyridine acceptor. We demonstrate that the chalcogen atom dictates molecular conformation: phenoxazine derivative exclusively adopts the QE conformation, phenothiazine derivative predominantly favors QE, while phenoselenazine derivative stabilizes in the QA form. Notably, heating induces a phase transition in polymorphs toward their thermodynamically favored conformations. Furthermore, Zn2+ coordination enhances intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) strength, shifting the thermodynamically preferred conformation and triggering a switch from room‐temperature phosphorescence (RTP) to dual RTP–delayed fluorescence (DF) emission. This work validates the chalcogen‐determined conformation and ICT strength can effectively modulates DF/RTP performance, deepening the fundamental understanding of the chalcogen‐mediated conformation and properties for the rational design of organic luminescent materials.

articles.title: Characterization of a Fungal Modular Polyketide Synthase System Reveals an Unusual Strategy for Polyketide Chain Initiation
articles.abstract: Polyketides constitute a major class of natural products with remarkable structural diversity and biological activities. While bacteria predominantly produce polyketides via modular type I polyketide synthases (PKSs), eukaryotic modular PKSs remain largely unexplored. Here, we report the functional characterization of a fungal modular PKS system from Lasiodiplodia theobromae through heterologous expression in Aspergillus oryzae, leading to the production of the antimalarial macrolide strasseriolide C (1). Intriguingly, biosynthesis of 1 involves C‐methylation of the starter malonyl unit despite the absence of a methyltransferase domain in the loading module. Furthermore, module 2 of the PKS system contains an unusual arrangement of four consecutive acyl carrier protein (ACP) domains. Although the catalytic basis of this methylation remains unresolved, our isotope‐labeling experiments, mutational analyses, and in vitro biochemical assays support a model in which the malonyl unit loaded onto the module 2 ACPs is transferred to the loading ACP, where starter‐unit methylation is proposed to occur prior to chain initiation. Our study reveals unexpected biosynthetic logic and establishes a foundation for mechanistic studies and engineering of eukaryotic modular PKSs.

articles.title: Chiroptical Switching by Stereoselective Photochemical Sigmatropic Rearrangements: Experimental Realization of Calderoselectivity
articles.abstract: The stereochemical outcomes of pericyclic reactions provide direct insight into the geometry and directionality of concerted bond reorganization. Although torquoselectivity has emerged as a defining concept for electrocyclizations, an analogous principle for sigmatropic rearrangements on a single cyclic π system has remained unknown. We report that a homoannulene‐based photoswitch undergoes an auxiliary‐controlled, stereoselective photochemical [1,11]‐sigmatropic rearrangement, thereby establishing selectivity over directional migration on a single cyclic π framework. We coin the term calderoselectivity for such an unreported stereoselective sigmatropic rearrangement. The switching process is reversible, proceeds to photostationary mixtures of homoannulene and iso‐homoannulene isomers, and furnishes diastereomeric products in a 56:44 ratio; combined chiral HPLC, NMR, ECD, and DFT studies assign the major directionality of acyl migration in pro‐R directionality. This study provides the first experimental realization of calderoselectivity and reveals a direct analogue in sigmatropic rearrangements to torquoselectivity with implications for both mechanistic physical organic chemistry and chiroptical switch design.

articles.title: Cobalt‐Catalyzed Desymmetrizing Hydrogenation of Cyclic Anhydrides
articles.abstract: Achieving general asymmetric catalytic manifolds that accommodate broad substrate diversity remains a long‐standing and highly sought‐after goal in synthetic chemistry. Herein, we report an efficient cobalt‐catalyzed desymmetric hydrogenation of structurally diverse cyclic 1,2‐ and 1,3‐diacid anhydrides, enabling access to pharmaceutically relevant chiral γ‐ and δ‐lactones with broad substrate scope and excellent enantioselectivity (up to 99% ee). The reaction is readily scalable, as demonstrated by gram‐scale synthesis of several representative products. Notably, this 3d‐metal catalytic platform represents a rare example that outperforms platinum‐group‐metal‐based counterparts in both generality and stereoselectivity. DFT studies identify a catalytically active d7 Co(II) dihydride complex with an outer‐sphere hydride transfer mechanism, wherein a relatively flexible chiral pocket underlies the broad substrate compatibility of this catalytic system.

articles.title: Cobalt‐Catalyzed [2σ+2π] Cycloaddition via Site‐Selective Capture of Bicyclobutane Diradical
articles.abstract: Strained bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs) have emerged as versatile precursors for accessing highly reactive intermediates, enabling unconventional bond constructions through strain‐release pathways. Herein, we report a cobalt(II)‐catalyzed strategy that combines thermal activation of BCBs with selective radical capture by Co(II) to afford head‐to‐head fused bicyclo[2.1.1]hexanes (BCHex). We propose that thermal activation of the BCB generates a reactive diradical intermediate, which is intercepted by a tailored bidentate phosphine Co(II) cationic complex via oxidative radical coupling, followed by a [2σ+2π] cycloaddition with indoles. Mechanistic investigations, including 31P NMR spectroscopy, cyclic voltammetry, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), and density functional theory (DFT) studies, provide insights into the plausible reaction pathway. The involvement of paramagnetic Co(II) species is consistent with the broad features observed in both EPR and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra of the catalyst. In addition, four structurally distinct Co(II) complexes were synthesized, fully characterized by UV–Vis and Fourier‐transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and evaluated as catalysts for the transformation. The cationic nature of the Co(II) species was further confirmed by phosphine oxide trapping experiments and single‐crystal X‐ray crystallography.

articles.title: Collision‐programmed Selectivity in CO2 Electrochemical Reduction via Co‐engineering Electron Transfer Duty Cycle and Proton Transport
articles.abstract: Selectivity of electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (ECO2RR) is typically pursued by optimizing immobilized catalyst films biased at constant potential, an approach referred to as “catalyst‐fixed electrochemistry”. This architecture hinges on two variables that are difficult to tune: the electron‐transfer (ET) environment and local mass transport. Here we introduce a fundamentally different concept: a “catalyst‐fluidized electrochemistry” platform, where freely suspended catalyst particles make stochastic, short‐lived contacts with the electrode. This dynamic system co‐engineers the ET duty cycle (intermittent vs. continuous) and the local proton supply (spherical/fast vs. planar/slow transport), transforming two traditional constraints into tunable operating parameters. Co‐modulating these levers and, when desired varying them independently, improves the selectivity of high‐value products and reveals how each steers pathway branching. Using AuCu2 nanoparticles as a model catalyst, fluidization boosts 9.2‐fold and 2.5‐fold enhancement in Faradaic efficiency (FE) for ethylene (C2H4) and formic acid (HCOOH) under high and low overpotentials, respectively, relative to the corresponding fixed‐film configuration. Pulsed‐potential emulation isolates ET intermittency, while experiments together with DFT‐informed microkinetic modeling indicate that increased surface proton availability further biases the reaction toward C2 formation at high overpotentials. Reaction environment programming thus emerges as a catalyst‐agnostic lever for reconfiguring reaction networks, complementing conventional materials design.

articles.title: Combinatorial Biosynthesis of Antithrombotic Flavonoid 6‐O‐Glycosides From Carthamus tinctorius
articles.abstract: Flavonoid 6‐O‐glycosides from Carthamus tinctorius (safflower) represent a unique class of potential antithrombotic agents. However, their pharmaceutical development has been hindered by limited natural resources. In this study, we characterized four key biosynthetic enzymes from C. tinctorius: Ct6OGT (6‐O‐glycosyltransferase), Ct7OGT (7‐O‐glycosyltransferase), Ct3OGT (3‐O‐glycosyltransferase), and CtFLS (flavonol synthase). Among them, Ct6OGT is the first identified high‐regioselectivity flavonoid 6‐O‐glycosyltransferase. By combining these enzymes with upstream genes identified from safflower, we established an in vitro enzymatic approach for the synthesis of 6‐hydroxykaempferol 3,6,7‐tri‐O‐glycosides. Notably, enzymatic assays demonstrated that the 3,6,7‐O‐triglycosides were synthesized via a sequential linear glycosylation pathway, in the order of 6‐O‐, 7‐O‐, and finally 3‐O‐glycosylation. Through combinatorial biosynthesis, we further produced 26 flavonoid 6‐O‐glycosides, including naturally occurring compounds from C. tinctorius and novel analogs. Subsequent evaluation in a zebrafish model revealed these flavonoid 6‐O‐glycosides exhibited antithrombotic activities, with 6‐hydroxylation and 6‐O‐glycosylation remarkably enhancing the potency. This work represents the first report of an enzymatic synthetic method for flavonoid 6‐O‐glycosides, and provides a valuable foundation for their future drug development.

articles.title: Complementary Eigen–Zundel Interpretation Reconciles Thermodynamics and Spectroscopy of Excess Protons in Aqueous HF Solutions
articles.abstract: Aqueous solutions of HF and HCl behave very differently at intermediate concentrations: HCl dissociates completely, whereas HF only partially dissociates and forms bifluoride (HF2−${\rm HF}_2^-$). This should lead to markedly different excess‐proton spectra in HF and HCl solutions, in contrast to experimental reports. Using ab initio molecular dynamics, we show that in HF the proton is not firmly bound to F−${\rm F}^-$, as suggested by textbook chemistry, but dynamically shared with a hydrating water molecule. This is rationalized by a modified Eigen‐picture description which also explains the formation of HF2−${\rm HF}_2^-$. The similar vibrational spectra of HF and HCl solutions are explained by a complementary Zundel picture in terms of almost identical excess proton transfer free‐energy profiles for HF and HCl. These results reconcile thermodynamic and spectroscopic observations and provide a unified microscopic picture of excess protons in aqueous solution.

articles.title: Conformation‐Selective Binding Domains of Intramolecular Chemically Induced Protein Dimerisation Systems
articles.abstract: Chemically induced protein dimerisation (CID) is a widely used approach for detecting and actuating small‐molecule‐protein interactions. Here, we demonstrate that CID systems can be used as building blocks for higher‐order ligand‐controlled protein systems. To this end, we converted classical FK506‐ and cyclosporine A‐controlled CIDs into single‐chain pseudo‐allosteric proteins. These systems displayed 15‐ and 50‐fold gains in ligand affinity compared with the parental components operating in trans. Using these fusion proteins as baits in mRNA display, we identified FN3con binding domains that recognise the holo state of each bait with subnanomolar affinity and >100‐fold selectivity over the apo form. Integration of the binding domains and intramolecular CIDs into two‐component enzymatic protein biosensors enabled quantification of the cognate ligands with low‐nanomolar limits of detection (LODs). ELISA assays based on the developed systems displayed mid‐picomolar LODs and accurately quantified FK506 and cyclosporine A in unprocessed blood samples from transplant patients with accuracy comparable to that of LC‐MS/MS. This work establishes a generalisable strategy for harnessing the affinity gains of intramolecular CID systems to create gain‐of‐signal assays for small molecules and ions.

articles.title: Controlling Adaptive Flexibility for Efficient Purification of Ethylene From Ethane
articles.abstract: Ethane‐selective adsorbents enable direct production of high‐purity ethylene, yet rational improvement of selectivity and productivity remains challenging. Here, we report a strategy of adaptive flexibility control. A family of isostructural metal azolate frameworks featuring bent linkers and size‐tunable substituents were designed and synthesized. Single‐crystal X‐ray diffraction and computational simulations unveiled a bending‐adsorption coupling mechanism: the stronger ethane binding drives more pronounced linker flattening to reinforce itself. Crucially, bulkier substituents reinforce this adaptive response, further elevating ethane selectivity. Notably, mixture breakthrough experiments demonstrated that navigating the selectivity–capacity trade‐off via substituent‐tuned adaptive flexibility afforded superior ethylene purification productivity.

articles.title: Cooperation of PtO2 and Adjacent Pt1 on In2O3 Photocatalysts for Unity‐Selective Propane Dehydrogenation
articles.abstract: Solar‐driven direct propane dehydrogenation (PDH) represents a promising strategy to overcome the high‐temperature demands and selectivity limitations of conventional thermocatalysis, yet the identification of effective photoactive phases remains challenging. Herein, we demonstrate that photoactivated PtO2 enables regenerable and highly selective PDH over a PtO2/Pt1‐In2O3 catalyst under mild conditions. Under simulated sunlight without external heating, the catalyst achieves a propylene formation rate of 1322.35 µmol g−1 h−1 with unity selectivity, while remaining inactive under comparable thermocatalytic conditions. In situ spectroscopic analyses combined with density functional theory calculations reveal a photoactivated dual‐site mechanism, in which PtO2 nanoparticles function as oxidation centers for hole‐driven C─H bond activation, whereas neighboring interfacial Pt single atoms act as electron‐accepting sites to promote H2 evolution, enabling efficient spatial separation and utilization of photogenerated charge carriers. Catalyst deactivation arises from partial reduction of PtO2, which can be exactly regenerated via a facile oxidative annealing process in air, affording excellent reusability. These findings identify photoactivated PtO2 as a distinct active phase for selective PDH and provide a design principle for solar‐driven alkane valorization.

articles.title: Coordination‐Triggered Coupling‐Pathway Control in Organic Diradical Cations
articles.abstract: Organic diradicals with stimuli‐responsive spin interaction tunability have attracted considerable interest due to their unique controllable magnetic behaviors. However, due to the challenges of introducing tuning centers into the highly reactive diradical systems, only limited cases of tunable diradicals have been reported. Herein, we demonstrated that a boron center placed directly between two spin sources can serve as a coordination‐responsive antiferromagnetic coupling unit to modulate magnetic interactions in an organic diradical system. We developed a boron‐based diradical cation which can be readily coordinated by acetonitrile. Both the non‐coordinated diradical cation and the adduct were comprehensively characterized by single‐crystal X‐ray diffraction, SQUID magnetometry, EPR spectroscopy, and further analyzed by DFT calculations. After coordination, the spin interaction through boron is weakened, resulting in a significant reduction in the antiferromagnetic coupling strength while shortening the average spin‐spin distance. The non‐coordinated form possesses a singlet ground state, while the adduct has nearly degenerate singlet and triplet states. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first experimental demonstration of coordination‐triggered coupling pathway control in organic diradical cations, thereby providing a new approach for controlling spin interactions through chemical coordination.

articles.title: Correction to “Achieving Stable and Fast Ion Transport in Regenerated LiFePO4 Via Vacancy‐Mediated Upcycling”

articles.abstract: Cooks and coworkers (Angewandte Chemie 65 (2026), e1888676, https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.1888676) claim that cyclic ketones are oxidized by H2O•+. Formation of this species requires a substantial input of energy to be formed and is, even if it were to be formed, too short‐lived to participate in bimolecular reactions.

articles.title: Covalently Preorganized (Thio)Urea–Alkoxide Organocatalysts Enable Controlled Synthesis of High‐Molecular‐Weight Polyglycolide
articles.abstract: Polyglycolide (PGA) is a leading biodegradable polyester, but controlled access to high‐molecular‐weight PGA remains challenging. Here, we introduce a covalent preorganization strategy that merges H‐bond‐mediated monomer activation and alkoxide‐based chain propagation within a single molecular scaffold. Systematic variation of the H‐bond donor, substituent electronics, tether length, and counter cation identifies the thiourea‐based sodium alkoxide Cat. 7 as an optimal catalyst/initiator. Under mild conditions, Cat. 7 enables rapid and selective ring‐opening polymerization of glycolide, affording PGA with number‐average molecular weights up to 222.4 kDa (dispersity of 1.57, turnover number of 11 600, and turnover frequency of 483 h−1). Crystallographic, kinetic, spectroscopic, and computational studies support an intramolecular cooperative mechanism. The resulting high‐molecular‐weight PGA exhibits high crystallinity and tensile strength, highlighting (thio)urea‐alkoxide covalent integration as a powerful strategy for the precision synthesis of high‐performance biodegradable polyesters.

articles.title: Crossing the Threshold: Using Photostationary States to Control Supramolecular Polymerisation
articles.abstract: The completeness of photoswitching is a key figure of merit for molecular photoswitches. In azo‐based switches, quantitative conversion between the E and Z isomers is typically sought to maximise change in properties, while intermediate photostationary states (PSSs) receive less attention. Here, we show that intermediate PSSs can be functionally useful when coupled to threshold‐regulated processes. We demonstrate this by using a photoswitchable monomer that undergoes cooperative supramolecular polymerisation. The irradiation wavelength controls the concentration of polymerisation‐active monomer; once this concentration crosses the nucleation threshold, small wavelength‐dependent changes in PSS composition produce large changes in aggregation state. The resulting supramolecular polymer assembles in aqueous media and undergoes light‐induced disassembly in the condensed phase. In the broader context, coupling photoswitching to threshold‐dependent assembly provides a novel route to convert subtle changes in PSS composition into an amplified, non‐linear supramolecular response.

articles.title: Customized Flexibility in Soft Porous Crystals with Coupled Dynamics for Matching Separation of Light Hydrocarbons
articles.abstract: Soft porous crystals exploit adaptive structural dynamics for molecular recognition, yet their elusive nature hinders the fundamental understanding of rational design and reliable applications. Here, the correlation dynamics intrinsic to layered M(pbe)‐α (M = Co2+, Zn2+, Cu2+), transmitting from mono‐vertex to strained‐linker and to self‐adaptive grid/stack, are orchestrated into node‐encoded flexibility. In‐situ tracking of dynamic structural evolution (including vertex distortion, linker rotation, layer motion, and pore resculpting) reveals the cation‐induced flexibility gradient Co > Zn > Cu, evidenced by changes in coordination bond lengths, unit cell volumes, and inter/intra‐layer interactions. The activated phase Co(pbe)‐β exhibits strong flexibility, undergoing a polarizability‐driven response for acetylene, achieving a record acetylene/carbon dioxide uptake ratio of 75. Zn(pbe)‐β with moderate flexibility displays a marked difference in response to propylene versus propane. Cu(pbe)‐β with the weakest flexibility shows high selectivity for dispersion‐driven adsorption of butadiene over n‐butene. Breakthrough experiments confirm exceptional separation and cyclic performance, where efficient desorption yields high‐purity (≥ 99.5%) acetylene, propylene, and butadiene. Thus, correlating the local dynamic extent of coordination bonds with weak interaction constraints, as well as global cell volume expansion extent in these finely fabricated layered soft crystals, enables customized flexibility for the matched separation of challenging C2‐C4 mixtures.

articles.title: Difluoromethylenation of Alkynes: Streamlined Access to Allyl Difluorides
articles.abstract: A direct difluoromethylenation of alkynes has been developed using HF/pyridine as a dual acidic and fluorinating medium. The reaction proceeds via in situ generation of a primary oxocarbenium ion from formaldehyde, enabling efficient formation of two C(sp3)─F bonds and one C(sp2)═C(sp2) bond in a single step without the need for pre‐functionalized reagents. This strategy offers a concise route to allyl difluorides as a complementary approach to incorporate difluoromethylene motifs into complex molecular frameworks. Additional spectroscopic and computational investigations provide insights into this mechanism.

articles.title: Direct Asymmetric Synthesis of Chiral β‐Hydroxy‐α‐Amino Amides via PLP‐Inspired Biomimetic Aldol Reaction
articles.abstract: Chiral β‐hydroxy‐α‐amino amides represent important structural motifs ubiquitous in pharmaceuticals and bioactive molecules. Current synthetic approaches typically rely on multistep conversion from the corresponding β‐hydroxy‐α‐amino acids, resulting in poor step‐economy and potential α‐racemization during amidation. However, direct asymmetric synthesis of these compounds via aldol reactions remains highly challenging because of the low reactivity of glycinamides and the instability of the corresponding aldol products. Herein, we report a chiral pyridoxal‐catalyzed biomimetic aldol reaction of glycinamides with aldehydes, producing a broad range of structurally diverse chiral β‐hydroxy‐α‐amino amides in up to 98% yield, >20:1 dr, and 99% ee. Notably, this biomimetic strategy accommodates structurally complex dipeptides and polypeptides, allowing direct modification of peptide chains and providing efficient access to these significant peptide‐based chiral β‐hydroxy‐α‐amino amides. The key intermediate of the drug eliglustat was also readily synthesized via this strategy. Mechanistic studies suggest a cooperative carbonyl catalysis pathway analogous to threonine aldolase, accounting for the high reactivity and stereocontrol.

articles.title: Discovery and Bioinspired Synthesis of Neuroprotective Geranylated Chalcones From Artocarpus communis
articles.abstract: Two geranylated chalcone oligomers, artocarpusones A (1) and B (2), featuring a highly functionalized 6/5/6/5/6‐fused pentacyclic hemiketal, were discovered from the medicinal plant Artocarpus communis, along with six related compounds 3−8. Their structures with absolute configurations were established using comprehensive spectroscopic analyses that were supported by computational calculations. Biosynthetic considerations suggest that 1−7 could be derived from a single precursor 8. Guided by this insight, a bioinspired synthesis of 1−7 was achieved in a total of 7−9 steps from 8. The synthesis is enabled by bioinspired cascade reactions encompassing oxidative rearrangement, Michael additions, hemiketalizations, 6π‐electrocyclization, and hetero‐Diels–Alder reaction. Notably, congener 2 exhibited anti‐ischemic stroke activity both in vitro and in vivo, suggesting its potential as a neuroprotective candidate for further therapeutic evaluation.

articles.title: Discriminating Monomers and Fibrils of Amyloid‐β1–42 With Site‐Ordered Peptide‐QMFluors
articles.abstract: The detection of soluble amyloid-β (Aβ), the most neurotoxic species in early Alzheimer's disease (AD), remains a major analytical challenge. Conventional probes are designed to target the β-sheet structures of mature fibrils and are thus blind to these transient, nonfibrillar species. Here, we introduce “site-ordered engineering” strategy, a peptide-conjugated QMFluors conjugate designed to selectively target Aβ 1–42 monomers with high fidelity. We identified the conjugation site order on the fluorophore as the key parameter controlling this molecular topology and self-assembly behavior. This breakthrough is enabled by a hydrogen-bond-driven recognition mechanism, fundamentally departing from classical dyes that target the β-sheets of mature fibrils. This yields an unprecedented “inverted selectivity” with a 20-fold fluorescence enhancement for monomers over fibrils. Using probe N-QM-KLVFF with super-resolution microscopy, we reveal the nanoscale “core-shell” biophysical phase diagram of plaques, visualizing dense fibrillar cores surrounded by monomeric/oligomeric halos. Furthermore, the probe demonstrates a limit of detection of pg/mL level and excellent linearity, meeting the stringent requirements for trace cerebrospinal-fluid-biomarker analysis. This work provides not only a powerful tool for early diagnosis and pathological investigation, but also establishes “aggregation-regulated accessibility” as a generalizable principle for designing probes for other dynamic amyloid protein targets.

articles.title: Divergent Chiral Self‐Sorting of Covalent Organic Pillars Switched by Subtle Conformational Preferences
articles.abstract: Chiral self‐sorting enables molecular systems to translate stereochemical information from small building blocks into highly organized architectures across length scales, echoing the hierarchical expression of chirality in biological systems. However, predicting whether a system will favor homochiral or heterochiral organization, let alone rationally controlling the sorting outcome, remains challenging. Here we show that the chiral self‐sorting of covalent organic pillars (COPs) can be selectively switched through minimal structural variation in the linker units. Two diamine linkers, 2,6‐bis(aminomethyl)pyridine and m‐xylylenediamine, were used to connect pairs of stereolabile penta‐aldehyde tiara[5]arene macrocycles through dynamic covalent [2+5] imine condensation. Despite their close resemblance, these linkers lead to divergent outcomes. Whereas 2,6‐bis(aminomethyl)pyridine directs social chiral self‐sorting to give a meso COP, m‐xylylenediamine promotes narcissistic chiral self‐sorting to afford enantiomeric COPs. In both cases, the products form cleanly without detectable stereoisomeric byproducts, and their stereochemical assignments are confirmed by X‐ray crystallography. Computational analyses support the view that distinct linker conformational preferences provide a rationale for the divergent sorting pathways. This work establishes COPs as a model platform for understanding chiral self‐sorting and provides a conceptual basis for selecting, amplifying, and expressing stereochemical information in complex molecular architectures.

articles.title: Diverting Reaction Pathways: Shunt Catalysis for Robust C═O Hydrogenation
articles.abstract: Manipulating the spillover of reactants represents a pivotal strategy to govern reaction pathways and boost the efficiency of heterogeneous catalysis, enabling reactive species to spontaneously navigate the path of least kinetic resistance. Herein, we establish a “catalytic shunt” by integrating discrete Ag/SiO2 and Ag/CeO2 nanounits into a unique Ag/CeO2||SiO2 architecture that decouples competing reaction steps in dimethyl oxalate (DMO) hydrogenation to methyl glycolate (MG). Notably, Ag/CeO2 with well‐defined polyhedral Ag nanoparticles is catalytically inert, due to overwhelming C═O adsorption on positively charged Agδ+ sites. However, mechanically integrating with Ag/SiO2 (featuring spherical Ag NPs) unlocks unprecedented activity for C═O hydrogenation. In this featured configuration (Ag/CeO2||SiO2), in‐depth characterizations and theoretical calculations reveal that H2 is activated on metallic Ag0 (Ag/SiO2 moieties) and efficiently spills over to activate DMO pre‐polarized on Agδ+ (Ag/CeO2 subunits). Remarkably, even with only 5% of Ag nanoparticles on CeO2, the Ag/CeO2||SiO2 system delivers a turnover frequency (TOF) 6‐fold higher than benchmark Ag/SiO2. The engineered configuration ensures ultra‐high H2 utilization and enhanced thermal stability, maintaining robust stability over 1000 h. This spatial shunting strategy thus provides a powerful paradigm for the rational design of cooperative catalytic interfaces that circumvent competitive adsorption limits.

articles.title: Dual‐Function Cosubstrates Enable Threonine Dehydrogenase‐Driven Chemoenzymatic Pyrrole Synthesis
articles.abstract: Preparative biocatalytic synthesis of substituted pyrroles remains challenging despite recent advances in enzymatic α‐aminoketone generation. In this study, we report a concurrent chemoenzymatic cascade to disubstituted pyrroles based on threonine dehydrogenase (ThrDH)‐catalyzed generation of aminoacetone from l‐threonine that is intercepted in situ by Knorr pyrrole condensation with β‐dicarbonyl compounds. To overcome cofactor limitations at high substrate concentrations, Escherichia coli ThrDH was coupled to an alcohol dehydrogenase from Rhodococcus ruber DSM 44541 (ADH‐A), enabling dual‐function of the β‐dicarbonyl cosubstrate as both a hydride acceptor and pyrrole building‐block. The whole‐cell catalyst tolerated up to 8% (v/v) β‐dicarbonyl and afforded pyrrole products in up to 90% yield and space‐time yields of 4.5 g L−1 h−1. Preparative synthesis on a 100 mL scale furnished 4.3 g of pyrrole (279 mM, 93% isolated yield). Among the products obtained, the cascade provides direct access to a reported sunitinib intermediate, illustrating its potential utility for pharmaceutical synthesis. This work establishes ThrDHs as outstanding biocatalysts for heterocycle synthesis and demonstrates that amino acid feedstocks can be efficiently converted into substituted pyrroles through a scalable chemoenzymatic cascade.

articles.title: Routes to cleaner critical metals
Diffusion Models for Small-Molecule Design
articles.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a class of generative models for controllable small-molecule design in drug discovery capable of progressively transforming noisy or partially specified molecular states into candidate structures under structural, geometric, and property constraints. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological foundations and representative applications of diffusion-based molecular generation, emphasizing the alignment among molecular representations, generative dynamics, controllable design, and evaluation and validation. Particular attention is given to recent advances in property- and structure-guided generation, target-aware and fragment-based design, multiobjective optimization, and synthesis-aware generation. We also discuss the roles of data sets, computational evaluation, and prospective experiments in assessing the chemical and biological relevance of generated molecules. By organizing these developments within a unified conceptual framework, we provide computational chemists and drug discovery researchers with a structured roadmap that balances the mathematical rigor with chemical intuition. Throughout, we highlight current methodological limitations and unresolved challenges and conclude with future directions toward chemically credible and experimentally grounded molecular design. To facilitate navigation of this rapidly evolving field, we introduce an interactive companion platform (https://diffsmd.scbdd.com) that provides a curated, continuously updated repository of model architectures and visualizations.

articles.title: Electrochemical conversion of low-concentration carbon dioxide to multicarbon products: advances, challenges, and perspectives

articles.title: Magnetic Skyrmions in CrGaTe3 Monolayer
articles.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) magnetic skyrmions hold great promise for next-generation high-density information storage, yet their low-dimensional behavior and controllable size remain challenging. Here, combining first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations, we identify monolayer CrGaTe3, derived from the Ga2S3 structure, as a ferromagnetic half-metal and a robust platform for hosting topological spin textures. The system exhibits a substantial Dzyaloshinskii−Moriya interaction (DMI) of 2.36 m V, arising from intrinsic inversion asymmetry and strong spin−orbit coupling, alongside sizable Kitaev exchange and magnetic anisotropy. At zero field, the ground state adopts a Néel-type cycloid state, which evolves into stable skyrmion phases under moderate external magnetic fields. Remarkably, beyond field tuning, we find that biaxial strain not only modulates the skyrmion size but also induces skyrmion states under tensile conditions, offering an additional degree of freedom for topological phase engineering. Furthermore, our parameter-resolved analysis reveals that while DMI is pivotal for skyrmion nucleation, the Kitaev interaction and magnetic anisotropy collectively govern the size and density of the skyrmion lattice. These findings establish monolayer CrGaTe3 as a promising candidate for sub-10 nm spintronic devices and demonstrate that the synergy between intrinsic symmetry breaking and external stimuli provides a generalizable strategy for designing functional 2D magnets.

articles.title: ZnO Vacancy Homojunction for Phonon-Enhanced Directional Charge Transfer
articles.abstract: Directional charge transport is essential for efficient photocatalysis, yet carrier transfer in semiconductor nanocrystals is often random and limited by recombination. Although electron−phonon coupling strongly influences carrier dynamics, phonons are more commonly associated with energy dissipation than with enhanced charge transport. Here, we construct a ZnO vacancy homojunction composed of donor-type oxygen vacancies and acceptor-type zinc vacancies, establishing an intrinsic pathway for directional charge transfer. The resulting n−p junction introduces both an internal electric field and asymmetric lattice distortion, enabling phonon-assisted directional carrier transport under ultrasonication and leading to significantly enhanced photocatalytic performance in methylene blue degradation compared with conventional ZnO. Combined spectroscopic measurements, radical-trapping experiments, and density functional theory calculations reveal a phonon-enhanced directional charge-transfer mechanism. These findings provide a general strategy for regulating directional charge transport through lattice dynamics.

articles.title: Generation of Human Cardiomyocytes With Adult-Like Metabolism by a Chemically Defined Medium for Mitochondrial Disease Modeling
articles.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC cardiomyocytes) as a model for cardiac disease have become increasingly important, bolstered by the Food and Drug Administration’s initiative to promote novel alternative methods for biomedical research. A key limitation of metabolically immature iPSC cardiomyocytes is their limited ability to accurately recapitulate mitochondria-dependent pathologies, such as Friedreich ataxia–associated cardiomyopathy. Adult cardiomyocytes are characterized by a high density of interfibrillar mitochondria, abundant respiratory complexes (I–V) that form supercomplexes, and efficient utilization of fatty acids to drive mitochondrial respiration. These unique metabolic structures and functions are largely missing in iPSC cardiomyocytes. Further, whether iPSC cardiomyocytes can efficiently utilize fatty acids for respiration in the presence of glucose, a unique adult feature, remains unclear. We developed a chemically defined, 11-component maturation medium (MM11) designed using a bioinformatics-guided strategy that identified high-fidelity transcriptional markers of adult cardiac metabolic maturity. Human iPSC cardiomyocytes were treated with MM11 for 2 weeks and evaluated at the molecular, structural, and functional levels, with an emphasis on mitochondrial maturity. We benchmarked our results with isolated primary adult human cardiomyocytes. Last, we tested whether this method could enable us to more accurately model Friedreich ataxia cardiomyopathy. MM11 treatment increased expression of metabolic pathways, including mitochondrial respiration and fatty acid metabolism, at the transcript and protein levels. Ultrastructural analyses revealed the formation of interfibrillar mitochondria and mitochondrial respiratory supercomplexes, a feature never shown in previous reports. Functionally, MM11-treated iPSC cardiomyocytes exhibited substantially increased oxidative phosphorylation and a metabolic preference for fatty acid utilization in the presence of physiologic substrates, as determined by oxygen consumption assays and 13 C isotope tracing. MM11 promotes robust metabolic maturation of human iPSC cardiomyocytes, enabling sophisticated mitochondrial architecture and substrate utilization. These metabolically matured cardiomyocytes more faithfully model mitochondria-dependent cardiac pathologies, including ischemia-reperfusion injury and Friedreich ataxia cardiomyopathy, improving the use of iPSC cardiomyocytes for mechanistic studies of human heart disease.

articles.title: Off-Pump versus On-Pump Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting in Prefrail and Frail Patients: 30-Day and 1-Year Outcomes From the FRAGILE Randomized Trial
articles.abstract: Frailty is associated with worse outcomes after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). However, the comparative effectiveness of off-pump CABG (OPCAB) versus on-pump CABG (ONCAB) in prefrail and frail patients remains uncertain. This multicenter, randomized, open-label trial enrolled patients ≥60 years of age classified as prefrail or frail, randomized 1:1, between January 2018 and December 2024. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, or reoperation for bleeding. Secondary outcomes included ventilation time, intensive care unit and hospital stay, transfusion requirements, completeness of revascularization, surgical wound infection at 30 days, and neurocognitive function preoperatively and at 1 year. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle; relative risks with 95% CIs were estimated. A total of 508 patients were included (OPCAB, n=258; ONCAB, n=250; median age, 68 years [interquartile range, 65.0–73]; 30.5% female). The primary composite outcome occurred in 28 patients receiving OPCAB (10.9%) and 40 patients receiving ONCAB (16.0%; relative risk, 1.47 [95% CI, 0.94–2.31]; P =0.09). Surgical wound infection was more frequent with ONCAB (20 [8.0%] versus 9 [3.5%]; P =0.04). No significant differences were observed in neurocognitive or quality of life outcomes at 1 year. Estimated 1-year survival probabilities were 96.1% and 92.8% in the OPCAB and ONCAB groups, respectively ( P =0.099). In prefrail and frail patients undergoing CABG, OPCAB and ONCAB resulted in similar rates of the primary composite outcome. No significant differences between OPCAB and ONCAB were found in neurocognitive outcomes. URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT02338947.

articles.title: A Comparison of Owl Pellet Analysis and Conventional Trapping: A Review of Central European Cases for the Study of Small Mammal Communities and More Efficient Paleoenvironmental Reconstructions
articles.abstract: Due to their rapid reproductive cycles and short generation times, small mammals—particularly rodents and shrews—are widely used as bioindicators in ecological studies. While traditional live trapping provides detailed demographic data for such monitoring, it is labour‐intensive and subject to sampling bias. In contrast, owl pellet analysis presents a non‐invasive and cost‐effective alternative for evaluating small mammal community structure over broad spatial and temporal scales, though potential prey preferences should be considered. This study evaluates the effectiveness of owl pellet analysis in comparison to conventional trapping methods for monitoring small mammal communities. We synthesised data from 26 published studies and additional unpublished field reports, comprising a uniquely robust dataset of 40 systematically processed case studies across seven countries in Central Europe, a biogeographically coherent region. In all cases, trapping and pellet collection were carried out at the same locations and during the same periods, allowing for an exceptional level of methodological consistency. Results reveal that owl pellet analysis detects higher species diversity and provides a more efficient, non‐invasive means of monitoring small mammal assemblages over larger spatial and temporal scales. However, prey preferences and hunting behaviour of owls introduce biases, often overrepresenting abundant prey such as the common vole, Microtus arvalis and underrepresenting species associated with specific habitats or microclimates. These biases have significant implications for biodiversity assessments and paleoenvironmental reconstructions, where accurate community composition is essential. Our findings indicate that while owl pellet analysis is a valuable tool for ecological monitoring, careful consideration of predator selectivity is necessary to accurately interpret the results. Further research into owl hunting ecology is recommended to refine the application of this method in biodiversity studies and paleoecology.

articles.title: Building a Framework for Peatland Assessment in Europe by Combining Spectral and Molecular Data
articles.abstract: Peatlands provide critical ecosystem services, including carbon storage, water regulation, and climate mitigation, yet spatial information on their ecological condition remains limited despite widespread degradation. Specific biogeochemical analyses (e.g., biomarkers, molecular compounds, compound specific stable isotopes) can characterize drainage‐related changes in peat properties but are time‐consuming, costly, linked to sophisticated analytical set‐up and thus spatially restricted. We therefore investigated whether high‐resolution PlanetScope imagery capture consistent spectral differences between pristine and drained areas and explored their multivariate correspondence with complementary site‐level biogeochemical properties. Spectral indices, including NDVI, EVI, gNDVI, Greenness Index, and albedo were derived from PlanetScope Analysis‐Ready Surface Reflectance (ARPS) data for nine European peatland sites spanning three climatic zones and contrasting open and sparsely treed vegetation structures. Peat biogeochemistry was characterized using elemental carbon and nitrogen contents and molecular composition determined by pyrolysis–GC/MS. NDVI and Greenness Index differed most consistently between the investigated pristine and drained areas, with higher values under drained conditions across both vegetation structures. In contrast, EVI and albedo, even though also suitable indicators, depended more strongly on vegetation structure and the patterns differed between open and sparsely treed systems. Spectral differences were most pronounced during May and June, identifying the early growing season as the period of strongest spectral separation within the investigated dataset. Drained areas were additionally characterized by higher nitrogen contents, lower C/N ratios, and a greater relative abundance of compounds indicative of metabolized organic matter. Exploratory principal component analyses indicated complementary site‐level patterns between spectral and biogeochemical variables associated with hydrological condition. Consequently, this study demonstrates the potential of high‐resolution PlanetScope spectral data to differentiate between pristine and drained peatland conditions across the investigated sites. However, predictive classification of previously unknown peatland areas will require dedicated modeling and independent validation especially in differentiating from surrounding transition peats and mineral grassland soils.

articles.title: Ecological and Structural Drivers of Song Amplitude Variation in Passerines
articles.abstract: Song amplitude is an important but comparatively understudied dimension of avian acoustic communication, influencing signal transmission, detectability and social interactions. We investigated ecological and structural drivers of song amplitude variation in six passerine species using 3265 songs recorded from 120 territorial males. Body size was associated with cross‐species variation in amplitude only when the largest and loudest species, the Great Reed Warbler, was included. Across species, song amplitude declined with increasing temperature, relative humidity and time after sunrise, whereas ambient noise showed no evidence of a generalised Lombard effect. Song rate, song length and peak frequency were consistent predictors of amplitude, with peak frequency showing the strongest association. Within‐species analyses revealed substantial heterogeneity in environmental effects, whereas relationships between amplitude and song structure were more consistent across species. Individual identity explained considerable variation in amplitude, indicating pronounced within‐species variability in vocal output. Overall, our results suggest that song amplitude is a flexible component of vocal performance shaped primarily by song structure and signalling context rather than by body size alone. These findings emphasise the importance of considering both behavioural and ecological sources of variation when interpreting patterns of acoustic signalling in birds.

articles.title: Genomic Diversity and Population Structure of Tibetan Antelopes Sampled From the Selincuo Region
articles.abstract: Based on genome‐wide SNP data, this study assessed genomic diversity and population structure in Tibetan antelopes sampled from the Selincuo National Nature Reserve. The analyses included runs of homozygosity (ROH), genomic inbreeding coefficients, genetic diversity, linkage disequilibrium (LD), effective population size, genomic relatedness, principal component analysis (PCA), and sNMF. Genomic inbreeding varied among the sampled individuals, with substantial variation among individuals. Short and medium‐length ROHs predominated, whereas long ROHs contributed little to total ROH coverage. This pattern indicates that population‐wide homozygosity is mainly associated with older shared ancestry, genetic drift, and historical demographic change, with limited evidence of severe recent inbreeding. Several individuals had relatively high ROH‐based inbreeding coefficients, indicating heterogeneous individual‐level autozygosity. The samples retained considerable genome‐wide SNP variation, although allele frequencies were unevenly distributed. PCA showed dispersion among individuals, while sNMF identified multiple ancestry components with substantial overlap in individual genetic backgrounds. Kinship analysis detected no first‐ or second‐degree relatives among the sampled individuals. Linkage disequilibrium declined with increasing physical distance between markers, providing a basis for estimating recent effective population size and evaluating demographic history. Overall, the analyzed individuals showed variation in genomic autozygosity, with several exhibiting elevated homozygosity. The LD‐based estimate of recent effective population size provides a baseline for continued genomic monitoring of Tibetan antelopes sampled from the Selincuo region. Broader geographic and temporal sampling is needed to assess population boundaries and changes in genetic diversity. Future work should expand sampling across geographic regions and time periods and compare multiple populations using genome‐wide differentiation, IBD sharing, isolation‐by‐distance analysis, demographic modeling, and direct estimates of migration or gene flow. These analyses will clarify historical demographic changes, recent effective population size variation, and genetic connectivity among protected areas.

articles.title: Population Genetics of Small Hive Beetles in Their Native Range Indicates High Gene Flow and Male‐Biased Dispersal
articles.abstract: The success of biological invasions depends strongly on the genetic diversity and dispersal abilities of invading populations. In many species, males and females differ in their dispersal behavior, potentially contributing unequally to the establishment and spread of invasive populations. Population genetic approaches provide powerful tools for investigating genetic diversity and dispersal patterns. When applied to populations in their native range, these approaches can improve our ability to predict the spread and potential impacts of species following their introduction into new environments. However, such studies remain scarce for many invasive species. This holds true for small hive beetles (SHB), Aethina tumida, which are free‐flying parasites of social bee colonies native to sub‐Saharan Africa that have recently become a widespread invasive species. Here, we show high gene flow across A. tumida populations from Western Kenya. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and nuclear DNA (nuDNA) markers were used to study SHB genetic diversity and differentiation and to infer short‐ and medium‐range dispersal across host colonies (N = 15) and neighboring apiaries (N = 5; ≤ 30 km apart). The mtDNA diversity was high (29 haplotypes in 87 samples), but no significant differences were detected in haplotype diversity and distribution within and across apiaries. The nuDNA diversity and differentiation levels also did not differ significantly between apiaries. However, genetic differentiation among apiaries was significantly lower in males than in females. Moreover, significant isolation by distance was detected in the females but not in the males, suggesting sex‐biased dispersal. Overall, the results suggest that the observed high gene flow underlies the high genetic diversity of SHB, which may contribute to its invasion success.

articles.title: Primary Cavity Excavators in Community‐Managed Lowland Forest of Nepal: Woodpecker Assemblage, Nest‐Tree Preference, and Its Implications for Forest Management
articles.abstract: Woodpeckers are keystone species playing a crucial role as ecosystem engineers, with their highest species richness and diversity in the tropical and subtropical regions. Although most research on the species' ecology originates from the temperate regions, it leaves a substantial gap in woodpecker assemblage and nesting ecology in tropical and subtropical areas. Our study fills this gap in the subtropical region of South Asia, exploring woodpecker diversity, abundance, and factors influencing cavity nest occurrence in the lowland sal Shorea robusta forests of Nepal. The study was carried out in May and June 2024 in the Pathlaiya Community Forest (CF), with 24 line transects established. Each transect was surveyed twice for woodpecker abundance and nesting cavities, with data gathered on the perpendicular distance of woodpecker observation from the transect, tree characteristics, and nesting variables. Distance sampling analysis was used to estimate an overall woodpecker density and detection probability in the study area, which were found to be 0.54 ± 0.07 birds/ha and 0.79 ± 0.05, respectively. Overall, 51 individuals from nine woodpecker species were recorded. In Nepal's lowland sal forests, the nesting occurrence of woodpeckers was significantly influenced by factors: canopy cover, tree condition and tree Diameter at Breast Height (DBH), with emphasis on sal and jamun Syzygium cumini as preferred tree species. It was found that woodpecker cavity nest occurrence depends substantially on mature forest structure for nesting, highlighting the importance of retaining adequate amount of snags and larger trees, aligning with sustainable forest management practices. These findings emphasize community‐managed tropical sal forests as important habitats for primary cavity excavators, particularly Picidae. Our study highlights the importance of retaining large native trees, snags, and cavity‐bearing tree species in forest management plans to support woodpeckers and the larger cavity‐nesting species in South Asia.

articles.title: Temperature‐Dependent Warning Colour Variation in an Aposematic Insect
articles.abstract: Aposematic colouration in animals advertises prey toxicity and unpalatability to predators. However, intra‐specific variation in aposematic signals is widespread and often thought to be the result of environmental factors such as temperature. To investigate how temperature affects warning colour, we used the aposematic seed bug Lygaeus simulans as a model. Wild‐type adults of this species exhibit the typical red and black pattern common among many aposematic insects, while “pale” mutants are yellow and black. Here, we investigated how rearing temperatures affect their warning colour, fitness traits, and protein expression. We found that L. simulans warning colouration is temperature sensitive, with both pale‐mutant and wild‐type individuals redder at lower temperatures (24°C) compared to higher (32°C) temperatures. Reduced body size (weight and length) was also found at this lower temperature. Utilising SWATH‐proteomic analysis, we identified 15 differentially expressed proteins between the two morphs, including Glutathione S‐transferase (GST), a protein involved in oxidative states. Subsequent analysis of GST activity showed higher activity in pale‐mutants compared to wild‐types at 29°C. Furthermore, in males, this difference between morphs mirrored the colour change as it was not evident at 24°C, although this was not the case in females. Our research reveals a distinctive temperature‐dependent variation in aposematic colouration, providing a greater understanding of how warning signals evolve with temperature changes.

Bridging the hearing data gap in the endangered Australian sea lion (Neophoca cinerea) through biomechanical modelling
articles.abstract: The endangered Australian sea lion (Neophoca cinerea) divides its functional ecology between land (for mating and pup-rearing) and sea (for foraging). Given this amphibious lifestyle, it is susceptible to natural and anthropogenic sound exposure in both air and water. Hearing data for the species are limited to a small sample size (two individuals) of behavioural measurements in air at only a few frequencies, and no underwater hearing thresholds are currently available. Understanding its auditory sensitivity is important for assessing potential risks from anthropogenic sound across its habitat. This study used computed tomography-based finite-element modelling of three post-mortem Australian sea lion heads to simulate frequency-dependent sound reception across broad frequency ranges in air and under water. Transfer functions were calculated as the ratio of stapes-footplate velocity to incident sound pressure, providing a quantitative measure of mechanical sound transmission to the inner ear. The models indicated differences in sound reception between the two media. The transfer functions were subsequently converted into estimated audiogram curves by anchoring the minimum thresholds to published values for Australian sea lions and closely related otariid species. The resulting curves were broadly consistent with published otariid audiograms. This study provides a mechanistic description of aerial and underwater sound reception in Australian sea lions, together with an anatomically informed basis for estimating hearing sensitivity and identifying frequency ranges relevant to anthropogenic sound exposure. More broadly, it provides the first mechanistic estimate of underwater hearing in ASLs and demonstrates the potential of CT-based finite-element modelling as a conservation physiology tool for inaccessible marine mammals.

articles.title: Consistent specialization on roe deer across contrasting prey communities: diet and prey selection of Eurasian lynx in the Western Carpathians
articles.abstract: The Carpathian population of the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx carpathicus) represents one of the most important native source populations for lynx conservation and reinforcement in Central Europe, yet ecological drivers of prey selection remain poorly understood. We investigated diet composition, and factors influencing prey selection in the Western Carpathians using an integrated approach combining GPS telemetry and systematic kill-site inspections, snow tracking, scat analysis, camera trapping and microsatellite genotyping for individual lynx identification from scats. Based on 446 prey remains and 386 scat samples collected across several mountain regions, we found that the lynx diet was overwhelmingly dominated by wild ungulates, which accounted for 96.0% of prey remains and 96.3% of total consumed biomass. Roe deer (Capreolus capreolus) was the main prey species, representing 64.6% of prey remains and 69.0% of consumed biomass, followed by red deer (Cervus elaphus; 27.6% and 24.8%, respectively). Despite substantial variation in ungulate community composition and the availability of alternative prey, roe deer remained consistently positively selected across all study areas. In contrast, red deer consumption increased with its relative availability and was more frequent in males, particularly during winter, indicating context-dependent flexibility in prey use. Non-ungulate prey contributed only marginally to the diet, and we found little evidence that lynx age, social status or population density substantially influenced prey selection. Our results demonstrate that Carpathian lynx remain strongly specialized on roe deer while retaining capacity to exploit alternative ungulate prey under specific ecological conditions. These findings improve our understanding of predator–prey interactions in a key European lynx population and provide an important scientific basis for conservation and management of lynx and its prey. Our integrated approach and findings also provide an ecological benchmark for anticipating predator–prey relationships as lynx recover across their former range through natural recolonization, reinforcement and reintroduction.

articles.title: Ecological context supports image-based fungal species recognition in citizen-science observations
articles.abstract: Citizen-science initiatives generate large numbers of image-supported fungal observations that can contribute to biodiversity recording, but their scientific value depends partly on reliable species identification. Recognition from field photographs is challenged by variable imaging conditions, a long-tailed species-frequency distribution, and visual similarity, while ecological descriptors recorded with the same observations provide context unavailable to image-only models. We examined whether habitat, substrate, and month improve fungal species recognition and compared matched strategies for incorporating these fields. Using Danish Fungi 2024-Mini (36,393 images from 20,618 observations of 182 species), we developed the Multi-scale Ecological Fusion Network (MEF-Net), which combines pooled multi-scale ConvNeXt descriptors with ecological descriptors through direct fusion and bounded channel recalibration. At an input resolution of 224 × 224 pixels, MEF-Net achieved mean Top-1 accuracy, Top-3 accuracy, and Macro-F1 values of 72.21%, 88.35%, and 61.68%, respectively, across five independent runs, a 5.51-percentage-point increase in Macro-F1 over the matched image-only ConvNeXt-Base model. At 384 × 384 pixels, mean Macro-F1 was 63.72%, 4.21 percentage points higher than the matched image-only model. These overall gains reflected the combined contributions of the multi-scale visual representation and ecological-context integration. Habitat produced the largest mean gain among the individual fields, whereas using all three fields jointly produced the best metadata-aware result. In the controlled strategy comparison, ecological conditioning of the pooled visual descriptors achieved the highest mean performance, while direct concatenation and calibrated Bayesian Late Fusion also improved upon the matched multi-scale image-only reference. MEF-Net achieved higher Macro-F1 across rare, medium-frequency, and frequent species, with the largest difference in the rare group. These findings indicate that ecological observation context can complement image evidence and support candidate ranking within human-validated fungal biodiversity-recording workflows.

articles.title: Seasonal shifts in phthalate ester composition and ecological risks along the Mudanjiang River–Jingpo Lake continuum
articles.abstract: Phthalate esters (PAEs) are widespread contaminants in freshwater ecosystems, yet how temporal shifts in congener composition relate to environmental gradients and ecological-risk patterns remains poorly understood in connected river–lake systems. In this study, 16 PAEs were investigated in 36 surface-water samples collected from 12 sites along the Mudanjiang River–Jingpo Lake system during spring, summer, and autumn 2024. Water-quality conditions and surrounding landscape pressures were also examined to evaluate the environmental context of PAE variation. Thirteen PAEs were detected, with Σ16PAEs concentrations ranging from 210.90 to 852.11 ng L−1 and averaging 513.35 ± 144.86 ng L−1. DBP was the predominant congener, accounting for 31.9% of Σ16PAEs, whereas DNP showed the highest detection frequency (86.1%). Σ16PAEs concentrations were highest in summer. The congener profile shifted from DBP dominance in spring and summer to a more even composition of DNP, DNPP, DPhP, and DNOP in autumn. PAE composition was associated with water-quality and landscape gradients, indicating that contaminant profiles varied across the observed environmental conditions. Σ16PAEs concentrations were positively associated with cumulative fish risk, but concentration dominance did not correspond directly to congener-specific risk contribution. DBP dominated the PAE burden, whereas DPhP contributed most strongly to fish risk. Non-priority PAEs also contributed substantially to both mixture composition and ecological risk. These results show that ecological-risk patterns in connected freshwater systems are shaped not only by total contaminant burden but also by temporal changes in mixture composition and environmental context. Considering congener-specific composition, non-priority contaminants, and multiple environmental pressures may therefore improve ecological-risk assessment and monitoring of river–lake ecosystems.

articles.title: End-of-Life Care for People Who Are Incarcerated—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We appreciate the response to our article by Ms Ofori-Darko and Dr McClelland and agree wholeheartedly that the definition of palliative care for incarcerated patients should be comprehensive and match the community standard. This standard includes all evidence-based interventions that palliate symptoms during serious, life-limiting illness. We also agree that short-course or single-fraction regimens of radiation therapy may be indicated for incarcerated patients with serious illness who may face additional barriers to longer-duration treatments. Other palliative treatments may also include some forms of chemotherapy, immunotherapy, antibiotics, blood transfusions, and diuresis. Some treatments may lose palliative effectiveness over time and thus be stopped as a person transitions to hospice care.

articles.title: Etiologies: Seeking Causation in Medicine and Poetry
articles.abstract: One of the most central animating questions in medicine is “What is the cause?” Clinicians assiduously seek the diagnosis of a patient’s perplexing symptoms or probe what pathophysiology underlies the disease. Poetry is similarly engaged in a quest for knowing and by its enlarging of the field of inquiry as to the deepest roots of human suffering, it is complementary to, and thus useful in, medical practice. In the poem “Etiology,” medical language (“neoplastic transformation,” “terminology”) is placed beside unscientific explanatory systems (“feng shui,” “fortune stick[s]”), suggesting that illness may arise from several causal worlds at once. A malignancy may be cellular, environmental, familial, cultural, and even spiritual, depending on the kind of history being taken and by whom. “[A]bbreviations and poor penmanship” evokes the insufficiency patients may feel when their illness is summarily translated into clinical shorthand or technical jargon; poetry re-expands the diagnostic arena, restoring texture and richness to causation (“…white rice you relish/is it incense you burnt for your parents, black/on your fingertips blooming dust on the wall”). The poem’s cascading interrogatives become like a differential diagnosis, its syntax and persistent rhetorical questioning resembling good clinical reasoning. Yet the poem tolerates uncertainty, without discounting rigor. In the end, “Etiology” does not oppose medicine’s pursuit of an explanation, but rather amplifies it: “is it the blood you own, now rushing back to you again?” it concludes without really concluding, helping us understand that merely naming or owning is never the end of our questions.

articles.title: Intravenous Vitamin C and Mortality and Organ Dysfunction in Severe Burn Injury
articles.abstract: To the Editor We read with interest the article from the recent VICTORY trial that reported increased mortality in patients with severe burns who were randomized to 4-day administration of vitamin C vs placebo. The rationale for vitamin C administration was the massive release of oxygen free radicals following severe burns. However, the median time to discharge alive from the intensive care unit was 42.5 days in the placebo group, suggesting that a 4-day course of vitamin C may have been too short to affect outcomes. Notably, 2 previous randomized clinical trials in critically ill patients reported that abrupt discontinuation of a 4-day course of vitamin C was associated with increased mortality.

articles.title: Intravenous Vitamin C and Mortality and Organ Dysfunction in Severe Burn Injury—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We thank Dr Hemilä and Ms Chalker for their interest in our VICTORY trial. They propose that the increased mortality in the vitamin C group reflected a rebound effect following abrupt discontinuation of therapy after 96 hours, rather than a direct effect of the drug itself. While one can never definitively rule out that different timing or dosing of a treatment could result in different outcomes, based on a post hoc analysis of the precise timing of treatment and subsequent mortality, we do not believe the VICTORY study provides evidence to suggest that the higher mortality rate observed in the vitamin C group was due to its abrupt termination.

Results demonstrated that the highly motivated DPP cohort derived significant benefit from the original intervention’s 16 individualized, hour-long health coaching sessions during 6 months, reinforced by monthly group and individualized follow-up meetings during the next 1.5 years. However, when the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention later assumed management of the program, this staff-intensive individualized coaching was eliminated for budgetary efficiency, altering a motivationally core feature of the intervention.

articles.title: Lifestyle and Metformin Interventions and Risk of Multimorbidity in Individuals With Prediabetes—In Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We thank Dr McCarthy and colleagues for their letter about our study, which demonstrated less multimorbidity among persons with prediabetes who underwent a lifestyle intervention. They raise the central implementation challenge of maintaining the essential components of an intervention that ensure its proven effectiveness while making necessary adaptations for real-world application. Incorporating new scientific findings that offer potentially short-term benefits must be done cautiously to avoid undermining the intervention’s long-term outcomes. We appreciate recent advances in pharmacotherapy, nutrition, and gut microbiome science and the evolving understanding of disease prevention. Although contemporary science has expanded available treatment modalities, lifestyle interventions continue to serve as a cornerstone of public health strategies for chronic disease prevention, with the behavior modification strategies to address energy balance remaining a core principle.

articles.title: Neuroprotective Therapy for Acute Ischemic Stroke
articles.abstract: A remarkable era in acute ischemic stroke care is now coming to a close—the period of the “reperfusion revolution.” Over the past few decades, pharmacological and mechanical flow restoration therapies became steadily more effective. By restoring blood flow and terminating the ischemic period, reperfusion salvages those cerebral tissues not yet irreversibly injured. However, the reperfusion strategy in acute stroke care is now reaching its limits. Current endovascular thrombectomy approaches reopen over 85% of occluded arteries, leaving little scope for further advance. And successful reperfusion treatment alone clearly only partially solves the therapeutic challenge. Among patients with ischemic stroke due to large-vessel occlusion who receive endovascular thrombectomy, more than two-thirds nevertheless have a disabled final outcome. Restoring blood flow yields incomplete recoveries because some irreversible injury accrues before recanalization can be achieved and additional injury is generated by reperfusion itself. To fully eradicate stroke-related disability, complementary therapies are needed, including: bridging neuroprotection agents, which allow brain cells to tolerate ischemia until reperfusion is attained; reperfusion neuroprotection agents, which avert reperfusion injury; and neuroreparative agents, which promote postinjury reorganization of neurons and synapses.
