Light-Induced Néel Vector Reversal in 2D van der Waals Antiferromagnets
articles.abstract: Antiferromagnetic spintronics promises ultrafast device performance, yet the essential Néel vector reversal is hindered by its intrinsic immunity to external magnetic fields. Here, we propose a mechanism for deterministic Néel vector reversal in 2D van der Waals antiferromagnets enabled by ultrafast laser pulses. The core physics involves light-induced asymmetric interlayer demagnetization, which drives the antiferromagnet into a transient ferrimagnetic state with a finite net moment. This transient symmetry breaking allows the Néel vector to be controlled by an external magnetic field. We identify that the intrinsic structural and electronic asymmetries and spin–orbit-coupling mediated spin flips are essential for this process. Using first-principles calculations and real-time time-dependent density functional theory, we further demonstrate this mechanism in bilayer NiICl and YI2. Our work establishes a general strategy for the optical manipulation of 2D antiferromagnetic order.

articles.title: Molecular and Nanoscale Control of Exciton Transfer in TADF-Sensitized Fluorescence
articles.abstract: TADF-sensitized fluorescence (TSF), also known as hyperfluorescence, combines efficient triplet exciton harvesting with the narrowband emission of fluorescent emitters. Yet, its performance depends on the interplay between exciton conversion, energy transfer, and molecular organization across different length scales. Herein, we review recent progress in nanoscale exciton-transfer engineering for TSF, with emphasis on molecular excited-state dynamics, sensitizer-dopant spatial control, diversified energy-transfer pathways, and interlayer sensitization. These approaches regulate exciton conversion and lifetime, balance Förster and Dexter energy transfer, and control exciton distribution within emissive layers and across interfaces. We also discuss emerging directions including kinetic matching, spatial organization, and multiscale modeling for understanding the links between molecular structure, energy-transfer dynamics, and device performance. This Mini-Review provides profound insights into transforming random blend systems into controllable nanoscale exciton-transfer networks, paving the way for efficient narrowband TSF OLEDs.

articles.title: Sequence-Switchable MOF-on-MOF Photonic Crystals for Broadband Visible Structural Color Modulation
articles.abstract: Structural colors generated by photonic crystals (PCs) have attracted interest in optical sensing. However, the sensing behavior of porous PCs is commonly tailored through material composition, pore structure, or surface chemistry. Here, we show that the spatial configuration of sequence-switchable MOF-on-MOF Bragg stacks regulates molecular access and adsorption while preserving the constituent metal–organic frameworks (MOFs). The reflection wavelength is continuously tuned across the visible spectrum by controlling layer thickness and refractive-index contrast, producing blue-to-red structural colors with a peak reflectance of approximately 90%. Reversing the layer sequence generates distinct optical response amplitudes and kinetics toward volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Combined optical analysis and molecular dynamics simulations further show that the sensing responses depend not only on molecular uptake but also on spatial adsorption distribution and framework–guest interactions. These findings establish molecular transport pathway control through spatial configuration as an additional strategy for regulating the sensing behavior of porous photonic materials.

articles.title: The prospects for standardization of optical brightness of satellites
articles.abstract: Protecting the night sky from optical interference by satellites needs a standard that goes beyond a simple brightness limit to consider the aggregate impact of constellations. We discuss the infrastructure and tools required to achieve this.

articles.title: Basophils boost early antitumor immunity by restraining Treg cells
articles.abstract: Basophils are rare immune cells best known for their roles in allergies. We find that they also restrict early metastatic seeding by suppressing regulatory T (Treg) cells through histamine–HRH1 signaling and MCPT8-mediated cleavage of CD25, thereby enhancing antitumor immunity. Progressing tumors subsequently reprogram basophils into a distinct, less protective state.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal control of CAR-T cell TNF release via tumor-targeted irradiation
articles.abstract: Masoumi et al. engineered CAR-T cells with a radiation-inducible promoter controlling the expression and local release of the cytokine TNF upon tumor irradiation.

articles.title: A binuclear copper enzyme platform for enantioconvergent radical (pseudo)halogenation
articles.abstract: Binuclear metalloenzymes remain underexplored for new-to-nature biocatalytic reactions. Now binuclear copper enzymes, particularly a Bacillus megaterium tyrosinase, are used as a catalytic platform for stereoselective radical azidation, bromination, chlorination and isothiocyanation reactions, expanding metalloenzyme catalysis beyond mononuclear systems.

articles.title: Aptamers enable a distinct mode of conformational DNA recognition
articles.abstract: Aptamers have generally been understood as nucleic acids that recognize a specific ligand. Now it has been shown that secondary aptamers can recognize the ligand-bound conformation of a primary aptamer, enabling recognition of molecules that lack multiple binding sites for sandwich assays. This mechanism can be integrated into lateral flow assays for targets, including serotonin.

articles.title: Author Correction: Hippocampal-prefrontal orchestration supports higher-order learning for creative ideation
articles.abstract: Author Correction: Hippocampal-prefrontal orchestration supports higher-order learning for creative ideation

articles.title: Count the climate losses we prevent
articles.abstract: Climate adaptation reduces losses, but successful risk reduction often leaves no claim or expenditure that records the benefit. Avoided-loss accounts would preserve intervention-specific estimates and evidence across insurance, lending and public finance, without recognizing counterfactual losses as assets.

articles.title: Diacylglycerol Metabolism Drives Host–pathogen Responses During Enteric Infection in Drosophila
articles.abstract: Li et al. reveal a lipid-dependent signaling axis that links intestinal epithelial cells and intestinal muscle to gut motility and bacterial pathogen clearance, offering mechanistic insight into how lipid dynamics orchestrate host defenses.

articles.title: Energy-guided combinatorial co-optimization of antibody affinity and stability
articles.abstract: Here, Tennenhouse et al. develop LAffAb, a structure-based method for designing CDR mutations to improve affinity and developability. By filtering mutations predicted to disrupt stability and foldability, LAffAb enables accurate, one-shot design.

articles.title: Engineering filamentous myosins for optical control of contractility
articles.abstract: Zemsky and colleagues employ protein engineering to create filamentous myosins controlled by light. These optogenetic motors enable spatiotemporal control of contractility in vitro and in cells, providing a tool for probing contractile actomyosin systems.

articles.title: Entangled-to-packed crossover in nonlinear extensional rheology of entangled polymers
articles.abstract: Entanglements among long-chain macromolecules dictate the mechanical performance of polymeric materials and are described with the tube model but the validity of this model has been questioned for nonlinear extension. Here the authors reveal the key mechanism that governs the mechanical response during extension by elucidating the evolution of entanglements using computer simulations and theoretical analysis.

articles.title: Multiscale neural dynamics reveal how striatal subregions shape stress vulnerability and resilience
articles.abstract: This study shows that striatal subregions shape individual differences in stress vulnerability and resilience through distinct patterns of multiscale network dynamics during stress coping.

articles.title: Strong-gain water-window X-ray laser driven by plasma photocathode wakefield acceleration
articles.abstract: Plasma wakefield accelerators promise compact X-ray lasers but have so far lacked sufficiently bright, stable electron beams. The authors show that beam loading by plasma photocathode-injected electron beams boosts brightness and self-stabilises acceleration inside wakefields, paving the way to compact, robust water-window X-ray lasers.

articles.title: Germinal centers as evolutionary islands
articles.abstract: Antibody affinity maturation can favor a few high-affinity clones. Spatially isolated germinal centers limit clonal dominance and preserve antibody response breadth.

articles.title: Mechanical adaptation drives out-of-equilibrium network reorganization and self-strengthening in adapt-ring networks
articles.abstract: Adapt-ring networks consisting of dense, reconfigurable α-cyclodextrin crystalline domains and sparsely crosslinked polyethylene glycol form adaptive polymer materials that remodel and strengthen in response to mechanical stress.

articles.title: Model systems and integration strategies to capture human biology
articles.abstract: Predictive human-relevant model systems are outlined in a Review by integrating engineered materials and microenvironments, human tissue and organ models, computational approaches, and closed-loop strategies. Controlling the boundary conditions, biological organization, measurements and model calibration can improve mechanistic insight, reproducibility and translational relevance across applications.

articles.title: Digital readiness for cardiovascular care in high-burden US communities with cardiology workforce constraints
articles.abstract: As presented at 2026 AHA Scientific Sessions: Analysis of U.S. Census and other national health data identifies communities with high cardiovascular care needs and assess health system readiness for digital care deployment.

articles.title: Opposing microbiome-mediated axes link modifiable lifestyles to health and chronic diseases
articles.abstract: Fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort and microbiome-based prediction scores validated across 13 independent and geographically diverse cohorts revealed two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases.

articles.title: Automated identification of individual birds by song enables multi-year recapture from passive acoustic monitoring data
articles.abstract: A machine learning-based method distinguishes individual ovenbirds in the wild by their distinct vocalizations, collected by passive acoustic recording.

articles.title: Biological foundation models
articles.abstract: A foundation model is trained on a broad body of data to learn general patterns and can then be adapted to many tasks.

articles.title: DIRAC makes complex spatial multi-omic data simpler to analyze
articles.abstract: DIRAC (‘domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration’) is a framework that helps researchers to analyze complex spatial multi-omic data through two connected tasks: integrating omics layers within a sample and transferring annotations from reference datasets to new ones. Thus, DIRAC makes it easier to build interpretable tissue maps across multi-omic assays, platforms and biological systems.

articles.title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC
articles.abstract: DIRAC is a geometric deep learning model that enables both vertical and horizontal integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data.

articles.title: Making AI approachable, one byte at a time
articles.abstract: Introducing AI Bytes, a new educational column at Nature Methods that aims to simplify technical concepts in artificial intelligence for the life sciences research community.

articles.title: Nondisruptive 3D profiling of combinations of epigenetic marks in single cells
articles.abstract: Epi-PHR is an imaging method that maps combinations of epigenetic marks at single genes while preserving 3D genome structure, revealing how chromatin folding and histone modifications are linked among single-chromatin copies.

articles.title: Unlocking spatial diversity of circular RNAs with abcFISH
articles.abstract: A new technique called abcFISH, a multiplex single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization strategy, enables spatial imaging of circular RNAs.

articles.title: abcFISH enables multiplexed, single-molecule visualization of circular RNA spatial heterogeneity
articles.abstract: abcFISH is an imaging method for multiplexed, single‑molecule circular RNA detection in cells and in vivo, revealing single-cell expression heterogeneity and direct therapeutic efficacy of circular aptamers.

articles.title: Atomically resolved exciton emission from single defects in MoS2
articles.abstract: Scanning tunnelling luminescence resolves exciton emission from individual defects in monolayer MoS2 and identifies carbon–hydrogen complexes as the source of a ubiquitous defect emission band.

articles.title: Endogenous virus-like extracellular vesicles enhance the efficacy of cancer vaccines
articles.abstract: Harnessing viral mimicry mechanisms enhances cancer vaccination by improving long-range antigen presentation and T cell activation.

articles.title: Repurposed endogenous virus-like vesicles mediate dendritic cell long-range antigen presentation and T cell activation for enhanced cancer vaccination
articles.abstract: Engineered dendritic-cell vesicles enrich antigen-presentation ligands and viral-mimicry programmes to drive T cell immunity and melanoma control.

articles.title: Editorial Expression of Concern: NgR1 and NgR3 are receptors for chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans
articles.abstract: Editorial Expression of Concern: NgR1 and NgR3 are receptors for chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans

articles.title: Degraders take on GPCRs
The contextual pathogenicity of Porphyromonas gingivalis
articles.abstract: In this Review, Lamont and Hajishengallis explore how the pathogenicity of Porphyromonas gingivalis is determined by microbial, metabolic and host context. They discuss how community interactions, nutrient-sensing and immune subversion regulate virulence and drive dysbiosis, inflammation and periodontitis progression.

articles.title: A novel method based on high‐resolution imaging spectroscopy to predict fine‐root traits and the economics space of fresh tree roots
articles.abstract: Maps of the estimated root nitrogen concentration in the < 0.5‐mm‐diameter classes of 20 woody species based on the imaging spectroscopy using the shortwave infrared spectral region. See also the Commentary on this article by Rewald, 252: 1695–1699. Summary Tree fine‐root morphological, anatomical, and chemical traits are important to reflect belowground resource acquisition strategies to support tree growth, but their measurements involve several labor‐intensive and time‐consuming procedures. We examined the efficacy of visible (VIS), near‐infrared (NIR), and shortwave infrared region (SWIR) spectral reflectance for predicting a comprehensive set of fine‐root traits. Spectral features of fresh fine roots in 20 tree species were analyzed using three distinct spectral datasets: the VIS–NIR (458–960 nm), the SWIR (967–2391 nm), and the combined spectral region (full‐range; 458–2391 nm). The partial least square regression (PLSR) model using root spectral reflectance was developed to estimate nine functional root traits. Comparison of the models revealed that the prediction accuracy was higher when using the SWIR and full‐range datasets than when using the VIS–NIR dataset. The trait with the highest prediction accuracy was root diameter. The predicted multiple root traits successfully reproduced the ordination of the multidimensional trait space, exhibiting a pattern highly similar to that of the observed traits. This method can advance our understanding of multidimensional fine‐root trait spaces and resource strategies by enabling efficient measurement and spatial modeling of root traits across diameter classes.

articles.title: Apoplast multi‐omics profiling during fungal infection uncovers new players of basal and early induced immunity in Arabidopsis thaliana
articles.abstract: Important processes taking place in the apoplast during plant–pathogen interaction identified by multi‐omics profiling of the apoplastic fluid. Summary The extracellular space in plant tissues, known as the apoplast, remains one of the least characterized cellular compartments. The apoplastic fluid, akin to mammalian extracellular fluid, serves as the primary interface between pathogens and their host. It allows the exchange of signalling molecules, coordinates host cell responses and enables the circulation of pathogen effectors that modulate the immune response. We describe here a comprehensive multi‐omics analysis of the apoplastic washing fluids content just 6 h after the onset of Arabidopsis thaliana infection with Botrytis cinerea, a fast‐killing necrotrophic fungus. By varying plant nitrogen nutrition, known to affect both plant defenses and pathogen virulence, we identify candidates that do not stand out under optimal conditions. Our analysis uncovers novel nitrogen‐dependent mechanisms that regulate both basal and early induced apoplastic immunity, revealing the presence of previously unidentified, potentially protective apoplastic metabolites as well as RAN GTPase, a nuclear protein, thereby offering new insights into early apoplastic immune responses. Résumé L’espace extracellulaire des tissus végétaux constitue l’apoplasme, un des compartiments les moins bien caractérisés. De la même manière que chez les mammifères, chez les plantes le liquide apoplastique constitue une des premières interfaces entre les agents pathogènes et leurs hôtes. L’apoplasme permet l’échange de molécules, la coordination des réponses des cellules hôtes, ainsi que la circulation des effecteurs des agents pathogènes qui modulent la réponse immunitaire de l’hôte. Nous avons réalisé une analyse multi‐omique détaillée du contenu de l’AWF 6 h après le début de l’infection de feuilles d’A. thaliana par le champignon nécrotrophe B. cinerea. En faisant varier la disponibilité en azote pour les plantes, qui module à la fois les défenses de la plante et l’agressivité des agents pathogènes, nous avons pu identifier des candidats qui n’apparaissent pas dans des conditions optimales de croissance. Notre analyse a permis d’identifier de nouveaux mécanismes azote‐dépendants qui régulent à la fois l’immunité apoplasmique basale et précocement induite, révélant la présence de métabolites potentiellement protecteurs non décrits jusqu’à présent, ainsi qu’une protéine impliquée dans le transport nucleo‐cytoplasmique de type RAN‐GTPase, offrant ainsi une nouvelle vision de la réponse immunitaire apoplasmique précoce.

articles.title: Avirulence genes of Magnaporthe oryzae are a pathogen defense arsenal shaped by cognate rice resistance genes in the field
articles.abstract: Population structure and AVR gene presence/absence of 383 single‐spore isolates from the US Mo population. Summary We examined the frequency of and variation in eight avirulence (AVR) genes from 840 Magnaporthe oryzae field isolates collected from the Southern United States relative to rice resistance (R) genes deployed from 1959 to 2017. Little coding or noncoding variation was detected in AVR‐Pi9, AVR‐Pib, ACE1 and AVR‐Pizt, which correspond to R genes not used in the United States. In the United States, AVR‐Pik, corresponding to rice R gene Pi‐k alleles deployed at varying levels since the late 1960s, was present in 37% of the isolates over six decades. AVR‐Pita1, corresponding to Pi‐ta deployed in the late 1990s, reached a low point in the 5‐yr period following Pi‐ta deployment and then recovered to 99% in recent years. Our results suggest a fitness penalty for M. oryzae isolates carrying nonfunctional AVR variants and provide concrete data on how changes in plant R gene composition can impact pathogen populations. These findings will inform localized strategies for R gene usage and durable control of blast disease. AVR frequencies differ over time between United States and global samples for AVR‐Pik, AVR‐Pi9, AVR‐Pii and AVR‐Pita1. Further whole genome analysis including additional US samples is necessary to confirm whether the United States is a geographically isolated population.

articles.title: Belowground growth is the primary driver of radial oxygen loss from Typha angustifolia to sediment
articles.abstract: Oxygen pool accompanying the growth of a new Typha angustifolia rhizome through anoxic sediment. Summary Wetland plants must supply oxygen to their rhizomes and roots to maintain aerobic respiration despite soil anoxia. Excess oxygen can diffuse into the environment, strongly affecting rhizosphere biogeochemistry. This radial oxygen loss (ROL) has often been observed to increase in the daytime, perhaps supported by photosynthetic oxygen production and stomatal opening. However, dynamics in rhizosphere oxygen pools do not derive exclusively from diel cycles. Using oxygen‐sensitive planar optodes (and simultaneous leaf gas exchange measurements), we compared the timing and magnitude of variation in rhizosphere oxygen pools due to diel cycles vs root and rhizome development in the widespread aquatic macrophyte Typha angustifolia. Diel cycles drove only slight variation in oxygen pool sizes (c. 5% oxygen saturation). Strongly oxygenated regions – regularly 25–30% oxygen saturation – appeared as roots and rhizomes grew, and then disappeared after several days of maturation. Expansive plumes of oxygen also developed upon the emergence of lateral roots and persisted for several weeks. These results indicate that root and rhizome development are dominant determinants of ROL in T. angustifolia. Seasonal and environmental controls over timing of belowground development likely have strong implications for rhizosphere biogeochemistry ranging from microbe‐controlled decomposition to redox‐sensitive transformation of metals in natural and managed systems.

articles.title: BpSRK1‐mediated phosphorylation of BpERF3 relieves HDA6‐dependent chromatin repression to enhance drought tolerance in birch
articles.abstract: The TF BpERF3 positively regulates drought tolerance and activates POD‐associated stress‐response genes in birch. Summary Drought tolerance in plants requires rapid conversion of water‐deficit signals into protective transcriptional and epigenetic programs. Although ERF transcription factors (TFs) are central regulators of stress‐responsive gene expression, how drought‐induced kinase signaling is coupled to chromatin regulation and antioxidant gene activation remains unclear. Here, we identify the ERF TF BpERF3 as a phosphorylation‐dependent regulator of drought tolerance in birch (Betula platyphylla). Using transgenic and CRISPR‐Cas9 mutant lines, protein interaction assays, immunoaffinity fluorescent electrophoresis (IAFE)‐based interactome mapping, post‐translational modification analysis, reactive oxygen species measurements, and drought phenotyping, we dissected the regulatory mechanism underlying BpERF3‐mediated stress adaptation. We show that BpERF3 activates the peroxidase (POD) genes BpPOD3 and BpPOD4, which are required for its drought‐protective function. Mechanistically, BpSRK1 phosphorylates BpERF3 at Ser355, enabling phosphorylated BpERF3 to competitively engage the HDAC domain of BpHDA6 and restrict BpHDA6‐dependent histone H3.1 deacetylation. Consequently, H3.1 acetylation is maintained, chromatin relaxes, downstream stress‐responsive genes are activated, and drought tolerance is enhanced in birch. Our findings reveal a BpSRK1‐BpERF3‐BpHDA6‐H3.1 regulatory module that links drought‐induced phosphorylation to local chromatin activation and redox homeostasis, providing mechanistic insight into plant stress adaptation.

articles.title: Climate drivers of mesophyll conductance: temperature and water deficit alter CO2 diffusion and leaf anatomy in cotton
articles.abstract: Temperature responses of photosynthesis, mesophyll conductance and stomatal conductance to water across Gossypium hirsutum cv Sicot 71, Gossypium arboreum, Gossypium bickii, Gossypium gossypioides and Gossypium sturtianum. Summary Mesophyll conductance (g m) limits CO2 delivery to Rubisco, yet its responses to temperature, heat and water deficit are poorly resolved in cotton (Gossypium hirsutum). We characterised photosynthetic and g m temperature responses in five Gossypium species, then examined cultivated G. hirsutum and the Australian native Gossypium bickii under combined elevated temperature and soil water deficit to link physiological responses with mesophyll anatomy. Plants were grown under controlled glasshouse conditions. We quantified g m using simultaneous gas exchange and online stable carbon isotope discrimination (Δ, ‰) and measured leaf anatomy. Across species, photosynthesis and g m exhibited broad thermal optima (33–36°C). In G. hirsutum, water deficit at control temperature reduced g m and induced thicker, more porous mesophyll and thicker cell walls, while assimilation declined only under combined heat and water deficit. In G. bickii, g m and assimilation remained stable under combined stress, and g m was stimulated by elevated temperature without anatomical adjustment. g m emerged as a stress-sensitive trait in cultivated cotton, whereas G. bickii exhibited stress resilience, with responses incompletely explained by anatomical acclimation. Further research on g m responses to environmental stresses and on the mechanisms underpinning these responses is required to inform model development and identify traits for climate resilient crops.

articles.title: Control of organ size by TAS3A
articles.abstract: Regulation of Arabidopsis organ sizes by the TAS3‐ARF2‐GRFs regulatory network. Summary Plant organ size depends on the coordination of cell proliferation and expansion, a process regulated by numerous factors, including transcription factors and small RNAs. However, how different small‐RNA pathways are integrated with growth‐regulating transcriptional networks remains only partly understood. Here, we studied how the Arabidopsis TRANS‐ACTING siRNA3A (TAS3A)‐derived trans‐acting small RNA pathway controls organ size in Arabidopsis thaliana. We found that TAS3A overexpression increased leaf and floral organ size, whereas tas3a mutants showed reduced organ growth. We show that TAS3A acts by modulating AUXIN‐RESPONSE‐FACTOR2 (ARF2) activity and that plants expressing a trans‐acting siRNA (tasiRNA)‐resistant ARF2 allele showed reduced organ growth. In turn, ARF2 repressed several GROWTH‐REGULATING FACTOR (GRF) genes, including GRF3, which is a direct ARF2 target and is also controlled by microRNA miR396. Furthermore, uncoupling GRF activity from ARF2 repression was sufficient to increase floral organ size. Interestingly, whereas the TAS3A‐ARF2‐GRF module regulates leaf and petal growth predominantly through changes in cell proliferation, gynoecium growth involves a more complex balance between cell proliferation and elongation. Together, our results identify ARF2 as a central molecular node connecting tasiRNA‐ and miRNA‐dependent pathways and establish TAS3A as a key regulator of Arabidopsis aerial organ growth.

articles.title: Correction to ‘Mediator subunit MED8 interacts with heat shock transcription factor HSF3 to promote fucoxanthin synthesis in the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum’
Differential ubiquitin modifications of ESCRT‐I subunits VPS37‐1 and VPS28‐2 positively regulate plant immunity
articles.abstract: The RING type ubiquitin ligase (E3), XBAT35.2, positively regulates FLS2‐mediated plant immunity against bacterial pathogens by modifying the ESCRT‐I subunits VPS28‐2 and VPS37‐1 with distinct ubiquitin chain types. Summary Sensing of pathogen‐associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by pattern recognition receptors at the cell surface initiates the first layer of host immunity against invading microbial pathogens. In plants, the immune receptor Flagellin Sensing 2 (FLS2) perceives bacterial flagellin to trigger downstream signaling that culminates in PAMP‐triggered immunity (PTI). FLS2 protein levels are critical for effective PTI, yet the regulatory mechanisms governing its stability remain to be fully elucidated. Our previous work showed that the Arabidopsis Really Interesting Gene (RING) type ubiquitin ligase XBAT35.2 positively regulates plant immunity against bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas syringae pv tomato by promoting FLS2 stability. In this study, we demonstrate that XBAT35.2 interacts in vivo with two key ESCRT‐I complex components, VPS37‐1 and VPS28‐2. XBAT35.2 ubiquitinates VPS37‐1 with K48‐linked polyubiquitin chains, leading to its proteasomal degradation, and modifies VPS28‐2 with K63‐linked chains, reducing its interaction with FLS2. VPS37‐1 and VPS28‐2 play redundant, negative roles in FLS2‐mediated immunity by promoting vacuolar degradation of FLS2, displaying differential effects on distinct FLS2‐mediated immune responses. By targeting VPS37‐1 and VPS28‐2, XBAT35.2 intercepts this degradative pathway, thereby stabilizing FLS2 and enhancing host immunity. These findings uncover a novel regulatory circuit modulating FLS2 abundance and deepen our understanding of controlling the cell‐surface receptor homeostasis in plant immunity.

articles.title: Disrupting two Arabidopsis thaliana xylosyltransferase genes results in plants deficient in thermomorphogenesis
articles.abstract: Here, we reveal a PHYTOCHROME‐INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4)/ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 5 (HY5)–xyloglucan xylosyltransferase 1 (XXT1)/XXT2 regulatory module that mediates xyloglucan biosynthesis in response to warm ambient temperature in plants. Elevated temperatures promote the conversion of phyB to its inactive form, releasing PIF4‐mediated transcriptional activation of XXT1 and XXT2, which encode key enzymes for xyloglucan biosynthesis. HY5 antagonizes this process by competing with PIF4 for promoter binding, thereby suppressing XXT1/XXT2 expression. Our findings establish a mechanistic link between thermomorphogenesis and cell wall metabolism, highlighting the pivotal role of cell wall biosynthesis in plant adaptation to elevated ambient temperature. Summary Several cell‐wall‐modifying enzymes have been implicated in hypocotyl elongation; however, whether cell wall biosynthesis enzymes contribute to this process, particularly under warm temperature, remains largely unknown. In Arabidopsis, xyloglucan is a major component of the primary cell wall. Xyloglucan xylosyltransferase 1 (XXT1) and XXT2 are the major enzymes required for xyloglucan biosynthesis. Here, we investigated the roles of XXT1/2 in hypocotyl elongation with a focus under warm temperature using genetic, molecular, and transcriptomic approaches. We show that XXT1/2 are required for warm‐temperature‐promoted hypocotyl elongation and that the elongation phenotypes of PHYTOCHROME‐INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4) overexpression, Phytochrome B (phyB), and ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 5 (hy5) depend partly on XXT1/2. PIF4 directly binds to and activates the promoters of XXT1 and XXT2, whereas HY5 binds to the same promoter regions and represses their expression. Importantly, the warm‐temperature‐induced increase in xyloglucan content is antagonistically regulated by PIF4 and HY5. Transcriptomic analyses identified warm‐responsive genes whose induction depends on XXT1/2, including expansins (EXPs) and xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydrolases (XTHs). Mutants of some EXPs and XTHs showed compromised warm‐induced hypocotyl elongation. Together, our findings identify XXT1/2 as new components of the phyB–PIF4–HY5 growth network, linking environmental signaling to the cell wall biosynthetic machinery required for hypocotyl elongation.

articles.title: Distinct targeting of 5mC and 6mA DNA methylation during the onset of Flg22‐induced immunity between Arabidopsis and rice
articles.abstract: Using Oxford Nanopore sequencing, genome‐wide DNA methylation responses to Flg22 were compared between Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa. In both species, immune activation was marked by increased relative 5mC accumulation at (peri)centromeric regions compared with chromosome arms. In parallel, defence‐responsive genes displayed an enhanced bimodal 6mA distribution flanking transcription start and termination sites following Flg22 elicitation. These findings identify shared methylation features associated with immune activation across two evolutionarily distinct plant species and associate 6mA remodelling with activation of the immune‐responsive transcriptome. Summary Cytosine methylation drives transcriptional reprogramming during plant innate and acquired immunity. Beyond RNA adenosine methylation, DNA adenine methylation (6mA) has recently emerged as a candidate regulator of gene expression, though its role in plant immunity is unknown. Using the bacterial elicitor Flg22, we examined genome‐wide DNA methylation responses of Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa to identify shared epigenetic responses across divergent genomes. High‐resolution Oxford Nanopore sequencing enabled simultaneous detection of 5‐methylcytosine (5mC) and 6mA DNA modifications. In both species, early immune activation was marked by non‐CG 5mC hypomethylation at short euchromatic transposable elements. By 72 hpt, both species showed elevated 5mC levels at (peri)centromeric regions, targeted to pericentromeric non‐CG sites in Arabidopsis and accompanied by lasting chromosomal arm hypomethylation in rice. Despite species‐specific global 6mA responses, both species exhibited a conserved bimodal 6mA distribution flanking transcription start and termination sites of genes, intensified at defence‐related genes following Flg22 elicitation. In Arabidopsis, these 6mA signatures correlated with Flg22‐primed gene activation, while mutation of 6mA demethylase ALKBH1D increased susceptibility to Pseudomonas syringae and Meloidogyne incognita. Together, our findings reveal conserved 5mC dynamics during immune activation and highlight a role for 6mA in modulating defence‐related transcriptional reprogramming.

articles.title: Dual mechanisms give rise to biphasic stomatal opening in onion
articles.abstract: Anisotropic guard cell wall stiffness enhances onion stomatal pore opening by increasing guard cell arc length. Summary Stomata are controllable micropores on the leaf surface that regulate gas exchange and water loss. Pore aperture adjustment is a mechanical process whereby changes in guard cell turgor drive changes in cell shape, resulting in stomatal opening or closure. Previous computational models of kidney‐shaped stomata primarily relied on guard cells elongating upon turgor increase, a process dependent on cell wall properties, such as anisotropy in stiffness, strain‐stiffening, and polar fixing. Finite element method simulations using experimentally derived 3D meshes from confocal imaging of Allium cepa (onion) suggest an alternative mechanism for opening that is largely due to changes in guard cell cross‐sectional shape. This mechanism does not rely on the assumptions for cell wall parameters required in previous models based on idealised geometries. We propose that mechanical responsiveness of guard cells to turgor changes is determined by a combination of two processes: one dependent on shape and the other on wall material properties. This suggests the parameters governing guard cell dynamics can be viewed abstractly as a two‐dimensional (shape and material properties) ‘morphospace’, allowing multiple routes of shape adaptation to optimise gas exchange.

articles.title: Dynamic microbiome turnover and glycerol‐3‐phosphate‐linked metabolic adjustments underlie resilience to desiccation in intertidal algae
articles.abstract: A holobiont‐level desiccation strategy in intertidal red algae. Rapid dehydration restructures the microbiome, enriching stress‐tolerant taxa, like Sulfitobacter and Alteromonas, while host‐secreted G3P sustains key epiphytic bacteria that enhance antioxidant and osmoprotective functions. This cross‐domain metabolic coupling highlights a co‐evolved strategy for intertidal resilience. See also the Commentary on this article by Flores‐Uribe, 252: 1700–1701. Summary Tolerance to extreme dehydration has emerged across the tree of life, yet current understanding relies heavily on terrestrial host traits. Marine lineages facing rapid, tide‐driven hydration oscillations remain largely unexplored. We used Pyropia haitanensis as a model to determine if intertidal resilience arises from a coordinated holobiont strategy. We integrated time‐resolved microbiome profiling and metagenomics. Mechanisms were validated through multi‐omics of desiccation‐stressed bacterial isolates, inoculation, and antibiotic‐depletion experiments, and host physiological assessment. Rapid drying reshaped the microbiome through selective loss of osmosensitive taxa and occupation by stress‐tolerant lineages, whereas rehydration promoted selective recolonization and network recovery. Metagenomic analysis revealed enrichment of functional potential for microbial antioxidant, osmoprotective, and extracellular polysaccharide pathways, alongside enrichment of glycerol‐3‐phosphate (G3P) ABC transporter modules. Host G3P secretion increased, creating a selective nutrient niche that recruited symbionts possessing specialized G3P transporters. Inoculation and microbiota‐depletion experiments established a causal role for the microbiome in host resilience. Keystone isolates Sulfitobacter sp. and Alteromonas sp. utilized host‐derived G3P to fuel complementary protective mechanisms, with their combination outperforming either taxon alone. These findings highlight an integrated host–microbiome partnership shaped by tidal filtering, a cross‐domain strategy that buffers hydration stress and supports intertidal resilience and mariculture practices.

articles.title: Ecological determinants of stability in dryland plant communities
articles.abstract: Conceptual framework for partitioning the drivers of community stability. Summary Community stability is often presented as crucial for sustaining ecosystem services under environmental change. Yet, its determinants (dominance, asynchrony in species fluctuations, averaging effect of species diversity) have rarely been disentangled in natural systems, and their contributions across climates remain unclear. We disentangled the determinants of stability in 40 winter annual communities comprising 178 populations across four climates (arid, semi‐arid, Mediterranean, mesic‐Mediterranean) and two microhabitats (open areas and under perennial shrubs) over 13 yr in a dryland biodiversity hotspot. Asynchrony in species fluctuations and the averaging effect of species diversity emerged as the strongest stabilizing mechanisms. Asynchrony consistently stabilized communities across climates, independent of species richness, challenging the ‘Insurance Hypothesis’. The averaging effect was weaker in desert and mesic‐Mediterranean climates, suggesting biodiversity may not always determine stability. These findings stress the need to separate compensatory dynamics into asynchrony in species fluctuations and the averaging effect of species diversity to better predict community stability over time under increasing climatic variability.

articles.title: Engineering a TurboID‐based proximity labeling tool to track the dynamic secretomes under salt stress
articles.abstract: We developed a new method to specifically track proteins moving through the main secretion pathway. Using this tool, we discovered proteins involved in salt stress responses, including AED3 that helps plants better tolerate high salt conditions. Summary Secretory proteins are essential for plant development and environmental adaptation, yet selectively profiling cargoes transported through the conventional endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–Golgi pathway remains technically challenging because apoplastic secretomes contain proteins from multiple secretion routes. We developed an ER‐anchored TurboID proximity labeling method to selectively enrich proteins entering the conventional secretory pathway in Arabidopsis thaliana. Quantitative proteomics under control and salt stress conditions identified dynamic secretome changes and showed that most enriched proteins carry N‐terminal signal peptides, supporting the utility of this approach for profiling conventional secretory proteins. Using this method, we found that sodium chloride (NaCl) stress remodels the conventional secretome by enhancing the secretion of a subset of cell wall‐associated proteins. We further identified Apoplastic EDS1‐Dependent 3 (AED3) as a salt‐induced secretory protein, confirmed its ER–Golgi‐dependent secretion, and demonstrated its role in salt tolerance. Overall, this study provides a useful approach for pathway‐specific profiling of the conventional plant secretome, enabling the discovery of dynamic secretory proteins involved in plant environmental responses.

articles.title: Extending the limits of algal growth and stress resilience – the desert alga Chlorella ohadii as an emerging model
articles.abstract: Multiple facets of Chlorella ohadii biological properties and potential as a research model and biotechnology platform. Summary Since its isolation from the sand dunes of the Negev Desert over a decade ago, the unicellular green alga Chlorella ohadii has turned into a reference organism for studying photosynthesis, metabolism, and abiotic stress response. Much of C. ohadii's appeal as an emerging model lies in its robust fast growth, comparable to yeast even as a photoautotroph. Hence, the detailed physiological, biochemical, and molecular studies that followed rapidly, together with extensive omics datasets, have revealed several of its intriguing biological features. We provide a historical perspective unfolding the rise of this species from survival in the harsh desert crusts to a widely used standard for photodamage resistance, dynamic metabolism, and elevated growth and photosynthetic performance, frequently with prominent relevance for plant research. We also spotlight how this case study enables exploration of photosynthesis in harsh habitats. Further, we discuss challenges in the development of genetic tools for the growing community studying C. ohadii, and current biotechnological approaches aiming to exploit its prime genetic potential. Finally, we refer to guidelines of good practice for C. ohadii research as a highly stress‐resistant model.

articles.title: Genetic and molecular networks mediating potato tuber development
articles.abstract: Tuberigen and antituberigen control of potato tuberization. Summary Potato, the world's third most important food crop, is cultivated world‐wide for its tubers that store high‐energy photoassimilates, which are predominantly induced under short photoperiods with cooler night temperatures. The stored photoassimilates ensure plant survival by vegetative propagation and to support subsequent shoot growth. The leaf‐generated main tuberigen signal, StSP6A, upon its transport to stolon, forms tuber‐inducing Tuberigen Activation Complex (TAC). Misregulation or redirection of StSP6A transport toward lateral buds contributes to aerial tuber formation, thereby adversely affecting underground tuber yield. The activity of TAC is inhibited by antituberigens, such as StAST1 and StTFL1, which compete with StSP6A and constitute anti‐TAC. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying underground and aerial tuber formation, their regulation by antituberigen factors, key genes controlling stolon‐to‐tuber transitions, the role of StSWEET‐StSUT transporters in establishing the source–sink relationship essential for tuber development, and the evolution and global dissemination of modern potato cultivars. Collectively, insights from potato provide a valuable framework for understanding the conserved and divergent mechanisms governing storage organ development in other economically important crops. सारांश आलू, जो विश्व की तीसरी सबसे महत्वपूर्ण खाद्य फसल है, अपने कंदों के लिए पूरे विश्व में उगाया जाता है। इसके कंद उच्च‐ऊर्जा वाले प्रकाश‐संश्लेषणीय उत्पादों का भंडारण करते हैं, जिनका निर्माण मुख्यतः छोटे प्रकाश‐अवधि तथा अपेक्षाकृत कम रात्रिकालीन तापमान की परिस्थितियों में प्रेरित होता है। संचित प्रकाश‐संश्लेषणीय उत्पाद वनस्पतिक प्रवर्धन के माध्यम से पौधे के अस्तित्व को बनाए रखने तथा बाद में होने वाली प्ररोह वृद्धि को समर्थन देने में महत्वपूर्ण भूमिका निभाते हैं। पत्तियों में निर्मित प्रमुख कंदजनक संकेत, StSP6A, जब कंद बनाने वाली भूमिगत डंठल तक पहुँचता है, तो कंद निर्माण को प्रेरित करने वाले कंदजनक सक्रियण सम्मिश्र (Tuberigen Activation Complex, TAC) का निर्माण करता है। StSP6A के परिवहन में होने वाला अनियमित नियमन या उसके परिवहन का कक्षस्थ कलिकाओं की ओर पुनर्निर्देशन वायवीय कंद के निर्माण में योगदान देता है, जिससे भूमिगत कंदों की उपज पर प्रतिकूल प्रभाव पड़ता है। TAC की सक्रियता को StAST1 और StTFL1 जैसे कंदजनक विरोधी कारक अवरुद्ध करते हैं। ये कारक StSP6A के साथ प्रतिस्पर्धा करके प्रति‐कंदजनक सक्रियण सम्मिश्र (anti‐Tuberigen Activation Complex, anti‐TAC) का निर्माण करते हैं। इस समीक्षा में हम भूमिगत तथा वायवीय कंद निर्माण के अंतर्निहित आनुवंशिक और आणविक तंत्रों, प्रति‐कंदजनक कारकों द्वारा इनके नियमन, भूमिगत डंठल को कंद में परिवर्तन को नियंत्रित करने वाले प्रमुख जीनों, कंद विकास के लिए आवश्यक स्रोत‐उपभोक्ता संबंध स्थापित करने में StSWEET‐StSUT परिवाहकों की भूमिका तथा आधुनिक आलू किस्मों के विकास और वैश्विक प्रसार का व्यापक अवलोकन प्रस्तुत करते हैं। सामूहिक रूप से, आलू से प्राप्त ये अंतर्दृष्टियाँ अन्य आर्थिक रूप से महत्वपूर्ण फसलों में भंडारण अंगों के विकास को नियंत्रित करने वाले संरक्षित तथा विशिष्ट तंत्रों को समझने के लिए एक महत्वपूर्ण रूपरेखा प्रदान करती हैं।.

articles.title: Harnessing genetic variation for grain quality from diverse wheat landraces
articles.abstract: Grain protein content is usually measured on bulk samples, hiding variation between individual grains. We used hyperspectral imaging to predict protein in c. 15 000 single grains from over 500 Watkins wheat landraces grown in two environments, resolving both mean protein content and grain-to-grain uniformity. Genome-wide association mapping identified six protein loci, two grain weight loci and SGPH-A1 on chromosome 6A controlling uniformity. Haplotypes at 6D raised protein without reducing grain weight, and haplotypes at 1A and 6A raised grain weight without diluting protein, offering routes to break the protein–yield trade-off. Summary The grain quality traits of protein content, grain weight and size are socially and economically important for wheat (Triticum aestivum) breeding. Modern wheat germplasm has limited genetic variation for vital traits, including grain quality, underscoring the need to investigate ancestral varieties/landraces for beneficial allelic diversity. Here, we develop a reliable and sensitive single-seed hyperspectral imaging-based phenotyping platform to quantify grain protein, weight and size in 827 diverse wheat landraces, achieving improved predictive accuracy (R 2 = 0.91) vs previous methods. We identified novel genetic variants (or loci) for grain protein content and its heterogeneity between individual grains in a genotype, and grain weight, and validated them through bi-parental linkage mapping. Many loci we report are rare and absent from modern breeding germplasm. Beneficial haplotypes at these loci improved mean protein content and homogeneity without compromising grain weight; these haplotypes represent valuable genetic variation for agriculture. We identify a stable locus on chromosome 6A contributing to protein heterogeneity within single grains, suggesting homogeneity in protein content could be a selectable trait for breeding. Our findings demonstrate how integration of advanced phenotyping into breeding strategies can harness untapped genetic diversity for grain quality improvement in wheat, providing an opportunity to enhance grain nutritional value.

articles.title: How to build a shoot: insights from Physcomitrium patens
articles.abstract: Cladogram of the streptophytes illustrating the diversity of apical growth mechanisms in this group. Summary The evolution of body plans with multiple cell layers provided structural rigidity and enabled tissue specialisation, which were both essential for the colonisation of land by plants. Building such structure requires apical cell divisions that generate merophytes along all three axes (3D growth), as well as the spatial control of cell fate. The shoot (gametophore) of the moss Physcomitrium patens is an ideal model for studying these processes. Recent studies have identified a genetic network integrating hormone signalling, cell wall biosynthesis and cell shape to regulate division orientation in the gametophore. Additionally, reporter‐based markers have revealed localised hormone activity that maintains the gametophore apical cell. This review summarises these findings to provide an updated perspective on 3D growth in Physcomitrium patens.

articles.title: Intraspecific variation in an arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus affects a plant and an AMF community
articles.abstract: Mesocosm placement within the growing facility. Summary Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) show substantial genetic, trait, and functional variation within species. Whether this intraspecific variability has community‐level consequences for plant and AMF communities is unclear. This study investigated whether introduced conspecific AMF affected a resident AMF and plant community. Mesocosms containing natural soils and a mixed plant community were inoculated with three conspecific isolates of Rhizophagus irregularis and grown for 17 wk. We measured AMF isolate abundance, plant performance (aboveground biomass, foliar phosphorus, seed production), and plant and AMF community response (diversity and composition). AMF isolate identity affected AMF isolate abundance though effects varied with host identity. Isolate identity affected aboveground biomass of two host species. A small shift in plant community composition, but not diversity, occurred between two isolate treatments. The most abundant isolate affected turnover of rare AMF taxa in the soil community but did not alter the dominant AMF community. Whether small community shifts would compound or stabilize over time remains to be seen. Given the growing use of AMF‐based agricultural and forestry products, often represented by a single genetic isolate, there is a pressing need to understand how intraspecific AMF variation fits within ecological frameworks.

articles.title: Jasmonate control of barley grain size across generations
Mimicry of mantis and Selaginella from Cretaceous provides new evidence for the deep‐time co‐evolution of insects and plants
articles.abstract: Reconstruction of leaf mimicry in fossil insects and plants and their familial diversity from the Paleozoic to the Cenozoic. Summary Mimicry between insects and plants represents sophisticated survival strategies. Their long‐term evolutionary interactions led to mutual adaptation, creating a complex ecological symbiosis. However, the deep‐time ecological associations of mimicry between insects and plants remain limited due to the scarcity of preserved fossils. Here, we report the fossil evidences of mimicry between praying mantis and spike mosses in 98‐Myr‐old Kachin amber. The new Cretaceous mantis, Folimantis hyalinala gen. et sp. nov., has a rare form of leaf mimicry via abdominal leaf‐shaped extensions that resemble contemporaneous vegetative leaves (trophophylls) of Selaginella in shape, size, and pattern of arrangement. The new findings provide the earliest direct evidence of the co‐associations between mantis and its mimetic plants during the Cretaceous and suggest that the stem‐group had already developed distinct structural features that mimic plant leaves during the early divergences of Mantodea. A diversification analysis of mimicry between fossil insects and plants from the Late Paleozoic and Mesozoic indicates that, before the rise of angiosperms in the Late Cretaceous, mimicry between insects and gymnosperms, ferns, lichens, and even Selaginella had existed for a long time and that changes in mimicry forms paralleled the evolutionary succession of plant lineages.

articles.title: Navigating through complexity: a roadmap to disentangle multi‐level drivers of intraspecific seed‐trait variability and prioritise research efforts
articles.abstract: Examples of hierarchical drivers of intraspecific variation in seed traits. Summary Seed traits underpin plant regeneration and are central to predicting species' responses to environmental change, yet their intraspecific variability remains poorly integrated into trait‐based frameworks. Progress has been limited by the conflation of processes operating across nested levels, from regions and populations to mother plants and individual seeds, and by weak integration of genetic drivers with environmental and phenotypic data. Drawing on published literature and analyses of seed traits in wild tree populations, we show that substantial seed‐trait variation can occur among mother plants and individual seeds within populations, meaning that population‐level macroenvironmental variables often capture only part of the observed variation. To address these limitations, we propose a roadmap to disentangle hierarchical drivers of intraspecific trait variability (ITV) in seeds. We outline a strategic plan to quantify seed‐trait variation across hierarchical levels, investigate its drivers where variation is concentrated, and assess its consequences for recruitment and demographic outcomes. We recommend coordinated, standardised sampling and experiments that retain mother‐plant and individual‐seed identity, integrate genetic, environmental and phenotypic data, and use scalable approaches to link seed traits to performance across recruitment stages. Recognising and integrating ITV across nested levels is essential for improving predictions of plant regeneration under environmental change.

articles.title: Petal infrared transmission warms flowers and reduces microbial abundance
articles.abstract: Lyonia lucida and Lyonia fruticosa have translucent, unpigmented regions at the proximal end of the corolla (‘windows’). Summary Flowers create distinct internal microclimates, yet how these conditions filter microbial abundance remains poorly understood. We tested whether petal light transmission and internal floral temperature influence microbial abundance in two co‐occurring species, Lyonia lucida and Lyonia fruticosa (Ericaceae), which have translucent petal ‘windows’ that modify internal light environments. We measured internal and external floral temperatures, quantified culturable microbial abundance (yeasts, molds, bacteria), and assessed ultraviolet (UV) and infrared (IR) petal transmission using spectrometry. We then experimentally tested the UV resistance of microbial communities across 108 flowers from 18 plants. Additionally, we used manipulative light experiments to test whether IR radiation drove differences in floral warming between these two species. Petal windows transmitted more UV and IR radiation than pigmented tissue. Internal floral temperature predicted microbial abundance, with warmer flowers harboring fewer microbes. A spectral filter experiment confirmed that IR radiation warms L. lucida flowers but not L. fruticosa, while natural variation in UV transmission did not predict microbial abundance or UV resistance. Petal spectral traits shape floral microclimate and microbial abundance primarily through temperature‐mediated filtering linked to IR‐driven warming rather than passive UV sterilization. These results position flowers as microhabitats where petal traits constrain microbial communities.

articles.title: Phytochemical divergence between above‐ and belowground tree organs along elevational gradients
articles.abstract: Hypothesized patterns of phytochemical differentiation between aboveground (leaves) and belowground (roots) organs along elevational gradients. Summary Plants produce diverse metabolites to defend against biotic and abiotic stresses. However, quantification of plant chemical defenses along environmental gradients has largely focused on aboveground organs, leaving belowground patterns poorly understood. To address how leaf and root defense chemistry shifts with changing biotic and abiotic conditions, we compared untargeted metabolomics of 183 species across elevational gradients spanning tropical, subtropical, and subalpine forests. Leaves and roots showed distinct chemical compositions across elevations, with phytochemical diversity declining from tropical to subalpine forests, corresponding with shifts in herbivore pressure and soil conditions. These patterns suggest that local variation in biotic and abiotic pressures across elevations may be associated with gradients in phytochemical diversity. We also uncovered contrasting patterns of chemical strategies between organs. Leaf chemistry shifts from polar, fast‐turnover, low‐cost metabolites in tropical forests to less polar, aromatic, and energetically costly metabolites in subtropical and subalpine forests, whereas roots display contrasting metabolic adjustments. Our results suggest that elevation filters species by their distinct metabolomic profiles, with organ‐specific and context‐dependent chemical investment, highlighting the importance of integrating above‐ and belowground organs to understand plant chemical responses across gradients. We reveal that organs of the same tree tell distinct chemical stories, illuminating the chemical life of trees. 概括 植物产生多种代谢产物以抵御生物胁迫和非生物胁迫。然而，沿环境梯度对植物化学防御的定量研究主要集中在地上器官，而地下器官的变化规律至今尚不清楚。 为探究叶片和根系化学防御如何随生物与非生物条件的变化而改变，我们比较了跨越热带、亚热带和亚高山森林的海拔梯度上183个物种的非靶向代谢组学数据。 叶片和根系在不同海拔上表现出明显的化学组成差异，植物化学多样性从热带森林到亚高山森林呈下降趋势，这与植食性压力及土壤条件的变化相对应。这些模式表明，海拔梯度上生物与非生物压力的局部变化可能与化学多样性的梯度变化相关。我们还发现，不同器官之间的化学策略呈现出相反的模式。叶片化学组成从热带森林中以极性、快速周转、低成本的代谢产物为主，转向亚热带和亚高山森林中以极性较低、芳香性且能量成本较高的代谢产物为主；而根系则表现出相反的代谢调整趋势。 我们的结果表明，海拔通过器官特异性和环境依赖性的化学投入来筛选具有不同代谢组学特征的物种，这强调了整合地上与地下器官对于理解植物沿环境梯度的化学响应的重要性。我们发现，同一棵树的不同器官讲述着截然不同的化学故事，揭示了树木的化学生命图景。

articles.title: Rethinking the soil core microbiome
articles.abstract: Soil microbiome studies often define ‘core microbiomes’ using different operational criteria, including occurrence thresholds, abundance thresholds, or other selection methods. Using 1813 soil samples collected across four U.S. Department of Energy Bioenergy Research Centers, we show that these different operational choices identify different subsets of taxa, highlighting that operationally defined subsets should not automatically be interpreted as conserved core microbiomes. Instead, such subsets are better viewed as explanatory subsets of taxa selected for specific analytical purposes, providing a clearer conceptual framework for interpreting soil microbiome datasets. Summary The concept of a core microbiome emerged from host‐associated research to describe microbial members or functions conserved across clearly defined spatial, temporal, and biological boundaries. In soil‐ and plant‐associated microbiome research, however, the term has increasingly shifted toward analytically defined subsets selected using study‐specific thresholds or criteria. Synthesizing recent literature and cross‐site analyses of bioenergy crop field soils, we show that the original biological meaning of the core microbiome has been blurred by dataset‐specific analytical criteria. Taxa designated as ‘core’ were highly sensitive to methodological choices and often reflected explanatory value rather than conserved biological membership. Moreover, many studies that identify taxonomic ‘core’ members interpret their significance in functional terms, suggesting that functional conservation may be the biological interest. Taxonomic conservation may not be the most biologically meaningful target in highly heterogeneous soil and rhizosphere systems, where functional conservation may persist despite taxonomic turnover. Accordingly, ‘core microbiome’ should be reserved for microbial components explicitly demonstrated to be conserved across defined spatial, temporal, and environmental dimensions and linked to conserved ecological functions, while taxa selected for explanatory value are better described as ‘explanatory subsets of taxa’. Greater terminological precision will improve cross‐study comparability and strengthen ecological inference in plant–soil microbiome research.

articles.title: Roots to simplicity: when evolution removes a key organ
articles.abstract: Overlapping niches and life habits of rootless vascular plants. Summary The evolution of roots was an instrumental event in the colonisation of land by vascular plants. Roots have undergone extensive radiation and can take many diverse forms including taproots, fibrous roots, and adventitious roots. This includes specialist root types, such as pneumatophores in mangroves, that have allowed species to occupy new ecological niches. In some cases, the relationship between roots and soil has been broken, rendering roots unnecessary and ultimately resulting in loss of this organ in some species. We identify several ecological niches/life habits in which rootless vascular plants have evolved: aquatic environments, canopies, arid environments, and carnivory. Many of these plants are challenging to cultivate in a laboratory environment. The exception to this is duckweeds, which we propose as a powerful experimental model for studying organ loss in plants.

articles.title: STRONG3 promotes lignin biosynthesis and culm strength in rice
articles.abstract: Combined haplotype analysis of STRONG3 and 4CL4. Summary Lodging severely reduces rice yield and quality. Culm strength, mainly determined by lignin biosynthesis and secondary cell wall (SCW) formation, is core to lodging resistance. We identified an ethylene response factor (ERF) transcription factor STRONG3 via genome-wide association study (GWAS) of 405 rice accessions based on lignin content. Functional validation demonstrated that STRONG3 positively regulates lignin accumulation, culm diameter, and mechanical strength by promoting sclerenchyma tissue development, vascular bundle enlargement, and SCW thickening. Molecular analyses revealed that STRONG3 directly binds to the GCC-box motif in the promoter of 4CL4, a rate-limiting enzyme in the phenylpropanoid pathway, to activate its transcription. Genetic complementation confirmed that 4CL4 acts downstream of STRONG3 to mediate lignin biosynthesis and culm development. Haplotype analysis identified subspecies-specific favorable alleles: STRONG3 G in Geng rice, caused by a single nucleotide polymorphism (4349512) leading to an Ala289Thr substitution in the activation domain that enhances STRONG3's transcriptional activation of 4CL4, and 4CL4 TC in Xian rice. Combinatorial analysis showed these alleles synergistically improve culm traits in their respective subspecies. Overexpression of STRONG3 enhanced lodging resistance without compromising grain yield. Our findings uncover a critical regulatory pathway for rice culm development and provide valuable genetic resources and molecular markers for breeding high-yield, lodging-resistant rice varieties.

articles.title: SUMOylation of chloroplast GrpE homolog 1 regulates chloroplast biogenesis through maintaining TIC complex stability
articles.abstract: A proposed model illustrating how CGE1 SUMOylation regulates chloroplast protein import and TIC‐associated machinery homeostasis. Summary In Arabidopsis, chloroplast protein import relies on the stromal cpHsp70 motor system, whose nucleotide‐exchange factor CGE1 is indispensable, yet its regulatory mechanism remains poorly defined. We integrated bioinformatics prediction with in vitro and in vivo SUMOylation assays, biochemical analyses, confocal microscopy, and genetic complementation to elucidate the functional impact of CGE1 SUMOylation in chloroplast development. CGE1 undergoes SUMO3 conjugation, and Lys‐214 is required for efficient CGE1 SUMOylation. The SUMOylation‐defective variant CGE1K214R retained stromal localization but caused marked chlorosis of emerging leaves, reduced photosynthetic efficiency, and impaired chloroplast development. Moreover, import of cytosol‐synthesized preproteins is compromised in CGE1K214R‐complemented plants, accompanied by decreased abundance of TIC40 and TIC110. Loss of SUMOylation simultaneously strengthens the CGE1‐cpHsp70‐1 and CGE1‐TIC40 interactions, and overexpression of either cpHsp70‐1 or TIC40 in CGE1K214R‐complemented plants restores TIC40 and/or TIC110 levels and the photosynthetic phenotype. In conclusion, these findings reveal that SUMOylation of CGE1 plays an important role in regulating TIC complex abundance and precursor import efficiency through cpHsp70‐ and TIC40‐related routes. This study uncovers a SUMOylation‐mediated regulatory layer that fine‐tunes chloroplast biogenesis.

articles.title: Subversion of plant endomembrane trafficking by a Plasmodiophora brassicae effector PbALE that recruits membrane components at the host–pathogen interface to aid in colonization
articles.abstract: Schematics of ΔSPPbALE‐induced disruption of plant endomembrane trafficking impairs both preinvasive and postinvasive immunity against filamentous fungi and facilitates intracellular colonization by Plasmodiophora brassicae. Summary Plasmodiophora brassicae, an intracellular biotrophic protist that causes clubroot in crucifers, extensively alters the host endomembrane system for colonization. However, the molecular mechanisms and functions of effectors to achieve this remain poorly understood. Using fluorescent and transmission electron microscopy of P. brassicae‐infected Arabidopsis, we show that host endomembranes and organelles become closely associated with P. brassicae secondary plasmodial structures and are subsequently phagocytosed by the pathogen. PbALE is a secreted endomembrane‐targeting effector that binds a range of phospholipids. Overexpression of the effector results in plants with glossy leaves that progressively become chlorotic. Fluorescent protein‐tagged PbALE is observed in large condensates that cluster with plant organelles, disrupting endocytic recycling of plant membrane receptors and immune regulatory proteins, thereby impairing penetration resistance to nonadapted barley powdery mildew infection. PbALE's association with the P. brassicae plasmodial surface and the extrahaustorial membrane during adaptive powdery mildew infection, along with the recruitment of PI(4,5)P2 to these membrane contacts, supports a model in which the effector nucleates lipid‐rich compartments and enriches organelles at the host‐pathogen interface. Our findings reveal a lipid‐binding effector that remodels host endomembranes, disrupts immune trafficking, and aids pathogen colonization, offering insights into strategies for durable disease resistance.

articles.title: Ten rules for robust taxonomy in ecological datasets
articles.abstract: A workflow for better use and integration of taxonomic‐related information into ecological datasets. Summary Accurate taxonomy, including species identification and naming, underpins ecological inference, yet taxonomic information in ecological datasets is often inconsistently recorded or weakly standardized. With the increasing integration of ecological datasets across taxa and regions, datasets with poor taxonomic practices can hinder data exchange and propagate errors. We propose 10 rules to improve the storage and management of taxonomic information in ecological datasets. These rules draw on our experiences in plant ecology and taxonomy, but the conclusions may be generalized to other organisms and disciplines. They emphasize aspects from species identification to the permanent storage of verifiable records (e.g. voucher specimens) and include taxonomic standardization, nomenclature, validation, and updating. We also address the treatment of morphotypes and incomplete identifications, the use of automated name‐matching tools, and (meta)data standards. Closer collaboration between ecologists and taxonomists is key to ensuring more robust datasets. The application of these rules consumes more time and resources, but they enhance data quality and interoperability, saving time during data integration and improving the reliability and scalability of ecological research. Resumo Uma taxonomia precisa, incluindo a identificação e nomenclatura das espécies, é fundamental para a inferência em ecologia. Entretanto, as informações taxonômicas em conjuntos de dados ecológicos frequentemente são pouco padronizadas. Com a integração contínua de dados ecológicos entre diferentes grupos taxonômicos e regiões, a adoção de práticas inadequadas pode dificultar o intercâmbio de dados e propagar erros. Neste trabalho, nós propomos dez regras para aprimorar o armazenamento e curadoria de informações taxonômicas em conjuntos de dados ecológicos. Essas regras foram baseadas em nossa expertise em ecologia e taxonomia vegetal, mas suas conclusões podem ser generalizadas para outros organismos e disciplinas. As regras enfatizam aspectos que vão desde a identificação de espécies até o armazenamento permanente de registros verificáveis (por exemplo, espécimes‐voucher) e incluem assuntos referentes a nomenclatura, padronização, validação e atualização taxonômica. Também abordamos o tratamento de morfotipos e identificações incompletas, o uso de ferramentas automatizadas de correspondência de nomes e padrões de (meta)dados. Uma colaboração mais estreita entre ecólogos e taxonomistas é essencial para garantir conjuntos de dados mais robustos. A aplicação dessas regras demanda mais tempo e recursos, mas melhora a qualidade dos dados e a interoperabilidade, economizando tempo durante a integração de dados e aprimorando a confiabilidade e escalabilidade em ecologia. Resumen Una taxonomía precisa, que incluya la identificación y asignación de nombres científicos, es fundamental para la inferencia ecológica; sin embargo, la información taxonómica suele estar poco estandarizada en las bases de datos ecológicos. Con el aumento en la integración de bases de datos ecológicos de distintas taxones y regiones, los conjuntos de datos con prácticas taxonómicas precarias pueden propagar errores y dificultar el intercambio de datos. En este manuscrito, proponemos diez reglas para mejorar el almacenamiento y el manejo de información taxonómica en bases de datos ecológicos. Estas reglas se basan en nuestra experiencia en ecología y taxonomía de plantas, pero pueden extrapolarse a otros organismos y disciplinas. Estas reglas enfatizan aspectos desde la identificación de especies hasta el almacenamiento permanente de registros verificables (e.g. especímenes de colecciones), también incluyen estandarización taxonómica, nomenclatura, validación y actualizaciones.…

articles.abstract: The gemma developmental program in Marchantia polymorpha is coordinated by MpMIR166‐mediated repression of MpC3HDZ and auxin homeostasis. Summary MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non‐coding RNA molecules essential for growth and development in eukaryotes. In plants, the master gene DICER‐LIKE 1 (DCL1) catalyzes the biogenesis of miRNAs by processing double‐stranded precursors that give rise to mature miRNAs. We sought to understand the function and evolution of microRNAs using Marchantia polymorpha, a model bryophyte that allows comparative approaches to infer characteristics of the ancestral land plant. We functionally characterized loss‐of‐function mutants of MpDCL1 a generated by means of CRISPR‐Cas9‐mediated genomic edition and the miR166/CLASS III HD‐ZIP regulatory circuit in Marchantia polymorpha. We report that MpDCL1a is required for the biogenesis of miRNAs and uncovered a central role for miR166/Homeodomain Zipper Class III‐regulated auxin synthesis in the specification of cell identity, patterning, meristem function, laminar expansion, and the development of the body in the last common ancestor of the bryophytes and vascular plants. Our findings indicate that DCL1, Class III HD‐ZIP, miR166, and auxin functioned in the development of the body of the last common ancestor of extant land plants and provide a novel working framework to interrogate the basic principles of cell specification and patterning in plants.

Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
articles.abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

articles.title: Denoising the US Census: Succinct block hierarchical regression
articles.abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21 to 36% and of all county-level groupings by 9 to 58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38 to 61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of more than $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.

articles.title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
articles.abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

articles.title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening
articles.abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. We addressed this by combining DNA nanoswitch–based selection of nucleotide-encoded libraries with next-generation sequencing to create FIND (Functional Interaction–based Nanoswitch Discovery), which enables ultrahigh-throughput discovery of compounds that induce or increase protein-protein interactions. We demonstrate FIND by discovering nanobodies that stabilize the interaction between angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and the receptor-binding domain of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and by discovering agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor gamma from a DNA-barcoded small-molecule library. By enabling rapid discovery of molecular modulators, FIND could lead to new therapeutics across many conditions.

articles.title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
articles.abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

articles.title: Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor
articles.abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ . Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.
