Although similar surface alkali issues exist in lithium‐ion layered oxide cathodes, it brings distinct and more complex challenges in sodium‐ion batteries due to the unique presence of NaHCO3, the severe Na+/H+ exchange tendency, and the narrower processing windows, which, however, have received very limited attention in the last few years. This review discusses the residual alkali issue in layered oxide cathodes of sodium‐ion batteries from the formation mechanisms to characterization techniques as well as modification strategies. Particular emphasis is put on the aforementioned sodium‐specific chemistry (e.g., NaHCO3) and derived differences from the well‐established lithium‐ion systems, as well as related research perspectives in the future, aiming to stimulate the development of air‐stable, high‐performance sodium‐ion layered oxide cathodes toward practical applications.

articles.title: An Azacrown Electrolyte for High‐Performance Sodium‐Ion Batteries
articles.abstract: Sodium (Na)‐ion batteries (SIBs) are promising energy storage devices. However, they still do not exhibit satisfactory performance metrics largely because the relatively large ionic radius of Na+ results in unfavorable solvation structures. This work demonstrates that using an azacrown (i.e., 1,4,7,10,13‐pentamethyl‐1,4,7,10,13‐pentaazacyclopentadecane, PMPAC) as a co‐solvent of the electrolyte can overcome the fundamental issues associated with SIBs. PMPAC features a cavity that not only matches the ionic radius of Na+ but chelates the metal ions as well. As a result, PMPAC effectively encapsulates Na+ and affords a disc‐like solvation complex with a relatively small solvation radius. These characteristics bestow the PMPAC‐based electrolytes with high ion conductivity and Na+ transference number, which promote battery operation by enabling Na to plate in a homogeneous manner. The PMPAC also prompts anions to locate in the inner sheath of the Na+ solvation structure such that inorganic‐rich solid‐electrolyte interphase layers with high structural integrity and low charge transfer resistance are formed at the anodes. SIBs that utilize PMPAC‐based electrolytes exhibit outstanding rate capacities (38 mAh g−1 at 100 C), along with ultralow capacity decay rates (0.0024% per cycle over 20 000 cycles for a half cell and 0.0062% per cycle over 10 000 cycles for a full cell).

articles.title: Anion‐Driven Solvent Degradation Networks in High‐Concentration Battery Electrolytes
articles.abstract: High‐concentration electrolytes (HCEs) are investigated for their ability to form robust, inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphases (SEI). While the SEI composition in HCEs differs from that in dilute electrolytes, the specific anion‐mediated reaction network driving this transformation remain poorly understood. The network complexity and transient nature of the radical intermediates involved have precluded the development of a comprehensive mechanistic map of initial SEI formation. Here, the reaction networks governing anion‐mediated electrolyte degradation are established using automated reaction discovery and microkinetic modeling (MKM). The study encompasses the decomposition pathways of ethylene carbonate (EC), propylene carbonate (PC), dimethyl carbonate (DMC), and acetonitrile (AN) in the presence of reduced anion species derived from LiFSI and LiTFSI. The results reveal a kinetically accessible landscape for solvent decomposition driven by fluoride (F−${\rm F}^-$) and CF3${\rm CF}_3$ fragments, identifying specific pathways that favor the formation of inorganic LiF and open‐ring organic carbonates. Microkinetic modeling further indicates that F−${\rm F}^-$ acts as a rapidly consumed driver, shifting the product distribution toward thermodynamically stable fluoro‐organic species. These results provide a molecular‐level rationalization for the unique SEI chemistries observed in HCEs and suggest that tuning the anion‐solvent interaction is a viable pathway for controlling interphase growth.

articles.title: Asymmetric Solvent Enables Adaptive Electrolyte with Orientation‐Modulated Structure for Ultrafast Charging Magnesium Metal Batteries
articles.abstract: The further development of rechargeable magnesium batteries (RMBs) is limited by significantly degraded performance under harsh working conditions, such as high areal capacity and large current density. This work first explores the failure mechanism of the Mg metal anode during fast charging and reveals the critical role of interfacial strong solvent shielding in governing the high‐current performance. Then, we propose an electrolyte design strategy by introducing asymmetric cosolvents to regulate the interfacial solvation structure through electric‐field‐induced dipole reorientation. Specifically, the electric‐field‐induced orientational rearrangement of asymmetric cosolvents reduces the solvation reorganization energy, thereby lowering the electron‐transfer activation barrier and accelerating electron‐transfer kinetics. Simultaneously, this orientational reorganization also weakens solvent‐induced shielding of Mg2+ at the interface, enabling preferential electron localization on Mg2+ rather than solvent molecules. Consequently, this proposed electrolyte strategy enables rapid Mg2+ migration and ultra‐stable Mg plating/stripping (<0.3 V overpotential at 10 mA cm−2/1000 h). Moreover, the full cell paired with Mo6S8 delivers 65 mAh g−1 capacity at 5C current density and when paired with fluorinated graphite exhibits excellent rate performance (over 350 mAh g−1 at 10C), establishing a kinetic paradigm for high‐rate multivalent battery systems.

articles.title: CO2‐Free Formaldehyde Electro‐Reforming Fuel Cell
articles.abstract: Conventional electrochemical synthesis is often hampered by steep energy demands and catalyst degradation, limiting both efficiency and durability. Here we introduce a hybrid alkali/acid formaldehyde‐to‐hydrogen fuel cell (h‐A/AFHFC) that transcends these limitations by coupling alkaline formaldehyde oxidation conversion with acidic oxygen reduction. A columnar branched AgCu catalyst drives the h‐A/AFHFC to a striking 2.0 V output and peak power density of 482 mW cm−2, maintaining robust operation for over 110 h. Beyond electricity, the device leverages the exceptionally low oxidation potential of formaldehyde and its single‐electron dehydrogenation pathway to co‐produce hydrogen and formate in a *CO‐free, CO2‐free electrochemical process, reformulating the role of fuel cells. Each kilogram of hydrogen is inherently paired with 46.0 kg of formate and 33.2 kWh of electricity, offering a rare convergence of clean energy and high‐value chemical synthesis. This strategy extends to gaseous formaldehyde and diverse aldehydes, enabling integrated energy‐chemical platforms for sustainability.

articles.title: Complex Makes It Powerful: From Unidirectional to Bidirectional via Synergistic Volatile Solid Additives Enabling 20.16% Efficient and Stable Organic Solar Cells
articles.abstract: Traditional volatile solid additives (VSAs) often regulate only the donor or acceptor phase, limiting synergistic microstructure optimization. Here, we report two halogenated nitrobenzene‐based additives, 3,5‐dichloronitrobenzene (DCNB) and 3,5‐dibromonitrobenzene (DBNB), that enable bidirectional regulation of both components. Owing to their anisotropic electrostatic potential and large dipole moments, they simultaneously promote ordered crystallization of donor D18 and enhanced packing of acceptor L8‐BO. Characterizations confirm improved molecular ordering and optimized phase separation, forming a favorable interpenetrating network. Consequently, D18:L8‐BO devices with DCNB and DBNB achieve power conversion efficiencies of 20.16% and 19.80%, respectively, versus 17.87% for the control. The 20.16% efficiency ranks among the highest for binary OSCs processed with volatile solid additives. Charge dynamics and transient absorption spectroscopy reveal enhanced exciton dissociation, suppressed recombination, and accelerated interfacial hole transfer. This strategy also shows broad universality across multiple D‐A systems, retaining >90% initial efficiency after 1000 h. This work unveils a bidirectional synergistic regulation mechanism and offers new insights into morphology engineering for stable, high‐efficiency OSCs.

articles.title: Descriptor‐Guided Computational Screening of Non‐Fullerene Acceptor Cores for Organic Solar Cells
articles.abstract: Non‐fullerene acceptors (NFAs) have propelled organic photovoltaic efficiencies toward 21%, yet their modular acceptor–donor–acceptor chemistry creates a vast combinatorial design space that calls for efficient prescreening. Here we establish a computation‐driven screening workflow and apply it to over 4000 optimized A–B–(D–S)–B–A NFA molecules assembled from experimentally reported building blocks. Using a sequential set of device‐relevant criteria – suppressed dipole moment, a target quadrupole for efficient charge separation, trap‐free electron transport, sufficient interfacial energetic driving force, strong visible‐light absorption, and a sufficiently large photovoltaic gap – we downselect from over 4000 to the top 10 NFA candidates for common polymer donors (P3HT, PBDB‐T, PBDB‐T‐2F, and PBDB‐T‐SF). The top candidates recover established high‐performance motifs, including Y6‐type structures and an O‐IDTBR‐like candidate, supporting the validity of the descriptor set. Statistical analysis further reveals a clear division of control: donor building blocks primarily determine ionization energies, acceptor/end groups determine electron affinities, and the quadrupole moment provides a broadly tunable electrostatic handle that is only weakly correlated with frontier orbital energetics. Comparison to synthesized reference NFAs shows good agreement for thin‐film electronic and optical properties, while device performance highlights the importance of morphology beyond descriptor‐based prescreening.

articles.title: Dual Anchoring Effect Achieves Active and Ultrastable Oxygen Reduction Catalysis
articles.abstract: Suppressing the dissolution of transition metals in multi-component platinum (Pt)-based oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) catalysts is critical yet challenging for proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC). Herein, we employ a dual anchoring strategy of rare earth (RE) surface stabilization and metal-nitrogen-carbon (MNC) interaction with porous Pt-nickel-cobalt nanowires (PtNiCo PNWs) to achieve satisfactory ORR and membrane electrode assembly (MEA) performances. The single site and cluster of praseodymium (Pr) tune the Pt electronic structure and protect the Ni/Co sites from dissolution, while zinc-N-C (ZnNC) provides extra active sites and stronger anchoring effect, yielding 9.0/9.5 times higher than those of commercial Pt/C in ORR mass and specific activities. Furthermore, the MEA exhibits high peak power density of 2.33 W cm−2, mass activity of 0.79 A mgPt −1 at 0.9 ViR-free and long-term lifetime of operating 30000/90000 cycles with 8.2%/28.3% decay, further reflecting our reasonable design conception of Pt-based ORR catalysts for PEMFC device.

articles.title: Electrolyte Microenvironment and Alloy Interface Synergy Enables Wide‐Temperature Aqueous Aluminum‐Ion Batteries From −30 to 50°C
articles.abstract: Aqueous aluminum‐ion batteries (AAIBs) have attracted interest due to the high abundance, low cost, and high theoretical capacity of aluminum. However, their development is hindered by limited electrolyte stability, severe corrosion and passivation of the Al anode, and sluggish Al3+ diffusion kinetics, particularly under temperature extremes. Herein, an electrolyte–anode coupled strategy is developed by combining a hydrated eutectic electrolyte with an electrodeposited Al‐Zn alloy anode. The optimized electrolyte, denoted as AETH30, is composed of Al(ClO4)3·9H2O, ethylene glycol (EG), triethyl phosphate (TEP), and H2O at a molar ratio of 1:6:4:30. EG and TEP reorganize the hydrogen‐bond network and establish a dynamic mixed Al3+ solvation environment, reducing water‐dominated coordination and suppressing parasitic reactions. Electrolyte‐derived interfacial species improve surface stability, while the Al‐Zn alloy lowers interfacial resistance and facilitates reversible plating/stripping. Benefiting from the complementary regulation of the electrolyte microenvironment and alloy‐anode interface, the Al‐Zn || AETH30 || PANI full cell retains 88.81 mAh g−1 after 1700 cycles at 25°C. It also maintains capacities of 53.96 and 81.47 mAh g−1 after 850 cycles at −30°C and 1000 cycles at 50°C, respectively. This work demonstrates an electrolyte microenvironment and alloy interface synergy strategy for durable AAIBs capable of wide‐temperature operation.

articles.title: Fluorination‐Tuned Covalent Organic Framework Interphases for Controllable LiF Content in Dendrite‐Free Lithium Metal Batteries
articles.abstract: To tackle the challenge of precisely regulating LiF content within the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) of high‐energy‐density lithium metal batteries (LMBs), this work presents a fluorination‐gradient design strategy, enabling controllable LiF formation through a covalent organic framework‐based artificial SEI layer (0F‐, 2F‐, and 4F‐COF), and lays the foundation for uncovering the interfacial regulation mechanism. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the electron‐withdrawing F group not only forms an ultra‐low HOMO energy orbital but also promotes the dissociation of LiPF6 via charge delocalization, enabling an oxidation stability of up to 5.4 V (vs. Li+/Li). Consequently, the Li||Li symmetric cell sustains stable cycling for over 6000 h at 1 mA·cm−2, while 4F‐COF@Li cell enables capacity retentions of 90.0% (LiFePO4, 1000 cycles), 80.5% (LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2, 300 cycles), and 70.1% (LiNi0.9Co0.09Mo0.01O2, 300 cycles) at 5 C. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations combined with in situ characterizations further reveal that F‐rich microenvironment of 4F‐COF accelerates LiPF6 dissociation and inhibits dendrite growth while directing the formation of a robust LiF‐rich SEI interphase. Overall, this work establishes precision fluorination of COF‐based artificial SEI layers as a new design strategy for developing safe, high‐rate, and dendrite‐free LMBs.

articles.title: Harnessing Endogenous Quinones to Orchestrate Water Dynamics and Electron Transfer at a Self‐Reinforcing Bio‐Abiotic Interface
articles.abstract: The bio‐abiotic interface is the central bottleneck in bioelectrochemical CO2 conversion, where electron and mass transport are governed by an intricate interplay among the electrode, microbial mediators, and interfacial water. Here we show that endogenous quinone mediators serve two coupled roles: shuttling electrons and reconfiguring the interfacial hydrogen‑bond network. Using a CoP nanoparticle‐decorated carbon nanoforest electrode that actively modulates these mediators, we find that the nanoforest surface lowers the adsorption barrier for quinones, accelerating their redox cycling and reducing overpotential for electron injection. Molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that these quinones disrupt the rigid hydrogen‑bond network, creating a localized free‑water zone that minimizes proton transport resistance. The interplay of this accelerated redox cycling and water restructuring generates a self‐reinforcing synergy, reflected by a ten‐fold drop in charge‑transfer resistance at 2.5 V vs. bare carbon felt and a Faradaic efficiency of 89.8% for acetate. This closed‑loop regulation, where material chemistry programs mediator behavior and mediators orchestrate both water dynamics and electron flux, offers a paradigm for engineering bio‑abiotic interface beyond empirical optimization.

articles.title: Hydrogen‐Bond‐Regulated and Rheologically Adaptive Interphase for Corrosion‐Suppressed Dense Zinc Deposition in Long‐Lasting 4 Ah Zinc Metal Batteries
articles.abstract: The practical implementation of ampere-hour-scale aqueous zinc metal batteries is severely hindered by hydrogen evolution corrosion and dendritic growth under high-current operation. Although regulating electrode–electrolyte interphase water via hydrogen bonding has been recognized as an effective strategy to suppress parasitic reactions, achieving dense, and uniform zinc deposition at high current densities remains a critical challenge due to interfacial instability and stress accumulation. Here, we construct a hydrogen-bond-network-regulated ionic liquid layer coupled with a rheologically adaptive polydimethylsiloxane gel to establish a water-poor and mechanically resilient interphase. The modified hydrogen-bond network modulates the interfacial water environment, thereby contributing to suppressing corrosion. Simultaneously, the polydimethylsiloxane gel layer provides a hydrophobic barrier against water penetration and dynamically accommodates interfacial stress, enabling dense and uniform zinc deposition under high-rate conditions. As a result, Zn||Zn symmetric cells exhibit exceptional cycling stability exceeding 1800 h at 50 and 25 mAh cm− 2. More importantly, a 4 Ah pouch cell delivers stable cycling for 300 cycles with a cumulative capacity exceeding 1200 Ah. This work establishes a rational interphase engineering strategy for achieving durable, high-capacity aqueous zinc metal batteries under practical high-current conditions.

articles.title: Inside‐Out Joule Heating Enables Coke‐Resistant Dry Reforming of Methane to Near‐Stoichiometric Syngas Over LDH‐Derived NiCo Catalysts
articles.abstract: Electrifying endothermic reactions offers a promising route toward sustainable chemical manufacturing, yet its practical implementation is constrained by inefficient outside-in heat delivery. Herein, we report a Joule-heating catalyst, NiCo/(Ni,Co)O-AlOx/Ti, derived from layered double hydroxides (LDHs) rooted onto a Ti scaffold. This monolithic architecture establishes intimate electrical-thermal coupling and creates an inside‑out thermal field that generates heat directly at the catalytic interface, shortening the heat-transfer pathway and mitigating reaction-induced catalyst-surface cooling. Experimentally validated multiphysics simulations resolve the resulting inverted temperature field and reduced source-to-surface temperature drop compared with outside-in furnace heating. Guided by this thermal design principle, the optimized Ni:Co = 2:1 catalyst achieves a high rate of 6.65 mmol·gNi(Co) −1·s−1 with a near-unity H2/CO ratio, together with stable operation over 200 h and markedly suppressed carbon accumulation. Co-incorporation enriches vacancy-associated defect sites in the oxide lattice, promoting CO2 activation through carbonate intermediates and reducing the energy barrier for carbonate-mediated carbon removal. These findings demonstrate how interfacial heat-delivery engineering can be coupled with defect-modulated catalyst design to advance electrified endothermic catalysis.

articles.title: Integrated d‐p Orbital Coupling Within High‐Entropy Oxide/Halloysite Accelerates Sulfur Reduction Kinetics in Sodium‐Sulfur Batteries
articles.abstract: The sodium polysulfides (NaPSs) shuttle effect remains a major obstacle to achieving the high theoretical capacity of room‐temperature sodium‐sulfur (RT Na–S) batteries. Herein, the high‐entropy oxide/halloysite nanotube hybrid host (HEO/HNT) is developed by integrating multicomponent catalytic sites with a naturally abundant 1D clay scaffold for efficient sulfur conversion. The hollow tubular structure of HNT enables uniform HEO anchoring and effective confinement of sulfur species, while the robust Si─O and Al─OH framework enhances cathode stability during long‐term cycling. Density functional theory calculations reveal that interfacial coupling between the metal 3d orbitals of HEO and the Al/Si 3p orbitals of HNT induces extended orbital delocalization, thereby strengthening NaPSs adsorption and lowering the free energy barriers for stepwise polysulfide conversion. In situ and ex situ characterizations further verify accelerated NaPSs reduction kinetics and suppressed shuttling. Benefiting from these synergistic effects, the S@HEO/HNT cathode delivers a high reversible capacity of 1225 mAh g−1 after 450 cycles at 1 C and maintains 478 mAh g−1 over 2500 cycles at 10 C, corresponding to an ultralow capacity fading of 0.008% per cycle. This study bridges high‐entropy oxide with naturally abundant clay substrates, offering a scalable route toward durable, high‐rate RT Na–S batteries.

articles.title: Interfacial Electronic Modulation of Vacancy‐Stabilized Pt Sites in Mo‐NiSeO4/NiSe2 Heterostructures for Industrial Alkaline Water Electrolysis
articles.abstract: Developing bifunctional electrocatalysts that combine high activity, long‐term durability, and practical device compatibility remains a major challenge for alkaline water electrolysis. Herein, we report a heterostructure catalyst of a conductive Co2P nanowire scaffold integrated with a Mo‐regulated NiSeO4/NiSe2 heterophase shell, and atomically dispersed Pt species stabilized at O/Se‐coordinated vacancy sites (Pt,Mo‐NiSeO4/NiSe2@Co2P) grown on nickel foam via sequential electrodeposition, controlled selenization, and galvanic replacement. Benefiting from synergistic electronic modulation and heterointerface engineering, the catalyst requires only 24 and 98 mV to deliver 10 and 100 mA cm−2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction, and 242 and 330 mV for the oxygen evolution reaction, in 1.0 M KOH, with excellent durability. Operando Raman spectroscopy and X‐ray absorption spectroscopy reveal dynamic surface evolution during electrocatalysis and confirm the atomic dispersion of Pt. When assembled in a two‐electrode electrolyzer, the catalyst achieves cell voltages of 1.47 V at 10 mA cm−2 and 1.65 V at 100 mA cm−2 in 30 wt.% KOH. Furthermore, an anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer delivers 1.55 V at 0.3 A cm−2 and 1.76 V at 1.0 A cm−2 at 70 °C, demonstrating its promise for practical alkaline hydrogen production.

articles.title: Local Atomic Disorder‐Driven Deep Relaxor State for Ultrahigh Dielectric Energy Storage With High Thermal Stability
articles.abstract: Lead-free dielectric ceramic capacitors are indispensable for advanced high-power electronic pulse systems owing to their exceptional power density and rapid charge-discharge kinetics. However, the simultaneous realization of ultrahigh recoverable energy density (W rec) and high efficiency (η), especially with robust thermal stability, remains challenging. Here, we propose a local structural design strategy focused on implementing atomic-scale disorder within relaxor ferroelectrics to achieve a deep relaxor state across a wide temperature window. Atomic-scale structure characterizations reveal that this local chemical/structural disorder induces ultrafine, highly active polar nanoregions, fostering an optimized polarization response while remaining resilient against thermal fluctuations. Consequently, the designed ceramics exhibit superior energy-storage performance, characterized by a large W rec of 13.1 J cm−3 and ultrahigh η of 93%, leading to a high figure of merit up to 187.1. Notably, exceptional performance stability across diverse operating conditions is bestowed, with η remaining above 90% at temperatures up to 200°C. This study thus provides a robust paradigm for designing dielectric capacitors that deliver both high energy-storage performance and reliability in harsh working environments.

Decompression With or Without Fusion Across Subgroups With Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis
articles.abstract: Randomized trials have shown limited benefits and increased risks of adding spinal fusion surgery to decompression for degenerative spondylolisthesis. Decompression with fusion has increasingly been used in the United States. To examine the comparative effectiveness of decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for patient subgroups. Cohort study using the target trial framework. Norwegian Registry for Spine Surgery and nested NORDSTEN-DS (Norwegian degenerative spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis) randomized trial. Adults aged 18 to 80 years with lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis and symptomatic back or leg pain lasting at least 3 months. Lumbar spinal decompression surgery with fusion versus lumbar spinal decompression surgery alone. The primary outcomes were Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) score and reoperation at 12 months. Linear regression models with inverse probability weighting to control for baseline confounding were used to obtain effect estimates with 95% CIs for decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for prespecified subgroups, including sex, age, smoking, body mass index (BMI), back pain intensity, and American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade. Of 2252 patients, 236 were in the NORDSTEN-DS randomized trial. The mean age was 66 years, and 1576 (70%) women were included. A total of 1446 patients had decompression alone, and 806 had decompression with fusion; respective unadjusted baseline ODI scores were 38.9 (SD, 14.9) and 41.4 (SD, 14.7). At 12 months, the ODI score was 22.3 (95% CI, 15.5 to 29.1) for decompression alone and 20.0 (CI, 13.9 to 26.2) for decompression with fusion; the mean difference was 2.2 (CI, -1.6 to 6.1). In exploratory analyses, the ODI score was worse for decompression with fusion for men with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher. Reoperation risk at 12 months did not differ. Possible residual confounding. Patient subgroups did not have differential effects from the addition of fusion to decompression at 12 months. Research Council of Norway.

articles.title: Measles
articles.abstract: Measles is reemerging, with cases and outbreaks increasing across the United States and other countries where measles had previously been eliminated. Most U.S. physicians have no experience with treating measles. However, the increasing likelihood of encountering not only children but also adults with measles requires a clinical review of the epidemiology, prevention, diagnosis, and management of this previously uncommon infection for general internal medicine physicians and hospitalists who care for adults in settings with measles reemergence. Prompt clinical suspicion, infection control measures, and notification of public health departments support timely diagnosis and disease control.

articles.title: Q&A: Hospital medicine looks ahead
Timing of Long COVID Improvement in Prospectively Followed RECOVER-Adult Participants
articles.abstract: Long COVID (LC) is widespread; however, limited information has been reported on the likelihood that symptoms remit over time. To evaluate the likelihood of improvement among persons with likely LC. Prospective, multisite cohort study (RECOVER-Adult [Researching COVID to Enhance Recovery]). 83 U.S.-based sites across 33 states; Washington, DC; and Puerto Rico. 1019 persons in RECOVER-Adult with likely LC (LC Research Index [LCRI] ≥11) 12 months after first SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary outcome was time until 2 consecutive study visits with LCRI less than 11. Secondary outcomes were time until LCRI measure reduced 50% or more and quality of life was good or better, and LCRI decreased to 0. Unadjusted estimates of cumulative incidence and adjusted marginal cumulative incidence by age, sex, SARS-CoV-2 wave, and LC subtype were reported across all follow-up time points. An estimated 36.2% (95% CI, 33.0% to 39.5%) met the primary outcome by 24 months after infection, and 50.1% (CI, 46.1% to 54.0%) met the primary outcome by 36 months. An estimated 56.4% (CI, 52.2% to 60.4%) and 26.9% (CI, 23.3% to 30.5%), respectively, met the 2 secondary outcomes by 36 months. Among persons who still reported likely LC at 18 months and 24 months after first infection, relative timing of subsequent symptom improvement was similar. Findings in this observational cohort are interpretable in a population with prevalent likely LC and do not address causal relationships between individual characteristics and symptom improvement. Among persons with likely LC 12 months after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, one half experience meaningful reductions in symptoms by 36 months, whereas a quarter experience complete remission of symptoms. These findings underscore both the potential for natural recovery and the urgent need for placebo-controlled therapeutic intervention trials. National Institutes of Health.

articles.title: Use of GLP-1 RAs before or during pregnancy was not linked to maternal pregnancy complications
Clonality in Preleukemic Conditions
articles.abstract: Preleukemia, historically a morphological and cytogenetic diagnosis, is now understood as a continuous clonal process in which somatic mutations, environmental influences, and stem cell pool dynamics interact over decades. Clonal hematopoiesis, the expansion of blood cells carrying somatic mutations, is near-universal in adults over age 70 and confers elevated risk of hematological malignancy, while also acting as a risk factor for cardiovascular and other age-related diseases. Here, we review the genetic and environmental factors that predispose to clonal expansion, organize the mechanisms of clonal expansion into three overlapping and interacting mechanisms (cell-autonomous fitness gain, context-conditional fitness, and nongenetic heritable states), and trace the trajectories that lead from clonal expansion to specific myeloid and lymphoid malignancies. We also discuss methods that have enabled mapping of clonal architecture in human tissue and close on the key questions that we anticipate will define the next decade of research in this field.

articles.title: Labor Unions and Better Health
articles.abstract: Social-class inequities in health arise from power imbalances in our political-economic system. However, through labor-union organizing, workers can build power to improve their life chances and health. In our review, we describe the rich historical, theoretical, and mechanistic evidence linking unions and health and critically evaluate the state of quantitative research on the topic. Most individual-level and ecological studies have estimated small beneficial or null union-health associations. However, as we describe, the studies are limited in number, particularly outside the Global North, and face many technical and conceptual challenges, including feedback loops between unions and societies’ political-economic contexts. We conclude with recommendations for enhancing the rigor and utility of union-health research, including by richly contextualizing studies’ findings and by answering questions raised by workers themselves. As social and economic inequities intensify and workers face heightening attacks on their well-being, unions remain crucial organizations for advancing health justice.

articles.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: A Statistical Perspective
articles.journal: Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application
articles.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a central framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its practical success, RLHF raises fundamental statistical questions because it relies on noisy, subjective, and heterogeneous feedback to learn reward models and optimize policies. This review provides a statistical perspective on RLHF, focusing primarily on LLM alignment. We introduce the main components of RLHF, including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, and relate them to familiar statistical concepts such as the Bradley–Terry–Luce model, latent utility estimation, active learning, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification. We review methods for learning reward functions from pairwise preference data and for optimizing policies through both two-stage RLHF pipelines and emerging one-stage approaches such as direct preference optimization. We further discuss recent extensions including reinforcement learning from artificial intelligence feedback, inference-time algorithms, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, as well as benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and open-source frameworks that support RLHF research. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in RLHF.

articles.title: Cell death in context: From mechanisms to interventions
articles.abstract: When, how, and why cells die, and what happens when they survive, have profound consequences for development, immunity, and disease. To coincide with the Cell Press Symposium "Taking programmed cell death from mechanisms to interventions," we bring together perspectives from researchers across career stages and areas of cell death research. From emerging mechanisms and consequences of cell death to opportunities for therapeutic intervention, these voices highlight a rapidly evolving field and the questions that will shape its future.

articles.title: HRS dephosphorylation at membrane contact sites promotes sorting within multivesicular endosomes
articles.abstract: HRS is a receptor tyrosine kinase substrate and ESCRT machinery component. It enables sorting of ubiquitylated cargo into multivesicular endosomes (MVEs) for lysosomal degradation but also functions in receptor recycling. We show that co-depletion of its ESCRT-0 binding partners, STAM1 and STAM2, recapitulates defects in EGF receptor (EGFR) sorting onto intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) but does not mirror the increased MVE size evident after HRS depletion. Using mutagenesis of the endogenous gene or introduction of APEX2-tagged HRS variants, we find that HRS Y329/334 phosphorylation is dispensable for EGFR sorting and MVE size control. AnnexinA1 mediates ER:endosomal membrane contacts and promotes EGF-stimulated ILV formation. We show that reduced ILV formation on AnnexinA1 depletion is accompanied by increased HRS phosphorylation, likely through reduced HRS dephosphorylation by ER-localised PTP1B. Conversely, Y329/334 mutation renders ILV formation insensitive to AnnexinA1 depletion. Our data suggest that rapid HRS dephosphorylation at ER:MVE contacts promotes efficient ILV formation.

articles.title: A critical reflection on the application of hot product frameworks to explain the target selection of wildlife products
articles.abstract: The application of hot product frameworks, such as value, inertia, visibility, and accessibility (VIVA) and concealable, removable, available, (abundance and accessibility), valuable, enjoyable, and disposable (CRAVED/CRAAVED), to illegal markets to understand the selection of wildlife products in them has gained momentum. Originally developed to study property crimes, these frameworks have been adapted for predictive analysis of wildlife product selection. However, their utility in explaining target selection and their empirical testability remain ambiguous. This study critically examined the use of the VIVA and CRA(A)VED frameworks in analyzing wildlife product selection for illegal markets. By reviewing peer‐reviewed studies and conducting a case study on Southeast Asian monitor lizards (Varanus spp.), we identified the challenges of applying these frameworks to real‐world contexts. These challenges are not merely methodological shortcomings of individual studies but reflect systematic difficulties inherent to applying these frameworks to wildlife contexts. The application of these frameworks to Southeast Asian monitor lizards confirmed that these issues transcend species groups. We also examined issues related to intraspecific variation in measures and variation between harvesters. Our analysis revealed complex interactions between attributes that influence wildlife product selection and identified key challenges to applying these frameworks, including incomplete data, inconsistent attribute measurements, and the dynamic nature of decision‐making during wildlife harvesting. A significant concern is the reliance on trade data, which are typically collected much later in the wildlife trade chain, to infer harvesting decisions. Moreover, we argued that target selection is not solely determined by product attributes. A more problem‐oriented and individualized approach that accounts for opportunity structures relevant to individual harvesters is needed to prevent aggregation fallacies. Thus, applying hot product frameworks to study the selection of target wildlife products cannot be quantitatively tested using an additive equation, and these frameworks should not be applied alone but situated within other theories of crime. Reflexión crítica de la aplicación de marcos de productos de moda para explicar la selección de objetivos de los productos de fauna Resumen Resumen. Hoy en día ha cobrado impulso la aplicación de marcos de análisis de productos de moda, como el de «valor, inercia, visibilidad y accesibilidad» (VIVA) y el de «ocultable, extraíble, disponible (abundancia y accesibilidad), valioso, agradable y desechable» (CRAVED/CRAAVED), a los mercados ilegales para comprender cómo seleccionan los productos de fauna silvestre. Desarrollados originalmente para estudiar los delitos contra la propiedad, estos marcos se han adaptado para el análisis predictivo de la selección de productos de fauna silvestre. Sin embargo, su utilidad para explicar la selección de objetivos y su capacidad de comprobación empírica todavía son ambiguas. Este estudio examinó críticamente el uso de los marcos VIVA y CRA(A)VED en el análisis de la selección de productos de fauna silvestre para los mercados ilegales. Revisamos los estudios sometidos a revisión por pares y la realización de un estudio de caso sobre los varanos del sudeste asiático (Varanus spp.) para identificar los retos que plantea la aplicación de estos marcos a contextos del mundo real. Estos retos no son meras deficiencias metodológicas de estudios individuales, sino que reflejan dificultades sistemáticas inherentes a la aplicación de estos marcos a contextos relacionados con la fauna silvestre. La aplicación de estos marcos a los lagartos monitor del sudeste asiático confirmó que estas cuestiones trascienden los grupos de especies. También examinamos cuestiones relacionadas con la variación intraespecífica en las mediciones y la variación entre los recolectores.…

articles.title: Conceptual framework for the implementation of the Species Threat Abatement and Restoration metric's threat abatement component
articles.abstract: One important goal of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) aims to halt extinction of species and reduce extinction risk 10‐fold by 2050. To help ensure that the actions taken under the targets of the KMGBF contribute to reducing species’ extinction risk, the Species Threat Abatement and Restoration (STAR) metric was designed to enable science‐based target setting for species. STAR quantifies the potential contribution of threat abatement actions or habitat restoration to reducing species’ extinction risk in an area. To support the effective implementation of STAR, we developed a framework to move from determining the threat abatement component of STAR (START) using global data to calibrating START using local data to setting targets and calculating realized START scores to measure progress. The framework outlines the specific approaches that can be implemented to calculate these different START metrics. First, estimated START scores use global data to provide an initial indication of the species and threats expected to be present within an area. Then, calibrated START scores involve confirming the local presence of species and threats, and the locally verified data allow for setting robust threat abatement targets, which can be articulated as target START scores. Calibrated START can also inform both reactive and proactive threat management. Finally, changes in threat intensity are then monitored and used to calculate realized START. Achieving realized START requires actors to not only reduce existing threats but also prevent additional threats emerging within the area. This framework provides a means for all potential actors, working across varying spatial scales, to quantify, plan, monitor, and deliver interventions to address species threats and then report the impact of the interventions using a consistent method and metric that are comparable and aggregable across actors and locations. Marco conceptual para la aplicación del componente de reducción de amenazas de la medida de Reducción de Amenazas y Restauración de Especies (STAR) Resumen Uno de los objetivos principales del Marco Global de Biodiversidad de Kunming‐Montreal (KMGBF) es detener la extinción de especies y reducir el riesgo de extinción diez veces para 2050. Con el fin de garantizar que las medidas adoptadas en el marco de los objetivos del KMGBF contribuyan a reducir el riesgo de extinción de las especies, se diseñó el indicador «Reducción de amenazas y restauración de especies» (STAR), que permite establecer objetivos basados en la ciencia para las especies. STAR cuantifica la contribución potencial de las medidas de reducción de amenazas o de restauración del hábitat a la reducción del riesgo de extinción de las especies en una zona. Para apoyar la aplicación efectiva de STAR, desarrollamos un marco que permite pasar de determinar el componente de reducción de amenazas de STAR (START) con datos globales a calibrar START utilizando datos locales, para finalmente establecer objetivos y calcular las puntuaciones START reales para medir el progreso. El marco describe los enfoques específicos que pueden aplicarse para calcular estas diferentes métricas START. Primero, las puntuaciones estimadas de START utilizan datos globales para proporcionar una indicación inicial de las especies y las amenazas que se espera que estén presentes en una zona. A continuación, las puntuaciones calibradas de START implican confirmar la presencia local de especies y amenazas y los datos verificados a nivel local permiten establecer objetivos sólidos de mitigación de amenazas que pueden articularse como puntuaciones objetivo de START. El START calibrado también puede servir de base para la gestión reactiva y proactiva de las amenazas. Por último, se supervisan los cambios en la intensidad de las amenazas y se utilizan para calcular el START realizado.…

articles.title: Reduction of Tree Water Stress by Large Herbivores in an African Savanna
articles.abstract: Large mammalian herbivores (LMH) play complex roles in shaping tree cover and composition in savannas by suppressing trees through browsing and reducing competition from neighbouring trees and understory vegetation. Where LMH are declining, release from browsing and intensification of competition has unpredictable physiological consequences. To test how LMH removal affects tree growth and water stress, we combined 16 years of growth data with measurements of leaf water potential and gas exchange from a herbivore‐exclusion experiment in Kenya. Across tree species, LMH exclusion increased growth but elevated water stress, particularly under dry conditions. Moreover, the tree species with the most acquisitive water‐use strategy was most susceptible to increased water stress and reduced carbon assimilation under exclusion. These findings indicate that although LMH limit tree growth, they also reduce water stress. Ultimately, interspecific differences in tree physiology will affect how savanna communities respond to interacting pressures from climate change and LMH declines.

articles.title: Biogeography of Argentine Stem Weevil Invasion of Southern New Zealand and Two Offshore Islands
articles.abstract: Understanding the biogeography and genetics of the invasion of oceanic islands by pest species can provide insights into how to limit such incursions. The invasive pasture pest weevil, Listronotus bonariensis (Kuschel), has established in both New Zealand and some of its offshore islands, causing significant economic damage. The opportunity was therefore taken to compare both the species' morphology and genetics of populations collected from the New Zealand mainland, Stewart Island (30 km offshore) and Chatham Island (860 km offshore). The L. bonariensis individuals from both of the offshore populations were found to be significantly smaller than those of the mainland populations. However, based on classical and molecular taxonomy, no associated species‐level differences were found and it was concluded that the island's smaller populations were the result of relatively poor habitat quality. Further, no significant genetic differences were detected between Stewart Island and mainland populations, indicating a close connection. Conversely, at the genomic level, the Chatham Island population was significantly different from the two other populations and this was attributed to probable founder effects. The evidence points to a small subset of what was still a recently‐established New Zealand L. bonariensis population early in the 20th century being inadvertently transported to the Chatham Islands. Thereafter, this founding subset expanded such that more recent introductions have had little effect on the founding genetics of weevils on the island. This study investigates whether irregular, unintended human transportation of species to isolated islands can lead to the occupation of previously uninhabited niches, with founder effects leading to genetic divergence from conspecific source populations elsewhere.

articles.title: Linking Morphological and Genetic Differentiation Among Populations in Seagrass Species With Contrasting Dispersal Strategies
articles.abstract: Long-distance dispersal sustains genetic diversity across populations and facilitates recovery from disturbance, and dispersal also may shape how ecologically important morphological traits shift in response to environmental change. We examined links among morphology, genetic differentiation, and dispersal through surveys of traits and genetics for Thalassia testudinum and Halodule wrightii distributed across a naturally occurring gradient in concentrations of total phosphorus in the water column along Florida's Gulf Coast (USA). We expected the contrasting dispersal strategies of the two seagrasses would drive patterns in genetic differentiation: T. testudinum produces floating fruits that can disperse over longer distances than the negatively buoyant seeds of H. wrightii. Genetic differentiation among populations was higher for H. wrightii (G' ST = 0.02–0.15) than for T. testudinum (G' ST = 0.00–0.07), supporting the expectation that limited dispersal leads to more genetic structure. Morphology for both species varied along the phosphorus gradient, where leaves were generally shorter in the estuarine system with the lowest phosphorus concentrations, with more pronounced differences in leaf length observed for T. testudinum. The role of the environment in driving leaf length was tested in a common garden experiment with plants of both species collected from three estuarine systems along the phosphorus gradient. Initially, leaf lengths of both species differed across plants originating from different systems. Leaf lengths became more similar throughout the experiment, with leaves of H. wrightii from the northernmost system beginning to lengthen after 11 months. Together, our results suggest that responses to environmental change can differ across seagrass species, where the species capable of long-distance dispersal exhibited greater variability in a morphological trait along an environmental gradient despite less genetic differentiation than the species with more limited dispersal.

articles.title: Shifting Dietary Ecologies of Early Ungulates Across the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum in the Bighorn Basin, Wyoming
articles.abstract: Understanding the interplay between climate change and ecology is crucial when attempting to reconstruct the evolutionary history of species, as well as predicting how modern species may fare in light of current anthropogenic climate change and habitat destruction. Here we use dental microwear texture analysis (DMTA) to infer the foraging ecologies of three lineages of early ungulates (the phenacodontids Copecion and Ectocion and the early perissodactyl Sifrhippus) across the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) in the Bighorn Basin of western North America. The PETM was a period of rapid warming and aridification 56 million years ago that resulted in considerable evolutionary changes within these lineages, including phylogenetic dwarfing. Our results interpret both lineages of phenacodontid as frugivorous “mixed feeders” that likely incorporated a large diversity of plant species and tissues, while Sifrhippus shows strong evidence of frugivory. This is further supported by greater complexity and lesser scale of maximum complexity in both species of Sifrhippus compared to the co‐occurring species of phenacodontids. Notably, only minor changes in dental microwear across the PETM were recovered, limited to textural fill volume in Ectocion. These data show that dietary ecology was mostly unchanged within these lineages during the PETM, despite considerable floral turnover and competition from immigrant species. The results of our study detail how herbivorous mammals adapt to intensive climatic and environmental disruptions, hinting at possible responses of modern fauna to present and future anthropogenic climatic and environmental breakdown.

A comprehensive “past-future” framework for restoration priority areas identification in a coastal city: a case study of Tianjin
articles.abstract: Coastal cities, endowed with abundant ecological resources and convenient transportation, are epicenters where the tension between ecological protection and economic development is most pronounced. Precise identification of restoration priority areas (RPAs) is crucial for improving ecosystem service management and advancing sustainable development in coastal cities. However, how to integrate historical evolution and future trends into RPAs management remains insufficiently addressed. In this study, we selected Tianjin as a case study site, and developed a comprehensive analytical framework for identifying RPAs. This framework centers on the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics and interrelationships of four ESs, identifies ecological restoration areas (ERAs) through full-cycle dynamic assessment and simulation, and proposes multi-type optimization recommendations. The results indicated that the water yield (WY), soil conservation (SC), carbon storage (CS) and habitat quality (HQ) exhibited divergent temporal trajectories from 2000 to 2020, although localized improvements were observed in the peripheral zones of ring-shaped built-up areas and in coastal wetland regions. WY–HQ exhibited a robust and gradually strengthening trade-off from 2000 to 2020, while CS–SC maintained a relatively stable synergistic relationship. Based on the Ecological Restoration Priority Index (ERPI), this study delineated ecological ERAs and further classified them into three progressively differentiated zones: Core Protection Zones (defined as RPAs), Synergistic Optimization Zones, and Ecological Improvement Zones. Based on the analysis of land use composition and spatial distribution in RPAs, we proposed specific ecological restoration strategies and spatial planning recommendations. This “past-future” framework overcomes the constraints of traditional RPAs and provides a novel perspective on the evidence-based land management in coastal city.

articles.title: Waterfowl habitat conservation in the U.S. Prairie Pothole Region benefits more than ducks: evaluating overlaps and gaps across geographies and bird species
articles.abstract: The Prairie Pothole Region (PPR) is a working landscape of grasslands, cropland, and wetlands that supports some of the highest numbers of breeding waterfowl, waterbirds, shorebirds, and grassland birds in North America. Consequently, the PPR was identified as a high priority for waterfowl conservation by the North American Waterfowl Management Plan. Partners in the Prairie Pothole Joint Venture (PPJV) have used spatial decision-support tools to guide extensive land conservation efforts, primarily acquisition of wetland easements, grassland easements, and fee-title lands, to conserve waterfowl populations. However, effects of waterfowl conservation actions on waterfowl and non-waterfowl species groups across geographies are poorly understood. We used spatial predictions from models developed by eBird along with land protection data to assess effects of conservation on 77 species of birds across the PPJV. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service fee-title and easement lands covered <5% of the landscape, but have generally protected much larger percentages of species’ populations, thus demonstrating the value of spatial targeting tools and how conservationists can disproportionately move the needle for priority species through strategic protection. Proportions of PPJV populations supported by lands protected through waterfowl conservation varied within and among waterfowl (range 0.07 to 0.39), wetland-dependent (0.02 to 0.42), and grassland bird groups (0.01 to 0.28), as well as among geographies. Proportions of populations supported by waterfowl conservation lands were generally lower in the eastern and western portions of the PPJV, where less habitat protection has occurred than in the central PPJV. Protected lands not acquired for waterfowl conservation added to proportions of populations protected, particularly in the western PPJV, which has large amounts of public agency land relative to other portions of the PPJV. Fee-title lands and grassland easements protected through waterfowl conservation were estimated to support more than three times as many individuals of non-waterfowl species as waterfowl; wetland easements were estimated to support more than twice as many individuals of non-waterfowl species as waterfowl. Our results demonstrate that waterfowl conservation in the PPJV benefits many species of birds; variation in benefits can be used to guide future conservation efforts to address gaps in protection.

articles.title: Beyond observed diversity: Community completeness negatively affects ecosystem invasibility across scales
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Charles Elton proposed that species‐rich communities are more resistant to invasion, yet a well‐known paradox persists: native diversity suppresses invasion at small scales while correlating positively with non‐native species diversity at broad scales. Moving beyond native observed diversity alone to community completeness, defined as the ratio of native observed diversity to its specific species pool, may offer a potential framework to address this scale dependency. This is because the completeness index reflects the degree to which a habitat saturates its available niche space, shaped jointly by abiotic and biotic filtering in an origin‐blind manner. At small spatial scales, native observed diversity and dark diversity (suitable yet absent native species) are negatively correlated. This implies that high native observed diversity indicates high community completeness, leaving limited vacant niche opportunities for both un‐arrived native and non‐native species and thus reducing invasibility. In contrast, at large spatial scales, greater environmental heterogeneity can yield a vastly expanded regional species pool where dark diversity also accumulates more, potentially resulting in lower community completeness and heightened susceptibility. It should be noted that native community completeness, based on the extant species pool, fails to capture the niche spaces left by historical species losses—a gap tracked by temporal dark diversity dynamics—yet these hypervolume holes can instead be successfully exploited and predicted by non‐native community completeness. Following on this logic, I propose a Completeness‐Based Invasion Theory, which hypothesizes that community invasibility is inversely related to community completeness across spatial scales. While further empirical testing across diverse systems is required, measuring completeness alongside observed diversity may provide a novel, scale‐independent perspective to advance our understanding and management of biological invasions. Combining both native community completeness and non‐native community completeness to predict non‐native species invasions may currently represent the optimal approach. articles.title: Community assembly on inland cliffs is context‐dependent
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Under harsh environmental conditions, community assembly processes are expected to drive pronounced functional convergence, with communities dominated by stress‐tolerant species. Integrating local communities with their regional species pools enables evaluating environmental filtering and disentangling habitat‐specific assembly processes. To assess whether the strength and direction of environmental filtering in extreme habitats depends on regional climate and topography, we adopted a trait‐based approach on a relatively underexplored habitat such as inland limestone cliffs. To test whether limestone inland cliffs function as extreme habitats that filter regional species pools towards stress‐tolerant trait syndromes or alternative habitat‐specific assembly processes, we sampled vegetation on inland limestone cliffs along an aridity gradient in three study areas spanning different European biogeographic regions, namely Alpine, Continental and Mediterranean. We compiled regional species pools from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility and integrated them into trait‐based null models to compare observed community structure against expectations under stochastic assembly, using a combination of functional traits compiled from field measurements and from databases. Additionally, to assess whether community assembly rules are shared across regions or shaped by regional context and topography, we quantify trait‐based non‐random assembly and functional convergence across biogeographic regions and different cliff aspects. The results show that in inland limestone cliffs, extremeness is context‐dependent. It varies with the selected traits, intensifies in humid regions and weakens on pole‐facing slopes in dry regions. Cliff plants showed reduced plant height across all regions and aspects, whereas leaf dry matter content was higher and seed mass was lower under specific conditions. These patterns indicate non‐random trait distributions towards conservative leaf strategies and reduced plant size, while the prevalence of small propagules may facilitate colonization of suitable microsites for establishment, often scarce and spatially scattered. Functional convergence occurred in the Alpine region and on equator‐facing cliffs in the Mediterranean region, with slope and microtopographic heterogeneity showing limited effects. Overall, inland limestone cliffs showed evidence of non‐random trait assembly and localized abiotic filtering, suggesting that these patterns are context‐dependent. Riassunto In condizioni ambientali severe ci si aspetta che i processi di assemblaggio delle comunità determinino una marcata convergenza funzionale, con comunità dominate da specie tolleranti allo stress. Integrare le comunità locali con i rispettivi pool regionali di specie permette di valutare il filtro ambientale e di distinguere i processi di assemblaggio delle comunità specifici di un habitat. Per valutare se la forza e la direzione del filtro ambientale in habitat estremi dipendono dal clima regionale e dalla topografia, abbiamo adottato un approccio basato sui tratti funzionali in un habitat relativamente poco studiato, quale quello delle falesie calcaree dell’entroterra. Per verificare se le falesie calcaree dell’entroterra funzionino come habitat estremi in grado di filtrare i pool regionali di specie verso sindromi funzionali associate alla tolleranza allo stress o, alternativamente, verso processi di assemblaggio specifici dell’habitat, abbiamo campionato la vegetazione su falesie calcaree dell’entroterra lungo un gradiente di aridità in tre aree di studio appartenenti a diverse regioni biogeografiche europee, ossia Alpina, Continentale e Mediterranea.…

articles.title: Context‐dependent joint buffering of abiotic stress by parental care and sibling interactions
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Climate change represents one of the most complex challenges of the 21st century, increasing global temperatures and the occurrence of extreme events, such as heatwaves, cold snaps, floods or droughts. These changes exert significant pressure on biological systems, often resulting in altered behavioural patterns and impairments in fecundity, reproductive success and offspring survival. The evolution of parental care is hypothesized to represent an adaptive response to environmental challenges, with the potential to buffer offspring performance against stressors such as thermal extremes. While parental care is long regarded as the major evolutionary driver for family groups, an increasing number of studies highlight the beneficial effects of sibling interactions on offspring development, raising interest in sibling cooperation as an early driver of social life. Here, we tested whether the fitness consequences of sibling interactions depend on abiotic environmental conditions and whether sibling interactions buffer offspring against environmental stress, act synergistically with parental care or lose their beneficial effects under harsh conditions. To this end, we examined larval performance in the subsocial burying beetle Nicrophorus vespilloides. In two separate experiments, we manipulated the presence or absence of parents and siblings and exposed offspring to either temperature or soil moisture extremes. The capacity of cooperative behaviours to mitigate the effects of environmental stress depended strongly on environmental context, social constellation and the trait considered. Under low temperatures, parental care and sibling cooperation acted synergistically to buffer larval mass, whereas the benefits of sibling interactions disappeared in the absence of parents. In contrast, high temperatures reduced offspring performance when parents and siblings were present simultaneously but did not diminish the benefits associated with sibling interactions in the absence of parental care. Our findings demonstrate that the effects of social interactions under environmental stress are highly context dependent. Rather than consistently promoting or disrupting cooperation, abiotic stress modified the strength and expression of social effects across environmental conditions and social constellations. These results highlight the importance of sociality for resilience to environmental change, while showing that its buffering capacity is conditional rather than universal. articles.title: Functional variation in butterfly egg pore traits: The potential role of climate
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Immobile eggs of terrestrial animals are exposed to variable environmental conditions. Insect egg pores, critical for gas exchange (aeropyles) and fertilisation (micropyles), are ecologically important yet understudied. While aeropyles likely adapt to climatic respiratory demands, and micropyles may respond to environmental pressures, their inter‐ and intraspecific variation remains poorly studied. Here, we compared egg pore morphology of three closely related Pieris butterflies sampled in the Netherlands. In addition, we compared egg traits of different P. napi populations sampled along a 4000‐km latitudinal gradient from northern to southern Europe and linked these traits with available climatic data. After several generations under identical greenhouse conditions, egg pore traits remained highly variable within and between species and groups. Remarkably, P. napi populations from divergent climates differed more in pore number and size than did co‐occurring Pieris species. Aeropyle number and width were strongly associated with climatic variables such as summer temperature and precipitation, independent of egg size. Additionally, we observed the micropyles of older eggs to be covered by a substance more often than fresh eggs. Our findings indicate that insect egg pores are highly dynamic traits, which may be shaped by ecological, behavioural and climatic factors and an under‐recognised role of egg adaptation. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract De eitjes van landorganismen zijn statisch en daardoor direct blootgesteld aan wisselende omgevingsfactoren. Insecteneitjes hebben poriën die verantwoordelijk zijn voor gasuitwisseling (aeropyles) en bevruchting (micropyles). Deze poriën zijn ecologisch belangrijk maar desondanks weinig onderzocht. Terwijl aeropyles waarschijnlijk belangrijk zijn voor de door het klimaat beïnvloedde gasuitwisseling, en micropyles zich wellicht aanpassen aan de omgeving, is hun natuurlijke variatie maar weinig onderzocht zowel tussen als binnen insectensoorten. In deze studie hebben we de variatie van ei‐poriën vergeleken tussen drie zeer verwante Pieris vlindersoorten uit Nederland. Daarbuiten hebben we gekeken hoe ei‐eigenschappen van Pieris napi populaties verzameld over een Europese noord‐zuid‐as van 4000 km gelinkt zijn aan het lokale klimaat. Na enkele generaties onder identieke kascondities bleek dat ei‐poriën sterk variabel bleven tussen zowel soorten als populaties. De verschillen waren zelfs groter tussen populaties van P. napi, dan tussen de drie Pieris soorten. Het aantal en de groote van aeropyles was sterk geassocieerd met temperatuur en regenval, onafhankelijk van ei‐grootte. Tot slot bleken eitjes van enkele uren oud vaker een nog onbekende substantie te bevatten die de micropyles afdekt dan vers gelegde eitjes. Deze studie laat zien dat de poriën van insecteneitjes zeer variabel zijn, die wellicht beïnvloed worden door ecologische‐, gedrags‐, en klimaatfactoren, en zo een grotere rol kunnen spelen in de evolutie van insecteneitjes dan eerder gedacht.

articles.title: Fungal Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis infections proliferate during amphibian terrestrial dormancy
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract The spread and impact of wildlife pathogens is often seasonal, and identifying the season(s) of highest impact can be critical to biodiversity and public health management. We report new evidence that winter host dormancy, a period generally neglected in terms of pathogen seasonal dynamics, strongly promotes the proliferation of the globally threatening amphibian fungal pathogen, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) in an endangered high‐elevation anuran host species. Surveillance of Bd in Yosemite toads (Anaxyrus canorus) during their first year of life showed that Bd prevalence and intensity increased fourfold during their first terrestrial winter dormancy. High prevalence and intensity of Bd infections following winter dormancy were observed in terrestrial first‐year juveniles across multiple sites and three consecutive years, and their Bd prevalence was much higher than that observed in aquatically breeding adults during the same time frame. The infections persisted into the active season. We integrated these results into a framework summarizing possible mechanisms of overwinter Bd maintenance. We recommend a reconsideration of seasons promoting Bd proliferation (i.e. increases in prevalence and/or intensity) and highlight a mechanism of interannual Bd maintenance in dormant terrestrial juveniles. The importance of host dormancy to pathogen persistence and seasonal infection spread may be far greater than previously thought. articles.title: High‐dimensional elementomes outperform CNP models in explaining photosynthetic traits
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Links between plant elementomes (i.e. the concentration of chemical elements in plant tissue) and functional traits have the potential to improve predictions of plant physiological performance and ecosystem processes, and their response to environmental change. High-dimensional plant elementomes, which encompass not only macronutrients but also micronutrients and trace elements, have been associated with various morphological and physiological plant traits, but not with photosynthetic traits. We determined elementomes, comprising 21 elements and isotopic ratios of C and N, of 26 hygrophytic bryophyte species (16 mosses and 10 liverworts) in Mediterranean springs, and examined their relationship with four photosynthetic light response traits: maximum photosynthetic rates, apparent quantum yield, light compensation point and dark respiration rates. Results from linear mixed effects models showed that high-dimensional elementomes are strongly associated with photosynthetic traits, explaining substantially more variance (R 2 = 38%–61%; 72%–85% when also including taxonomic information) than models based solely on C, N and P (R 2 = 6%–45% and 35%–72%, respectively). Model selection and averaging revealed that each photosynthetic light response trait was optimally modelled by a set of 8–13 elemental variables, including various macronutrients (e.g. N, S, K), micronutrients (e.g. Zn, Cu), trace elements (e.g. Ni, Co) and isotopic ratios (δ13C and δ15N). We demonstrate that plant elementomes capture key drivers of photosynthetic variation, which adds to growing evidence of strong links between elementomes and various functional traits that underpin organismal and ecosystem functioning. Our results suggest that characterising plant elementomes could contribute to improved predictions of ecosystem-scale processes such as CO2 uptake. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Resum Els vincles entre els elementomes de les plantes (és a dir, la concentració d'elements químics en els teixits vegetals) i els trets funcionals poden millorar les prediccions sobre el rendiment fisiològic de les plantes i els processos ecosistèmics, i com aquests responen als canvis ambientals. Els elementomes d'alta dimensionalitat, que inclouen no només macronutrients, sinó també micronutrients i elements traça, s'han associat amb diversos trets morfològics i fisiològics vegetals, però no amb trets fotosintètics. Hem determinat els elementomes (incloent 21 elements i les proporcions isotòpiques de C i N) de 26 espècies de briòfits higròfits (16 molses i 10 hepàtiques) presents a fonts mediterrànies, i n'hem analitzat la relació amb quatre trets de resposta fotosintètica a la llum: taxes fotosintètiques màximes, rendiment quàntic aparent, punt de compensació de la llum i taxes de respiració. Els resultats dels models lineals d'efectes mixtos mostren que els elementomes d'alta dimensionalitat estan fortament associats amb els trets fotosintètics i expliquen una proporció substancialment més gran de la variància (R 2 = 38%–61%; 72%–85% quan també s'hi inclou la informació taxonòmica) que els models basats únicament en C, N i P (R 2 = 6%–45% i 35%–72%, respectivament). La selecció de models i la mitjana ponderada de les estimacions revelen que cada tret fotosintètic es pot modelitzar de manera òptima mitjançant un conjunt de 8–13 variables elementals, que inclouen diversos macronutrients (p. ex., N, S, K), micronutrients (p. ex., Zn, Cu), elements traça (p. ex., Ni, Co) i proporcions isotòpiques (δ13C i δ15N). Demostrem que els elementomes vegetals permeten identificar factors clau de variació fotosintètica, la qual cosa se suma a l'evidència creixent de l'existència de vincles estrets entre els elementomes i diversos trets funcionals que sustenten el funcionament dels organismes i dels ecosistemes.…

articles.title: Invasive insects outperform their native counterparts
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Invasive alien species cause substantial ecological damage worldwide, driving biodiversity loss and negatively impacting human livelihoods. Although invasive insects have some of the most severe impacts, the traits associated with their invasiveness remain unclear. We conducted a meta‐analysis comparing phenotypic traits of matched, co‐occurring invasive and native insect pairs (sympatric congeners or confamilials) in the invaded range. In total, we compared 922 invasive‐native pairs using 1327 effect sizes from 182 studies. These pairs comprised 144 unique invasive insect species and 403 unique native species. We found that invasive insects generally have greater fecundity, shorter development times, faster population growth rates and enhanced foraging and competitive capabilities compared with their native counterparts. However, some of these patterns changed after excluding the two most data‐rich families (i.e. Coccinellidae and Formicidae), likely due to divergent evolutionary histories, life history strategies and selection pressures. This study represents the most comprehensive systematic comparison of trait differences between co‐occurring native and invasive insect species and highlights that a diverse array of traits can contribute to invasiveness. Moreover, our open‐access database of insect trait data will facilitate further research into the causes and consequences of insect invasions.
