articles.title: Trends at 50: a mission that matters
articles.abstract: What makes a great review article in your field? As more research is published every day, it has become increasingly difficult to keep up with the latest developments and to ensure that you are hearing from the leading scientists driving these innovations and advances. How do you know what is new and what is valuable?

articles.title: What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
articles.abstract: For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural–behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.

articles.title: A validated antibody toolbox for ALS research
articles.abstract: A substantial fraction of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated proteins remains poorly characterized, in part because of the limited availability of validated research antibodies. We established knockout (KO)-based antibody characterization workflows and demonstrated that widely used antibodies against the major ALS-associated protein C9orf72 lacked specificity (Laflamme et al., 2019). We subsequently scaled this framework to systematically benchmark research antibodies, revealing that up to 61% fail to perform as recommended by manufacturers (Ayoubi et al., 2023b). Here, we extend this approach by establishing the ALS-Reproducible Antibody Platform (ALS-RAP), a comprehensive effort to generate a publicly available dataset of KO-validated antibodies targeting proteins encoded by ALS risk genes. In total, we characterized 303 antibodies against 33 ALS-associated proteins to identify high-quality reagents for use in western blot, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence. Using these antibodies, we profiled protein levels across human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary neurological cell types. These analyses revealed diverse cellular distributions and higher levels of several ALS-associated proteins in glial populations, consistent with emerging evidence for immune contributions to ALS. Together, ALS-RAP provides a validated antibody toolbox and protein expression resource to support the study of ALS-associated proteins.

articles.title: Class-wide sequence, structural, and docking-profile diversity of insect odorant receptors and structural specialization of Orco
articles.abstract: Insect olfaction is facilitated by a heterotetrameric odorant receptor–odorant receptor co-receptor (OR-Orco) complex. However, extensive sequence divergence and lineage-specific expansion have complicated large-scale comparisons of OR repertoires across insects. Here, we integrated sequence similarity, structural similarity, and molecular docking to analyze ORs from 115 insect species. OR repertoire size was associated with adult diet, larval diet, and habitat, but not with circadian rhythm. We developed a ‘trunk–branch’ network framework to classify ORs according to sequence and structural similarity and used large-scale molecular docking to derive comparative docking profiles. Despite marked differences in sequence- and structural-community composition, almost all sampled orders contained ORs assigned to all six docking-profile communities. Holometabolous insects showed higher OR sequence-community diversity than non-holometabolous insects, and docking-profile composition differed between extant lineages whose order-level origins predate or postdate the end-Permian mass extinction. Most notably, we identified a highly conserved extracellular β-sheet in Orco that restricts ligand access to the binding pocket and may contribute to its reduced capacity to bind natural odorants. The emergence of Orco represents a key evolutionary transition from homomeric receptors to heteromeric OR–Orco complexes, and our results suggest that this transition may have been accompanied by pronounced specialization of the extracellular domain and binding pocket. Together, these analyses provide a class-wide framework for comparing insect OR diversity and generate testable hypotheses for future experimental and evolutionary studies.

articles.title: Impacts of mutation accumulation and order on tumor initiation revealed by engineered murine colorectal cancer organoids
articles.abstract: Tumorigenesis typically follows a multi-hit trajectory, driven by accumulating oncogenic mutations. Colorectal cancer (CRC) has long served as a paradigmatic model of multi-hit tumorigenesis, characterized by adenoma-carcinoma transition accompanied by acquisition of specific oncogene and tumor suppressor mutations. However, how the temporal order of early mutations influences CRC initiation remains poorly understood. To address this, we established a CRC tumorigenesis model using murine intestinal organoids. By introducing defined combinations of key CRC driver mutations (Kras, Apc, and Trp53) in distinct orders, we systematically investigated how the order of mutation accumulation affects tumor initiation. Our results reveal that the mutation accumulation confers growth advantages in both in vitro and in vivo models. Strikingly, mutation order also influenced the tumorigenic properties of the organoids. Whereas organoids with Trp53 loss before or after Apc loss similarly affected organoid phenotypes in vitro or tumorigenicity in immunodeficient mice, organoids with Trp53 loss preceding Apc inactivation exhibited reduced tumor-forming potential in immunocompetent mice, likely due to their distinct immunological features. Collectively, our study reveals a critical role of ordered mutation accumulation in CRC initiation, an insight that may hold clinical relevance.

articles.title: Spyglass is a framework for reproducible and shareable neuroscience research
articles.abstract: Scientific progress depends on reliable and reproducible results. Progress can be accelerated when data are shared and re-analyzed to address new questions. Current approaches to storing and analyzing neural data involve bespoke formats and software that make replication and reuse of data difficult. To address these challenges, we created Spyglass, an open-source data management and analysis framework written in Python. Spyglass provides reproducible pipelines for common neuroscience analyses and sharing of raw data, intermediate analyses, and final results within and across labs. Spyglass uses the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) standard and includes pipelines for spectral filtering, spike sorting, pose tracking, and neural decoding. Spyglass can be extended to apply existing and newly developed pipelines to datasets from multiple sources. We demonstrate these features in the context of a cross-laboratory replication by applying advanced state space decoding algorithms to publicly available data. New users can try out Spyglass on a Jupyter Hub hosted by HHMI and 2i2c: https://spyglass.hhmi.2i2c.cloud/.

articles.title: Deciphering Complex Interfacial Dynamics via Operando Microbalance during Potential-Modulated Alkyne Hydrogenation
articles.abstract: Applied potentials can alter heterogeneous catalysis, but the roles of ions, solvent, and reactants at the polarized catalyst-electrolyte interface remain unclear. Here, we track potential-driven interfacial mass redistribution during aqueous Pd-catalyzed alkynol semi-hydrogenation using an operando electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (EQCM). By combining gravimetric measurements with a volumetric occupancy model, we quantify the competitive redistribution of ions, reactants, and hydrogen at the solid-liquid interface. The results show that hydrated Na+ promotes cathodic interfacial mass accumulation, forming a cation-bridged microenvironment that enriches alkynol and limits H2 availability. Positive polarization disrupts this microenvironment, promotes product removal, and restores surface hydrogen. Based on these results, we developed an oscillating potential program (100 s at –0.9 V, 20 s at +0.5 V) to control reactant enrichment, product removal, and hydrogen availability, increasing alkenol selectivity from ∼50% to 97% while enhancing activity by 173%.

articles.title: Divergent Reactivity toward Decarboxylative Protonation or Oxidation via Single-Component Organocatalysis
articles.abstract: Decarboxylative protonation/deuteration provides a powerful strategy for removing carboxylic acid handles and installing C–H/D bonds. However, existing catalytic methods typically rely on separate components to conduct the necessary proton-transfer, electron-transfer, and hydrogen-atom-transfer steps, restricting substrate scope and scalability. Herein we report a single-catalyst platform for decarboxylative protonation/deuteration that is broadly tolerant of carboxylic acids and readily scalable to 100 mmol in flow. Diarylquinoline organocatalysts function simultaneously as the base, photo-oxidant, and hydrogen-atom donor, demonstrating an underexplored reactivity mode for photocatalysts in which reductive quenching occurs by facilitating C–H bond formation rather than conventional electron transfer processes. Mechanistic studies indicate that oxidation is achieved through proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET), resulting in high chemoselectivity for carboxylic acid activation. Hammett analysis reveals that catalyst electronics strongly influence the reaction rate, and an uncommon inverse kinetic isotope effect provides evidence for a turnover-limiting, hydrogen-bonded transition state. Finally, reactivity can be diverted toward decarboxylative oxidation to form carbonyl compounds simply by changing the reaction atmosphere, offering versatile synthetic control.

articles.title: Exploring Liquid Metals as Dynamic Reaction Media
articles.abstract: Liquid metals often exhibit enhanced catalytic performance owing to their inherent characteristics, including the facile preparation of liquid alloys, atomic dispersion of dissolved elements, high-entropy surface structures, adaptive atomic configurations, and resistance to coking. These features fundamentally distinguish liquid metals from their solid counterparts, which possess fixed atomic arrangements. The transient geometries and electronic properties of liquid atoms within a dynamic matrix increase the possibility to align with various reactants, enabling energy-favorable adsorption patterns and reaction pathways. The catalytic properties of liquid media can be tuned by regulating the dissolved components and/or combining with other functional species. To date, a variety of bond dissociation and formation reactions, centering on C–C, C–H, C–O, C=C, C–N, and C–Cl, have been achieved using liquid metal media. The distinctive catalytic phenomena and the underlying mechanisms associated with liquid metals challenge the conventional understanding of catalysis based on solid-state catalysts. The use of liquid metal media for chemical reactions remains at an early stage, offering great opportunities for future exploration.

articles.title: Hydroxyl-Directed Anchoring and Electronic Structure of Pt–Sn on γ-Al2O3 for Propane Dehydrogenation
articles.abstract: Although γ-Al2O3-supported Pt–Sn catalysts are central to industrial propane dehydrogenation (PDH), conventional support design has primarily focused on structural properties, largely overlooking the role of surface hydroxyl chemistry in governing metal–support interactions. Here, we show that the distribution of surface hydroxyl types strongly affects Pt–Sn anchoring, particle growth, and performance of the catalyst supported on γ-Al2O3. By hydrothermally tailoring AlOOH precursors and exploiting a topotactic phase transition, three γ-Al2O3 supports (Al2O3-AIP, Al2O3-NP, and Al2O3-NF) with distinct distributions of terminal μ1-OH and doubly bridged μ2-OH sites were prepared. Systematic characterization showed that the hydroxyl-rich Al2O3-NP and Al2O3-NF supports produced substantially smaller Pt–Sn particles than Al2O3-AIP. Spectroscopic trends suggest preferential involvement of acidic μ1-OH sites at lower precursor loadings and progressively greater involvement of μ2-OH sites as the μ1-OH sites approached saturation. The μ2-OH-enriched surfaces favored precursor anchoring associated with highly dispersed Pt–Sn clusters (∼0.6 nm) after reduction. In propane dehydrogenation at 580 °C, the μ2-OH-enriched 0.5Pt–1.3Sn/Al2O3-NF catalyst achieved an initial propane conversion of 60% while maintaining a propylene selectivity above 97%. Site-occupancy experiments and C3H6-DRIFTS further suggest that precursor anchoring involving μ2-OH sites is associated with improved Pt–Sn dispersion and weaker propylene adsorption. These results show that controlling surface hydroxyl types can regulate metal anchoring and particle growth in Al2O3-supported dehydrogenation catalysts.

articles.title: Kinetic Multi-reaction Model of Platinum Nanoparticle Oxidation and Cathodic Dissolution in a Wide Potential Window
articles.abstract: Mathematical modeling provides a powerful framework for understanding and mitigating degradation in catalyst materials such as platinum nanoparticles. A hallmark of platinum degradation during voltage cycling is the appearance of two distinct maxima in the dissolved Pt concentration: a smaller peak upon increasing potential and a larger peak upon decreasing potential. To explain this observation, we propose a kinetic multi-reaction model of Pt nanoparticle oxidation and dissolution, which describes dissolution as an interplay between direct electrochemical dissolution, passivation of the Pt surface, and the electrochemical dissolution of Pt oxides. The model is calibrated using cyclic voltammograms and time traces of Pt ion concentrations measured for two Pt catalyst samples with different nanoparticle sizes and different supports (carbon-supported 3 nm and unsupported 30 nm particles). The model results show very good agreement with the experimental data and indicate that the dissolution dynamics are indeed governed by oxide surface passivation and dissolution. Furthermore, comparison of results for different catalysts shows that the observed differences in Pt dissolution arise not only from variations in reaction rates on particles of different sizes but also from differences in the catalysts’ microscopic structure, which significantly influence Pt loss through diffusion.

articles.title: Mechanistic Insights into Cobalt-Catalyzed Kumada C(sp2)–C(sp2) Cross-Coupling Enabled by High-Denticity Cobalt(I) Intermediates
articles.abstract: Understanding the role of low-valent cobalt species in cross-coupling catalysis remains a central challenge, particularly in distinguishing two-electron organometallic pathways from radical-based mechanisms. Herein, we report the isolation and comprehensive characterization of cobalt(II) and cobalt(I) intermediates supported by a tetradentate diazapyridinophane (tBuN4) ligand and elucidate their roles in Kumada cross-coupling reactions. Structural, spectroscopic, and computational studies reveal partial ligand-centered reduction in the “Co(I)” species, which function as single-electron initiators for halogen atom transfer from aryl bromides. Mechanistic investigations suggest that the resulting aryl radicals follow two distinct pathways: solvent-mediated hydrogen atom transfer leading to protodehalogenation, or interception by Grignard reagents to form C(sp2)–C(sp2) bonds through an SRN1-type mechanism (radical-nucleophilic aromatic substitution). Overall, these findings establish a radical-mediated framework for Co-catalyzed Kumada coupling and highlight ligand denticity as a key factor in governing reaction pathways.

articles.title: Spatial Coupling of Metal and Acid Sites via Amorphous Nb–O–Al Interfaces for Selective Polyolefin Hydrocracking
articles.abstract: Hydrocracking of polyolefin waste into liquid fuels over bifunctional catalysts requires efficient synergy between metal sites for H2 activation and acid sites for C–C bond cleavage. However, on nonzeolitic, oxide-based supports, these two functionalities are typically distributed in a random manner, limiting their spatial proximity and, consequently, the overall catalytic efficiency. Herein, we report an interface-design strategy that enforces nanoscale spatial coupling between metal and acid sites within a single structural unit, specifically tailored for polyolefin hydrocracking. The catalyst comprises highly dispersed rhodium (Rh) species anchored on an amorphous NbOx-doped γ-Al2O3 support. The amorphous Nb–O–Al interfaces generate electron-deficient Nb centers that function as medium-strong Lewis acid sites, while simultaneously modulating the electronic and coordination environment of the adjacent Rh species responsible for H2 activation. The nanoscale proximity of these complementary sites facilitates the coupling of acid-mediated C–C bond transformation with the subsequent hydrogenation of reactive intermediates. When applied to the hydrocracking of low-density polyethylene under mild conditions (240 °C, 2 MPa H2), the optimized Rh/10Nb–Al catalyst achieves a liquid product space-time yield of 283 gliquid·gmetal–1·h–1 with a methane selectivity of only 0.77%. Quantitative analysis reveals a linear correlation between the density of these interfacial strong Lewis acid sites and the hydrocracking activity, thereby directly linking the catalytic performance to the interfacial structure. This study establishes interfacial engineering as a rational strategy to encode metal–acid intimacy into the catalyst architecture, thereby offering a general design principle for selective plastic-to-fuel conversion.

articles.title: Synergistic Catalysis of Single-Site Rhenium and Ruthenium Nanoclusters for Ammonia Synthesis under Mild Conditions
articles.abstract: The development of high-efficiency NH3 synthesis catalysts under mild conditions is urgently required to alleviate the excessive energy consumption and carbon emissions in traditional Haber–Bosch processes. Although Ru-based catalysts show considerable potential, their catalytic activity is often severely constrained by hydrogen poisoning caused by strong H2 adsorption. Herein, we report the fabrication of a Ba/0.1Re–Ru/AC catalyst through the strategic integration of single-atom Re species into a conventional Ba/Ru/AC framework. Notably, the Ba/0.1Re–Ru/AC catalyst exhibits a high NH3 synthesis rate of 65.1 mmol g–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 1 MPa. Mechanistic investigations reveal that single-atom Re species function as a supplementary active site for H2 adsorption and activation. The incorporation of Re also facilitates H-spillover over the catalyst surface, which effectively alleviates the competitive adsorption between H2 and N2 on Ru sites and consequently mitigates hydrogen poisoning on Ru nanoclusters. Concurrently, the incorporation of single-atom Re modulates the defect density of the support and promotes the creation of additional strong Lewis basic sites. These structural changes induce a strong electronic metal–support interaction (EMSI) effect, which specifically tunes the electronic structure of the Ru nanoclusters. This synergistic interplay between single-atom Re sites and Ru nanoclusters establishes a compelling paradigm for the rational design of highly efficient NH3 synthesis catalysts.

articles.title: Diagnosis of Mechanisms of Kinetics in Lithium-Rich Manganese-Based Cathode Materials
articles.abstract: The rate-determining step (RDS), which determines rate capability in lithium-rich manganese-based oxide (LRMO) cathode materials, remains unclear. In this work, we establish a quantitative diagnostic method for the RDS in LRMOs using in-situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) at different states of charge (SOC) and C-rates. From our results, the SOC determines the intrinsic bottleneck of the RDS, while the C-rate drives the transition from single-step to mixed control. Upon discharging to 4.4 V, the RDS is dominated by electron transfer at the interface accompanied by layered-to-spinel phase transition, whereas it is strongly influenced by solid-state diffusion in the bulk with depletion of Li vacancies arising from Jahn–Teller distortion when discharging to 3.0 V. Furthermore, Li+ diffusion, instead of charge transfer, plays a major part in the RDS of LRMOs when the C-rates are increased. These findings establish quantitative criteria for designing future cathode materials.

articles.title: UV Exposure and Durability of Emerging Photovoltaics: Quantifying and Reporting Outdoor UV Doses
articles.abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation in sunlight is well known to harm components of solar modules, especially those of emerging photovoltaic technologies. Current accelerated UV tests, however, differ in spectral range and by orders of magnitude in intensity and dose. Their usual anchors, IEC 61215-2 preconditioning at 15 kW h m–2 and a fixed UV fraction of AM1.5G, do not represent long-term outdoor exposure. Here, we quantify annual outdoor UV doses (280–400 nm) across the contiguous United States from the National Solar Radiation Database for horizontal, fixed-tilt, and tracked mounting. Spectroradiometer measurements at two sites validate the model. Annual horizontal-plane doses span 72–133 kW h m–2, with a median of nearly 100 kW h m–2, so IEC 61215-2 preconditioning simulates only 1.4–2.5 months of outdoor exposure. Single-axis and dual-axis tracking typically add 10 and 18 kW h m–2, respectively. Finally, we propose reporting the source spectrum and expressing the test dose as a multiple of the annual outdoor dose for a stated location and mounting.

articles.title: Competing deformation mechanisms controlled by oxygen content lead to a strength-failure turnover in CuO-doped NiTi shape memory alloys
Critical role of austenite in yielding behavior of ultrahigh-strength maraging steels fabricated via laser powder bed fusion
Direct observation of chemical short-range ordering in multicomponent alloys by resonant and non-resonant X-ray diffraction
Can Policy Uncertainty Drive the Dollar?
articles.abstract: This article reviews the risk-based literature on international arbitrage deviations, exchange rates, and countries’ borrowing costs. It synthesizes recent work identifying policy uncertainty as a key primitive in risk-based models of global finance and investment. Volatile and unpredictable policy environments alter forward-looking investors’ expectations and portfolio decisions, thereby influencing exchange rates, excess currency returns, and the cost of capital—effects especially pronounced in emerging markets. We discuss how increased global policy uncertainty can create conditions under which a policy risk premium also arises for the US dollar. We present preliminary evidence consistent with this hypothesis.

articles.title: Corporate Boards: New Thinking
articles.abstract: In the face of global challenges, corporate boards may need to think differently. In this review, I explore how the finance literature addresses the challenges boards face. I focus on a key recent challenge: how boards navigate shifting expectations about their objectives beyond shareholder value. I highlight that the literatures on boards’ stakeholder objectives and diversity overlap. This raises interesting, and important, questions about how boards can develop “new thinking” more generally. Much research remains to be done in this area. To rise to the challenge, however, finance academia may also need to think differently. Using data that measure how individual directors think, I illustrate that many factors may influence how directors think, including selection. Recognizing path dependencies in approaches and assumptions may help the field of finance continue to generate influential research on boards.

articles.title: Improving Financial Literacy: From Corporate Finance to Personal Finance
articles.abstract: This article provides an overview of the literature on financial literacy. It covers the initial measurement that created the Big Three financial literacy questions and measures of personal finance knowledge featuring 28 questions. It shows that levels of financial literacy are low and have not been improving over time. This is true not only in the United States but also in countries worldwide. These findings matter because financial literacy is conducive to savvy financial behaviors, from holding precautionary savings to planning for retirement to many other financial decisions. Financial education programs have grown exponentially over time, providing important insights into their cost-effectiveness. Personal finance courses have been added to high school and college curricula, and the evidence indicates that they are useful initiatives to improve financial knowledge and downstream behavior.

articles.title: Investor Beliefs and Expectation Formation
articles.abstract: This article reviews the literature that uses survey data to study expectation formation among investors. We begin by outlining methods for eliciting investor beliefs and summarizing key empirical patterns documented in recent work. Highlighting the persistent cross-sectional heterogeneity in expectations, we then review evidence on the determinants of beliefs, including a new analysis of belief reactions to the tariff announcement in April 2025. Next, we examine how expectations shape financial decision-making, emphasizing the systematic but muted sensitivity of outcomes to belief changes. We conclude by pointing to promising directions for future research on belief measurement, the determinants of expectations, and their implications for policy makers.

articles.title: Option Pricing, Time-Varying Volatility, and Tail Risk
articles.abstract: This article surveys recent developments and important issues in option pricing with a particular focus on time-varying volatility and tail risks. We start by briefly reviewing the most important market events, financial innovations, and theoretical developments from the 1970s to the 1990s and then focus on a more detailed review of the current state of knowledge with a discussion of open questions.

articles.title: Two Tales of Debt
articles.abstract: Recent research suggests that corporate debt contracts in the modern economy follow two common approaches: Some contracts lend against the liquidation value of separable assets, while others focus on cash flows from operations and the going-concern value of the firm as a whole. This article summarizes the key contract features and default resolution mechanisms of these two types of debt used by nonfinancial firms. Firms with abundant liquidation values and physical assets rely on the former; firms with low liquidation values and limited physical assets resort to the latter. Among large firms and those with positive earnings, total borrowing does not depend on physical assets, whereas among small firms and those with negative earnings, total borrowing remains dependent on physical assets. The evidence sheds light on the evolving nature of debt contracting and financial intermediation, with implications for economic fluctuations and growth.

articles.title: Vasomotion of Brain Arteries: Ionic Dynamics Through Systems Physiology in Health and Vascular Disease
articles.abstract: The myogenic tone and thus diameter of brain arterioles varies on multiple time scales. These variations result from coordinated contraction and relaxation of electrically coupled smooth muscle cells in the arteriole wall that drive constriction. A prominent feature is a broad-band ∼0.1 Hz rhythmicity, designated vasomotion, in the pial arterioles spanning the cortical mantle and the penetrating arterioles that nourish the capillary bed. As characterized in the murine brain, vasomotion supports propagating waves with a typical wavelength of 20 mm (a speed of 2 mm/s) that modulate perfusion with a magnitude equal to that of functional hyperemia. The spectral and spatial properties reflect the interaction of smooth muscle dynamics with the underlying neuronal drive. Possible functional roles of vasomotion are to mitigate capillary stalls and to facilitate the exchange of solutes between interstitial and cerebrospinal fluid. Indeed, loss of vasomotion has been implicated in the pathophysiology of vascular disease, such as cerebral amyloid angiopathy.

articles.title: Convergent genomic evolution of human gut bacteria along an industrialization gradient
articles.abstract: Analysis of globally diverse gut bacterial isolate genomes shows that host environments across the industrialization gradient shape genome remodeling and convergent selection, while industrialization is linked to increased HGT-driven gene acquisition and expanded genome size.

articles.title: Fatty acid desaturation controls cellular fate decisions between senescence and ferroptosis
articles.abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism shapes cell fate decisions: loss of DGLA favors senescence, whereas DGLA repletion triggers ferroptosis.

articles.title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism
articles.abstract: Integration of microbiome omics and host data from globally diverse human populations shows that industrialization restructures gut microbial ecosystems and intestinal physiology. These shifts include reduced microbial diversity, compositional heterogeneity, and community stability; altered intestinal immune and physiological responses; and limited cross-population portability of microbiome-based disease predictors.

articles.title: Subsistence transition preceded population turnover in the eastern Colombian Andes
articles.abstract: Ancient DNA data and stable isotope data from the eastern Colombian Andes reveal that C4-enriched resources were incorporated into local food webs during five millennia of genetic continuity and that a later population turnover introduced people with ancestry admixed between that found in Chibchan-related groups and that found at the Amazonian-Andean interface.

articles.title: TECR palmitoylation triggers a necrotic cell death program driving acute liver injury
articles.abstract: We identify a TECR palmitoylation-dependent necrotic cell death (TPNCD) pathway. Blocking TPNCD genetically or pharmacologically protects against immune- and drug-induced liver injury, revealing a therapeutic strategy for hepatic injury.

articles.title: Rethinking lithium content in inorganic solid-state electrolytes
articles.abstract: Inorganic solid-state electrolytes are being developed for safer, energy-dense batteries, yet many contain nearly an order of magnitude more lithium than liquid electrolytes. This perspective proposes low-lithium-content electrolyte design and introduces a lithium-transport realization index connecting local ion motion with long-range conductivity. Evidence across existing materials shows that reduced lithium content does not necessarily sacrifice performance. The resulting design roadmap aims to preserve conductivity with less lithium, potentially easing resource, cost, and environmental burdens.

articles.title: Anions as catalysts: from organosilanes as pro-nucleophiles to base-embedding electrophiles
articles.abstract: Anions are efficient catalysts when combined with organosilanes as pro-nucleophiles or with base-embedding electrophiles, the latter is an emerging catalytic deprotonation strategy which disentangles turnover from acidity–basicity constraints.

articles.title: Chemistry-transforming applications of artificial intelligence
articles.abstract: This review critically assesses how AI is integrated into chemistry. We decompose the chemical research cycle, summarize the modern AI toolkit, and map them onto each other to discuss both near-term and longer-horizon prospects.

articles.title: Potassium-ion batteries for stationary energy storage solutions
articles.abstract: Potassium-ion batteries are a potentially sustainable and cost-competitive technology for large-scale stationary energy storage.

articles.title: Donor−Acceptor Engineering in Porphyrin-Based Two-Dimensional Polymers for Ultrafast Nonlinear Optical Response
articles.abstract: Leveraging their extended π-conjugation, structurally tunable backbones, and superior film-forming processability, two-dimensional (2D) organic polymers have emerged as a highly promising class of materials for third-order nonlinear optical (NLO) applications. Herein, a series of porphyrin-based donor−acceptor (D−A) 2D polymer films, namely, TAPP-TAPZ, TAPP-BATD, TAPP-TDAT, and TAPP-BDTA, are successfully fabricated via a liquid−liquid interfacial polymerization approach. These films exhibit broad absorption profiles across the visible region alongside markedly narrowed optical bandgaps, underscoring the extensive π-electron delocalization inherent to the 2D polymeric frameworks. Femtosecond open-aperture Z-scan measurements conducted at 515 and 800 nm unambiguously reveal pronounced reverse saturable absorption in all samples. Strikingly, the TAPP-TAPZ film delivers exceptional nonlinear absorption coefficients (β) of 8.8 × 103 cm GW−1 at 800 nm and 5.2 × 103 cm GW−1 at 515 nm, values that not only substantially outperform the analogous TAPP-BATD, TAPP-TDAT, and TAPP-BDTA counterparts but also rival or surpass those of numerous reported covalent organic frameworks, 2D inorganic nanomaterials, and small-molecule NLO systems. Complementary density functional theory calculations ascribe this remarkable performance to the incorporation of benzothiadiazole units, which stabilize a donor−donor−acceptor (D−D−A) electronic configuration and facilitate efficient intramolecular charge transfer. Collectively, our findings establish interfacial polymerization as a robust and generalizable route for constructing ordered, defect-minimized 2D films, thereby offering actionable design principles for the development of next-generation ultrafast photonic devices.

articles.title: Broadscale Distribution and Pronounced Mitochondrial Phylogeographic Structure in the Freshwater Minnow Opsariichthys bidens Across China's Major River Basins
articles.abstract: China's complex river basins constitute a critical biogeographic setting for investigating genetic differentiation and lineage divergence in freshwater fishes. Opsariichthys bidens is broadly distributed among multiple, hydrologically isolated river basins, rendering it a well-suited system for assessing mitochondrial phylogeographic structure across major river basins. Here, we used newly generated mitochondrial data to characterize broad-scale genetic variation in O. bidens across China's major river basins. We analyzed 379 cytochrome b (cyt b) sequences sampled from 13 geographically distinct populations, including seven populations from the Yangtze River and one population from each of six other major rivers, complemented by complete mitochondrial genomes from one individual from each population. Mitochondrial diversity was high at the species level (haplotype diversity, H d = 0.942; nucleotide diversity, π = 0.02526), but varied markedly among populations, with some populations showing haplotype fixation and others retaining divergent haplotypes. Genetic differentiation was pronounced, with 83.84% of variation attributable to differences among populations; 93.6% of pairwise F st values exceeded 0.25. Haplotype-network and phylogenetic analyses showed two deeply divergent mitochondrial lineages, broadly distributed in northern and southern China, respectively, with further substructure broadly associated with major river basins. Complete mitochondrial genomes exhibited high structural conservation across lineages, and the clearest lineage-associated annotation differences were observed in the termination codons of nd1 and cox3. Overall, these results provide a broad-scale mitochondrial phylogeographic assessment of O. bidens and reveal a general association between river-basin geography and mitochondrial lineage structure across China.

articles.title: Characteristics of Professionals Involved in Open Science in Ecology and Evolution
articles.abstract: Open science aims to improve research transparency, reuse and societal impact, yet its adoption and reach ultimately depend on people. Understanding how personal characteristics such as gender, work experience or professional role influence familiarity with, attitudes toward and engagement in open science is critical for the effective, widespread implementation of open science practices. We surveyed 342 individuals who produce, mobilise or use scientific knowledge in ecology and evolutionary biology. Their engagement was analysed using the open science change framework, which conceptualises open science as a progression from familiarity and perceptions to practices and support for societal goals, as outlined in the UNESCO Recommendations. Familiarity with open science emerged as a strongest and most consistent predictor of engagement: higher familiarity was associated with more positive attitudes, greater participation in open science practices and stronger agreement with UNESCO principles. Although these relationships are correlational and likely bidirectional, they highlight the central role of familiarity in open science engagement. Years of professional experience were associated with slightly less positive perceptions of open science, particularly among knowledge creators, while gender effects were weak across all stages of engagement. Stakeholder groups differed most in their familiarity with open science, while attitudes and support for broader goals were more similar once familiarity was considered. Together, these findings suggest that increasing familiarity with open science may be more effective than managing resistance or targeting specific demographic groups. Aligning incentives and practical support to increase familiarity offers actionable opportunities to strengthen open science engagement across the research ecosystem in ecology and evolutionary biology and enhance its societal impact.

articles.title: DNA Metabarcoding Reveals Flying Arthropod Diversity and Community Turnover Across Ancient Tea Agroforestry Landscapes in Southwest China
articles.abstract: Ancient tea agroforestry landscapes in Southwest China are structurally complex systems that may support high arthropod diversity, yet their biodiversity value remains poorly documented. We used COI metabarcoding of Malaise‐trap bulk samples to assess flying arthropod assemblages at four tea‐associated sites in the Mengku Ancient Tea and Cultural System, Yunnan, China: a wild ancient tea tree community, a village‐adjacent cultivated ancient tea garden, a forest‐adjacent cultivated ancient tea garden, and a young‐shrub tea plantation. Samples were collected from May to October 2024 and analyzed using OTU‐based diversity and community‐composition approaches. We recovered 5669 arthropod OTUs. Diptera dominated the assemblages, accounting for 57.5% of total OTU richness, followed by Hymenoptera, Lepidoptera, Hemiptera, Coleoptera, and other arthropod groups. OTU richness, alpha diversity, and community composition varied among the four sites. WJC had the highest total OTU richness and mean alpha‐diversity values, whereas DXS yielded the most compositionally distinct assemblage and the largest number of OTUs detected exclusively at that site during this survey. Dominant families included natural enemies, herbivores, and mixed‐function taxa. Seasonal patterns showed higher OTU richness in early summer and September, but lower richness during the main rainy‐season months and October. These findings document marked spatial and seasonal variation in Malaise‐trap‐sampled flying arthropod assemblages. Because each landscape context was represented by a single site, the observed differences cannot be attributed independently to forest association, habitat heterogeneity, or management.

articles.title: Diurnal Nest Site Selection and Thermal Buffering Capacity of Shelters for Rufous Bettongs in a Grazed Savanna Woodland
articles.abstract: Small‐ and medium‐sized mammals are vulnerable to temperature extremes due to their high surface‐area‐to‐volume ratios and elevated metabolic rates. Shelter sites that buffer ambient temperatures are critical for thermoregulation; however, shelter resources may be limited in agricultural landscapes. We examined shelter site selection and the thermal buffering capacity of rufous bettong (Aepyprymnus rufescens) shelters in a grazed tropical savanna woodland in Queensland, Australia. We radio‐tracked 15 rufous bettongs (nine females, six males) across five grazing strategies at Wambiana Station (2020–2021) to locate diurnal shelters. We assessed fine‐scale habitat composition at 133 shelter sites and 224 paired random locations using a MANOVA and NMDS ordination. We deployed iButton data loggers to record hourly temperatures within shelters and at paired ground‐level points 2 m away across wet and dry seasons, isolating the thermal effect of the constructed shelter at the locations the animals selected. Rufous bettongs selected shelter sites characterized by thorny shrubs (Carissa ovata), logs, and termite mounds. Grazing intensity did not significantly affect shelter site selection, though bettongs tended to avoid heavily grazed paddocks. Daytime shelter temperatures (0600–1800 h) were substantially less variable than those at random sites, with thermal buffering most pronounced during the day (0900–1700 h), when random sites exhibited 2–3 times greater temperature variability than bettong shelters. Shelters provided critical thermal refugia, buffering daily temperature extremes by over 20°C in a hot, seasonally variable environment. Retention of dense shrub thickets (C. ovata), logs, and adequate grass cover should be prioritised in grazing landscapes to support rufous bettong persistence under current and future climate conditions.

articles.title: Dynamic Resource Partitioning in a Marine Predator Community
articles.abstract: To avoid competition, species partition resource‐use along various niche axes. However, variable resource availability, especially within dynamic environments, may influence this partitioning. Theory predicts that species will contract their ecological niche to limit competition during times of resource scarcity. We analysed blood δ13C and δ15N composition in four albatrosses, four penguin, two giant petrel and two fur seal species breeding on sub‐Antarctic Marion Island, during two seasons (autumn and summer) over 3 years. Using the species' seasonal stable isotopic niche space as a proxy for trophic niche space, we investigated their trophic dynamics and maintenance of inter‐specific resource partitioning. There were significant variations in the seasonal and inter‐annual trophic niches of these predators. However, despite this high seasonal and annual variability, resource partitioning among the species was maintained over time. Between years, there was greater variability in the species' trophic niches in autumn than in summer. This might reflect species being better able to track productive dynamic oceanographic features during autumn, when most species are less spatially constrained by breeding commitments compared to during summer. Our results indicate that most of these marine predators have foraging behaviours that are either sufficiently flexible or general to cope with resources that are variable in space and time. Their foraging strategies minimise inter‐specific overlap in food or foraging habitat preferences, potentially resulting from historic or present competition for resources.

articles.title: Interspecific Interactions Constrain Individual Niche Divergence and Reveal Energetic Cost of Niche Expansion
articles.abstract: Individuals vary in resource use, generating trophic niche variation that shapes a population's niche width (PNW). Interspecific interactions are predicted to constrain PNW, though individual responses are often heterogeneous. The keystone niche individual (KNI) framework identifies individuals that disproportionately expand PNW by exploiting resources beyond the population's realized niche, but whether interspecific interactions limit their emergence is unknown. We tested this by comparing an allopatric and sympatric population of brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) and rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss). Fatty acid profiles from repeatedly sampled individuals were used to quantify individual trophic niches and their contributions to PNW. Individuals in sympatry exhibited more negative contributions to PNW (−2.70% ± 1.7%) than individuals in allopatry (−0.47% ± 1.8%) and showed a continuum of contributions rather than discrete KNI, indicating that interspecific interactions constrained niche expansion by reducing disproportionate contributions to PNW. Across both populations, individuals with greater contributions to PNW exhibited reduced trophic overlap with competitors and lower body condition, revealing energetic costs of niche expansion. These findings suggest that, in this study system, interspecific interactions can limit niche differentiation by reshaping how individuals contribute to population‐level trophic diversity, highlighting the need to evaluate the generality of these mechanisms across ecological contexts.

articles.title: Mapping Leopard Conservation Priorities in Southeast Asia
articles.abstract: The Indochinese leopard (Panthera pardus delacouri) is one of the most endangered leopard subspecies, restricted to < 4% of its historical range across Southeast Asia. With severe declines driven by poaching, habitat loss and fragmentation, and prey depletion, recovery requires urgent, spatially informed conservation action. This study presents the first connectivity analysis for the Indochinese leopard across its extant and former range, aiming to identify core habitats, priority connectivity areas and opportunities for population restoration. We used resistant kernel modelling through the CoLa Decision Support System to evaluate landscape connectivity across 14 forest complexes in the extant range and 11 potential reintroduction areas, considering scenarios of extant, reintroduction and combined range connectivity. Importance to connectivity was assessed based on Kernel Extent, Kernel Sum, movement density and protected area overlap. Our results confirmed the Dawna–Tenasserim landscape, spanning parts of Thailand and Myanmar, and Peninsular Malaysia as the most critical strongholds. In the former range, our analysis revealed potential for large‐scale metapopulation structural connectivity across Cambodia and Lao PDR, despite recent extirpations. We stress that reintroduction opportunities will require actions such as reducing poaching, restoring prey and improving habitat management. In some complexes, intensive landscape restoration may be needed to reconnect major core areas with smaller reintroduction complexes that could be critical for meta‐population connectivity. Despite increasing human pressure in the region, substantial habitat and connectivity potential remain. Our framework provides a spatial foundation to prioritise actions for preventing extinction of this subspecies and guiding large carnivore recovery across fragmented tropical landscapes.

articles.title: More Than Color: Floral Color Polymorphism Is Associated With Scent Differentiation and Pollination Success in the Deceptive Orchid Anacamptis pyramidalis
articles.abstract: Floral color polymorphism is widespread among flowering plants, yet the mechanisms underlying its maintenance remain poorly understood, particularly in food‐deceptive orchids where pollinator‐mediated selection may differ from that operating in rewarding species. Here, we investigated the relationship among floral color polymorphism, ploidy variation, floral scent composition, and pollination in the Mediterranean deceptive orchid Anacamptis pyramidalis. Cytotypes were determined by flow cytometry, and floral volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were analyzed using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) in white‐ and pink‐flowered individuals from multiple populations. VOC profiles were compared using multivariate and univariate statistical approaches. Pollination success was assessed in mixed‐color diploid and tetraploid populations by quantifying the number of mature fruits produced per individual. Floral color morph was significantly associated with floral scent composition, accounting for approximately 6.5% of the total multivariate variation. Five VOCs differed significantly in relative abundance after correction for multiple comparisons, whereas total VOC emission did not differ significantly between morphs when cultivated in a common garden. No significant association between VOCs and cytotype was detected. White morphs consistently showed higher pollination success than pink morphs, producing significantly more fruits. By showing that floral color polymorphism is associated with both scent differentiation and differences in pollination success, our study highlights the importance of considering floral polymorphism as an integrated phenotype rather than a simple variation in flower pigmentation and helps explain its maintenance in the natural populations of this orchid.

articles.title: Resource Availability Shaped the Female‐Biased Floral Sex Allocation With Plant Size in Andromonoecious Capparis spinosa in Desert
articles.abstract: Although classic models of size‐dependent sex allocation (SDS) generally predict that among animal‐pollinated plants, female allocation increases with individual size, male‐and female‐biased allocation patterns have also been reported. We hypothesized that Capparis spinosa growing in resource‐poor desert habitats would exhibit a female‐biased sex allocation with increasing plant size, and that this pattern would be directly regulated by resource availability, because female function is generally more resource‐demanding to verify this conjecture. We examined SDS patterns at the flowering stage in the andromonoecious desert plant C. spinosa and assessed the role of resource availability in shaping these patterns through resource supplementation and pruning treatments. The results indicated that male plants with a low biomass occurred at low frequencies (0.021–0.051) in seven of the nine assessed populations. Among andromonoecious individuals across the nine populations, with increasing plant size, we recorded increases in the numbers of male and hermaphroditic flowers, the proportion of hermaphroditic flowers, and values of Lloyd's phenotypic gender index. These findings indicate a strong female‐biased sex allocation in C. spinosa plants of larger size. In addition, 2‐year resource manipulation experiments revealed that both the supplementation of water and nutrients and pruning treatments significantly enhanced the proportion of hermaphroditic flowers, thereby indicating that floral sex allocation is directly regulated by resource availability. Our findings in this study highlight the role of resource availability in shaping size‐dependent sex allocation patterns, particularly for plants in resource‐poor desert habitats, and sheds light on the evolution of sexual systems in plants.

articles.title: Spotted Patterns of Glass Frogs Can Disguise Imperfections in Transparency to Improve Camouflage
articles.abstract: Transparency could be considered the idealized version of camouflage, capable of producing effective concealment across heterogeneous habitats. However, although examples of highly transparent species do exist, ‘transparent’ species are highly variable and are often either only partially transparent or better described as translucent. Exactly how these different forms of ‘imperfect’ transparency may act as camouflage remains largely unknown. The glass frogs (Centrolenidae) have long been thought of as a classic example of transparent camouflage due to their see‐through ventral skin. Yet even in these seemingly exemplary cases, glass frogs are better described as translucent due to the presence of obligate opaque structures, such as the internal organs, within the body and opaque color patterns in their dorsal skin. These opaque patterns could be predicted to detract from transparency, with the potential to increase detectability and therefore predation risk. One potential explanation is that the addition of opaque patterning could help to conceal the internal organs from view while maintaining the cryptic effects of translucency. Here we tested whether the presence of opaque spots could reduce predation risk for translucent frogs by presenting model frogs, which differed in opacity and dorsal patterning, to wild birds and recording the rate at which these models were attacked. We found that the addition of opaque dorsal patterning reduced predation risk but there was no effect of translucency on survival. These data suggest that opaque patterning in glass frogs may help to conceal conspicuous internal structures but that partial translucency does not necessarily guarantee effective concealment. Future work is needed to explore the full range of dorsal patterning found in translucent glass frogs and to further examine how patterns comprised of both opaque and transparent elements may function as camouflage in a wider range of taxa.

articles.title: Temporal Changes in the Climatic Predictors of Hatching Success in Leach's Storm‐Petrels
articles.abstract: Climate change is rapidly altering ecosystems worldwide and can modify the demographic rates of long‐lived vertebrates. For seabirds, which rely on ocean productivity, reproductive success is particularly sensitive to climatic variability. Identifying the scale and stability of climate drivers is therefore critical for predicting population dynamics. Previous work on Leach's storm‐petrels (Hydrobates leucorhous) breeding on Kent Island, New Brunswick, showed that Annual Global Mean Temperature (AGMT) best explained hatching success between 1955 and 2010, with a nonlinear response peaking in the late 1980s. Here, we extend this dataset through 2024 to test whether AGMT remains a reliable predictor given the recent rise of ocean temperatures. Using mixed‐effects models, we compared hatching success with multiple climatic indices at regional, basin, and global scales. While AGMT retained some explanatory power, the best performing model for predicting variation in hatching success for the historical dataset (1955–2010) also included the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), which was not evaluated in the original analyses, and the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) for the full dataset (1955–2024). Different pathways may be involved: SOI could reflect non‐breeding conditions and have a carry‐over effect, whereas AMO could change prey availability and foraging conditions during egg formation and incubation. The relationships of hatching success with environmental indices changed over time. These results provide evidence that climate–biology relationships can be temporally dynamic, with the effects of some climatic drivers on hatching success changing over the study period. The AMO has also been linked to variation in adult survival for this population; its emerging importance for hatching success implies a compounded demographic impact with consequences for the population vulnerability.

Reconstructing ancient ecosystems: guanaco and marine carrion as drivers of predator-prey networks in Southern South America
articles.abstract: Understanding ancient trophic dynamics and human integration in terrestrial high-latitude ecosystems requires moving beyond traditional taxonomic lists to evaluate structural biological interactions. This study presents the first probabilistic, trait-based bipartite network reconstruction of ancient predator-prey assemblages in northern Tierra del Fuego, Southern South America, based on archeological records. By integrating a comprehensive zooarcheological dataset spanning 50 spatial-temporal contexts from the late Pleistocene through the late Holocene across steppe and forest habitats, we model trophic interactions including human subsistence strategies. In this region, dominated by grassy steppes and the forest-steppe ecotone, terrestrial hunter-gatherer societies were embedded in a complex predator-prey network in which the guanaco (Lama guanicoe) played a central role. However, the trophic structure of these interactions and how the introduction of humans as an unprecedented predator affected community-level properties is poorly understood. Our results reveal a significant chronological transformation in network architecture and diet composition. During the late Pleistocene, communities exhibited lower interaction diversity and high specialization centered around megaherbivores and multiple large predators. Following megafaunal extinction and island isolation during the mid-Holocene, the guanaco emerged as an enduring keystone herbivore and dietary anchor, while marine-derived carrion and littoral resources (mollusks and pinnipeds) provided critical energy subsidies. Humans acted as highly plastic generalist consumers, influencing network architecture across diverse habitats. In the steppe, foragers employed broad-spectrum strategies, whereas forest assemblages reflected specialized reliance on coastal resources. Ultimately, this community-level framework demonstrates that despite intense environmental shifts and insularization, the guanaco and marine necromass served as foundational trophic stabilizers, maintaining ecosystem and subsistence resilience over millennia.

articles.title: Herbivore versus detritivore effect on decomposition through leaf conversion into faeces
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract In terrestrial ecosystems, plant residues can reach the soil as senesced leaf litter or green leaves, and both types can be transformed by invertebrates into detritivore or herbivore faeces. Yet, the consequences of this conversion on decomposition rates and soil fertility are largely unknown. To fill this knowledge gap, we collected faeces from caterpillars (Historis odius; herbivores) and millipedes (Anadenobolus monilicornis; detritivores), which were fed green and dead leaves of Cecropia schreberiana, respectively, in a tropical ecosystem context. We then incubated green leaves, herbivore faeces, dead leaves and detritivore faeces in a microcosm experiment for 180 days to measure their decomposition and underlying soil parameters. Our results showed significant effects of (1) leaf senescence, with green leaves decomposing faster than leaf litter, and of (2) leaf conversion to invertebrate faeces, with faeces decomposing faster than intact leaves for both herbivore and detritivore faeces. However, contrasting patterns emerged between carbon and nitrogen dynamics, as nitrogen cycling was generally slower for faeces than for litter, with a particularly notable reduction in nitrogen losses for herbivore faeces. Consequences for the biogeochemistry of the underlying soil, specifically soil mineral nitrogen, were also observed. This pioneering study on faeces decomposition in a tropical context suggests that leaf‐feeding invertebrates, whether herbivores or detritivores, accelerate decomposition processes by converting leaves into faeces. This consistent acceleration of decomposition could have important consequences for soil organic matter formation and nutrient returns to plants. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Résumé Dans les écosystèmes terrestres, les résidus végétaux atteignent le sol après la sénescence des feuilles sous forme de litière qui peut être consommée par les détritivores. Une autre voie de restitution est la chute des feuilles vertes suite à des événements météorologiques intenses (pluie, vent, sécheresse) ou à leur consommation par les herbivores dont les déjections atteignent le sol. Cependant, l’impact de ces transformations sur la dynamique de décomposition et le fonctionnement du sol demeure largement méconnu. Afin de combler ce manque de connaissance, nous avons mené une expérience en conditions contrôlées dans un écosystème tropical humide, en utilisant deux espèces d’invertébrés et une espèce végétale collectées en Martinique. Nous avons ainsi collecté des boulettes fécales produites par des chenilles herbivores (Historis odius) et des diplopodes détritivores (Anadenobolus monilicornis), nourris respectivement de feuilles vertes ou de litière de Bois Canon (Cecropia schreberiana). Ces quatre types de matière organique (feuilles vertes, boulettes fécales d'herbivores, litière et boulettes fécales de détritivores) ont ensuite été incubés en microcosmes pendant 180 jours afin d’évaluer leur décomposition et les effets sur les propriétés du sol sous‐jacent. Nos résultats montrent que la sénescence des feuilles influence fortement leur décomposition : les feuilles vertes se décomposent plus rapidement que la litière. De plus, la transformation des feuilles en boulettes fécales accélère significativement leur décomposition, que ce soit pour les herbivores ou les détritivores. Toutefois, nous avons observé des dynamiques contrastées entre la décomposition du carbone et celle de l’azote. Le cycle de l’azote s’avère généralement plus lent dans les boulettes fécales que dans les feuilles, avec une réduction particulièrement marquée des pertes d’azote pour les boulettes fécales d’herbivores. En outre, cette transformation influence significativement le fonctionnement du sol sous‐jacent, notamment en modifiant les niveaux d’azote minéral.…

articles.title: Plastic and adaptive mitochondrial responses help face hypoxia events in a freshwater fish
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Hypoxic events (i.e. reduction of dissolved oxygen in water) are natural events, which intensity and frequency have been amplified by human activities. As oxygen fuels aerobic metabolism, species unable to avoid those events must maintain their functions through phenotypic adjustments, that could occur both at the individual level (plasticity) and population genomic level (adaptation). To examine the adaptative and plastic responses to hypoxia, we exposed two generations of three‐spined sticklebacks, Gasterosteus aculeatus, from wild populations historically exposed to different oxygen levels, to two different experimental oxygen conditions (normoxia or intermittent hypoxia with 12 h normoxia: 12 h hypoxia; with nighttime O2 level at 20% for wild‐caught F0 during 4–6 weeks and at 35% for F1 throughout their entire 19‐month lifetime). By comparing the two generations, early‐life programming of the mitochondrial aerobic metabolism was revealed, conditioning the adult‐stage phenotypic and plastic response: F0 fish from the wild hypoxic environment had elevated pectoral muscle mitochondrial respiration and were able to increase their mitochondrial OXPHOS control efficiency under normoxia conditions at the adult stage. Signs of adaptations towards mitochondrial suppression were found in F1 hypoxia population fish livers while no differences were observed in their pectoral muscle, suggesting a downregulation of the hepatic, but not the pectoral muscle, aerobic activities through generations. In opposition to the adaptative trend, the plastic responses to experimental hypoxia were a decreased mitochondrial respiration in the pectoral muscle and an elevated liver mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation of the F1 fish, suggesting that inherited divergence rather countered than reinforced plastic responses. While both signs of adaptation and plasticity were found in the antioxidant defences of F1 fish, the absence of significant differences between experimental groups in terms of oxidative damage revealed that these fish were able to maintain oxidative balance. Our findings highlight that plasticity to hypoxia depends on the full organism life‐cycle, with the adult ability to face hypoxia depending on their early‐life environmental experience and provides valuable information on the potential evolutionary process of fish facing hypoxia. articles.title: Root‐associated fungi modulate plant recruitment in Mediterranean forests
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Established plants affect directly and indirectly the success of juvenile plants recruiting in their close vicinity, what is defined as a canopy–recruit interaction. Such interactions affect plant species demography and community dynamics. Root‐associated fungi (RAF) can influence plant performance and survival, thus contributing to the sign and intensity of canopy–recruit interactions. Pathogenic RAF negatively affect individual plants and their neighbours, while mycorrhizal fungi can positively counteract those effects. Additionally, saprotrophic RAF decompose organic matter, modifying nutrient availability in the soil, possibly enhancing recruitment. Therefore, understanding the role of RAFs in canopy–recruit interactions will help us understand their potential effect on the dynamics of natural plant communities. We combined information on canopy–recruit interactions for 24 woody species in two Mediterranean mixed forests with high‐throughput sequencing of root DNA from each species. We determined the relationships between plant recruitment and the similarity and richness of RAF communities among woody species associated with different mycorrhizal types. The probability of canopy–recruit interactions decreased between plants sharing more similar pathogenic RAF communities. However, their effect on the frequency of recruitment was modulated by the mycorrhizal association of the recruit, being negative for plant species associated with AM fungi but not significant for those associated with ECM. At the plant species level, plants hosting higher richness of pathogenic RAF presented scarcer recruitment and recruited under a narrower set of canopy species; on the other hand, canopy species associated with ECM fungi or hosting higher richness of saprotrophic RAF promoted denser recruit banks of any species in their vicinity. Our findings provide evidence of the importance of RAF for plant recruitment in natural habitats, and thus for plant population and community dynamics. They support the hypothesis that pathogenic RAF interact with mycorrhizal associations, and that plant species susceptibility to multiple pathogens limits its recruitment success. They also suggest that the positive effect of certain plant species on the recruitment of others (i.e. nurse effect) is likely mediated by a higher diversity of saprotrophic RAF. articles.title: Water amount, rather than watering frequency, structures root‐associated microbial communities and their links to plant performance
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Climate change is altering both the amount and temporal distribution of precipitation, yet drought is often simplified to a single gradient of water reduction. As a result, how experimentally imposed variation in water amount and watering frequency jointly shape root‐associated microbial communities and their links to plant performance remains poorly understood. Using a 3‐year full‐factorial drought experiment in a dry grassland system, we disentangled the individual and interactive effects of water amount, watering frequency and plant composition (conspecific stands versus two‐species mixtures) on root‐associated microbiome and tested whether microbial variation was linked to plant performance. Water amount emerged as the dominant driver of microbial structure, strongly shifting bacterial and fungal composition and reducing bacterial diversity. Watering frequency had weaker but detectable effects, acting mainly on bacterial communities and partly interacting with water amount, whereas the specific contrast between conspecific stands and two‐species mixtures had limited effects. Bacterial community composition was associated with root trait variation and plant fitness, suggesting that drought‐driven bacterial reassembly formed part of the pathway through which water regime influenced plant performance. Together, our results show that water amount and watering frequency represent distinct dimensions of experimental drought with partly independent effects and highlight bacterial reassembly as an important component of grassland responses to increasingly severe and temporally variable drought. articles.title: Within‐crown microclimatic variation and growth‐stage shape oak leaf chemistry with limited consequences for herbivore performance
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Mature trees exhibit distinct vertical gradients in temperature and light. These within‐crown microclimatic gradients have been linked to spatial variation in leaf chemistry and herbivory. However, phytochemical variation and resulting herbivore responses are also strongly influenced by tree phenology and genetic differences among individuals. In this study, we tested whether crown position influences the chemistry of mature leaves and whether these effects vary between distinct phenological stages within a growth cycle. We also examined whether microclimatic or growth‐stage‐related changes in phytochemistry influence herbivore performance. We exposed clonal pedunculate oak (Quercus robur) saplings within three crown strata (ground, middle and upper canopy) of mature trees at two forest sites in Germany and Switzerland. We measured targeted and untargeted leaf chemistry across growth stages and conducted bioassays with generalist spongy moth caterpillars (Lymantria dispar). We found that vertical crown position was a major driver of mature leaf chemistry. Growth stage had a significant additive effect on phytochemistry but explained less variation than crown position. We did not detect any interaction between crown position and growth stage on phytochemistry. Targeted analysis of flavonoids revealed differences among crown positions and between the two growth stages, with compounds showing distinct yet additive responses to these factors. Untargeted metabolomics revealed similar additive patterns, largely reflecting shifts in phenolic and terpenoid‐related metabolite classes. The relative growth rate of caterpillars (RGR) was affected by growth stage, declining during shoot elongation compared to the steady growth stage, but not by crown position. Among the measured metabolites, quercetin 3‐O‐glucuronide was negatively associated with caterpillar RGR, whereas higher triterpenoid levels were positively associated with RGR. Our findings demonstrate that within‐crown microclimatic variation and oak growth stage jointly shape mature leaf phytochemistry, but have only limited consequences for the performance of the generalist herbivore Lymantria dispar. Rather than reflecting broad metabolomic shifts, herbivore performance was associated with only a limited subset of measured metabolites, highlighting that pronounced chemical variation within‐tree crowns does not necessarily translate into equally strong ecological effects.
