Reconstructing ancient disease ecology through pathogen genomics and palaeoproteomics
articles.abstract: Ancient pathogen genomics and palaeoproteomics have transformed archaeological research on infectious disease by enabling the detection of pathogens, reconstruction of extinct lineages, and investigation of host responses in past populations. Yet pathogen identification alone addresses only part of retrospective diagnosis: whether an individual experienced disease, which tissues were affected, and how infection contributed to morbidity or death. Palaeoproteomics extends this enquiry through the recovery of pathogen proteins, host immune proteins, and tissue-associated molecules from ancient human remains and associated materials. This review evaluates its diagnostic contribution within the broader reconstruction of ancient disease ecology. Dental calculus provides a particularly rich record of oral host–microbe interactions, combining microbial signals with inflammatory and dietary proteins. Studies of mummified skin, muscle and other soft tissues, dental pulp, skeletal lesions, historical bloodstains, coprolites, and latrine residues further extend the range of evidence available for retrospective diagnosis. Protein-based investigations of intestinal infection also illustrate the need to distinguish antibody-based antigen detection from sequence-based proteomics. Published studies support several levels of inference, ranging from tissue identification and inflammatory processes to specific infection and, more cautiously, clinical disease. They also reveal continuing challenges involving peptide specificity, contamination, source attribution, and the interpretation of disease-associated proteins. Retrospective diagnosis is strongest when molecular findings are consistent with anatomical, archaeological, and historical evidence and help discriminate among plausible alternative diagnoses. Protein evidence therefore contributes not only to individual palaeopathological diagnosis but also to broader reconstructions of relationships among infection, diet, sanitation, care, and social conditions. Future progress will depend on comparative samples with and without independently supported pathological evidence, archaeological validation of diagnostic markers, transparent reporting, broader regional coverage, and sampling of finite human remains.

articles.title: Carbon Accumulation in Tropical Dry Forests and Savannas Despite Widespread Land‐Cover Change, Revealed by Radar Remote Sensing
articles.abstract: Accurate mapping of woody biomass and its temporal change is critical for understanding the global carbon balance, informing restoration and supporting evidence‐based policy on climate mitigation and livelihoods. The vegetation of the dry tropics, comprised largely of dry forests and savannas, holds substantial woody carbon stocks, but both stocks and change over time remain uncertain. Where Earth Observation (EO) data have been used to estimate change over time, different products give conflicting results on the direction, magnitude and location of change. We present pan‐dry‐tropical maps of aboveground carbon density (AGCD) and AGCD change at 100 m resolution for the years 2015–2024, developed using ALOS ScanSAR satellite radar observations calibrated with in situ measurements (n = 237). These maps suggest an aboveground woody carbon pool (AGC) in the dry tropics of 25.3 ±$$ \pm $$ 2.0 PgC, ~13.0% of global AGC. Net AGC has increased by 0.43 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.07 PgC yr−1, ~20.0% of the global net land sink. The overall net increase (0.43 PgC yr−1) is comprised of gross losses from deforestation and degradation (0.27 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.05 PgC yr−1) and gains due to densification and extensification of 0.59 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.1 PgC yr−1, with the balance accounted for by small changes (change < 20% of AGCD; 0.11 PgC yr−1). Losses are equally split between degradation and deforestation, while gains are divided roughly 2:1 between the densification of woody ecosystems and expansion into previously grass‐dominated areas. These new maps, created with a dry‐tropics‐specific EO method, highlight the importance of tropical dry forests and savannas in the global carbon cycle. The prominent role of degradation‐related losses suggests that climate change mitigation will need to focus much more on reducing losses from overharvesting than at present. The widespread increases in carbon density and the increase in tree biomass into open systems present major challenges for biodiversity conservation, restoration and livelihoods.

articles.title: Thermal Generalism Shapes Tolerance to Extreme Heatwaves in Estuarine Fishes
articles.abstract: Climate change is widely expected to push many taxa beyond their biological limits, yet some populations persist in environments that routinely experience climatic extremes. This raises a fundamental question: does their thermal tolerance reflect species‐level thermal generalism (an evolved capacity to maintain performance across a broad thermal range) or population‐specific acclimation to local conditions (phenotypic plasticity)? Distinguishing between these alternatives is key for predicting whether tolerance to climatic extremes will generalise across species distributions or remain restricted to heat‐tolerant populations. To test these competing hypotheses, we quantified physiological performance (at cellular and organismal levels) in three economically important estuarine fish (Acanthopagrus australis, Sillago ciliata and Rhabdosargus sarba) collected from 20 sites across 15 estuaries along a ~1000‐km latitudinal gradient spanning their core and poleward range edges. Sites differed in thermal variability, including some that intermittently exceeded the severest end‐of‐century climate projections. We then experimentally exposed two of the fish species from low and high thermal variability sites to moderate (+2°C, 14 days) or extreme (+4°C, 7 days) simulated marine heatwave events, assessing 12 physiological and behavioural proxies. All three species collected in situ maintained comparable physiological performance across sites of contrasting thermal variability. Both experimental species, each collected from a single high‐ and low‐variability site, tolerated heatwave conditions regardless of thermal history or heatwave intensity, supporting species‐level thermal generalism rather than population‐specific acclimation. In the absence of heatwave conditions, S. ciliata from high‐variability sites also showed steeper allometric scaling and faster growth at 26 versus 24°C experimental control temperatures, suggesting this species may benefit from the warmer baseline temperatures projected under gradual climate change. Combined, our findings support thermal generalism as the primary driver of tolerance in estuarine fishes to climatic extremes, with important implications for the fisheries they support under climate change.

articles.title: Separating oxidant contact from cobalt activation over O-P⋯Co intersites for leaching-suppressed acetaminophen oxidation
Integrated multi-yarn synergistic light-trapping cone evaporator for efficient steam and wire-structured thermoelectric cogeneration
articles.abstract: Facing global freshwater scarcity and energy shortages, this work designs a flower-inspired 3D solar evaporator made from modified ramie yarns that simultaneously generates clean water and electricity. Its conical structure traps sunlight to drive rapid evaporation (1.77 kg m−2 h−1) and produce thermoelectric voltage (38 mV) while resisting salt crystallization even in high-salinity brine, offering a sustainable, off-grid solution for water-electricity cogeneration.

articles.title: A new approach for detecting phenological change using Time of Emergence (ToE) methodology
articles.abstract: Many species are responding to environmental change by shifting the timings of phenological events such as migration or reproduction. These shifts are typically reported as rates of change, which do not indicate when such shifts transcend their original states, nor consider whether species experience novel environmental conditions or phenological mismatch with other species at their phenological events. We present a new, generalizable approach to detect and contextualize shifts in phenological data regardless of taxonomic group or location by applying statistical and empirical Time of Emergence (ToE) metrics derived from climate science. Our approach conclusively identifies when species depart from their baseline phenological event timings and determines whether they experience novel environmental conditions or phenological mismatch with other species during their phenological event. In combination, these metrics detect emergence in timing, environment and community synchrony for species' phenological responses. We explore these metrics using simulations then apply them to a diverse set of example datasets (butterflies, marine plankton and cherry blossoms). We then develop community‐wide indicators of phenological emergence, environmental emergence and species mismatch, which can be applied to inform biodiversity policy at any scale and for any taxa. These methods are available via the phenometrics R package.

articles.title: Estimating absolute DNA abundance from replicated metabarcoding
articles.abstract: Datasets derived from mixed‐template DNA amplification and sequencing (‘metabarcoding’) are common in environmental DNA (eDNA), microbiome or microbial ecology analyses. Such metabarcoding data have been broadly used to inform estimates of biodiversity, distribution and abundance across a wide range of species and habitats. Generally, data from metabarcoding consist of a table of read‐counts assigned to each of a set of taxa or sequence variants. As such, they appear to contain quantitative information about the environment under study, immediately eligible for traditional community ecology analyses. In fact, metabarcoding data are compositional, can be biased by variation in PCR amplification rates among taxa, and have other statistical attributes that are distinct from many other common ecological observations. The difficulty in understanding and accounting for the complexity of metabarcoding observations has hindered their ecological interpretation and limited their integration with other ecological data types. Here, we use both simulations and empirical observations to show that the variability among replicate metabarcoding observations is closely tied to the absolute quantities of DNA present in a sample. We then develop a general statistical model for estimating DNA abundance from metabarcoding observations using the relationship between mean and variance of metabarcoding reads. We demonstrate that the model can effectively estimate DNA abundances using simulations and from experimentally created DNA samples. The model can be applied to a single marker or to multiple markers simultaneously, allowing the direct integration of information from multiple genetic markers derived from a common biological sample. Estimates of absolute DNA abundance are the logical unit to connect DNA observations to organismal abundance or biomass. Our methods can be used to link together multiple types of DNA observations or to connect DNA observations with non‐genetic ecological methods for surveying ecosystems. However, important aspects of the ‘ecology of DNA’ remain unresolved and may limit our ability to link observed concentrations to organismal abundances in a general way.

articles.title: Seeing both the forest and the trees: An automated workflow for ultra‐high‐resolution drone imaging of tropical canopies
articles.abstract: Tropical forest canopies host diverse tree and liana assemblages, yet key foliar and reproductive traits needed for taxonomic identification of canopy plants are often difficult to see from the forest floor, creating a bottleneck in inventories. We introduce a drone-based workflow that automatically acquires hundreds of close-up, ultra-high-resolution photographs (~0.4 mm pixel−1) of selected tree crowns per day, enabling efficient botanical and ecological studies of canopy plants (demo: https://youtu.be/80goMEifpc4). The approach leverages a compact DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise (M3E) with wide-angle and telephoto cameras to (i) generate a high-resolution digital surface model and orthomosaic via structure-from-motion photogrammetry and (ii) capture close-up photographs from ~6 m above the canopy at preplanned locations. Photographs are accurately (<13 cm error) geolocated with real-time kinematic (RTK) global navigation satellite system to support spatial co-registration with photogrammetric products. In field deployments, we acquired close-up photographs for up to ~300 selected canopy trees per day and maintained RTK corrections over operational distances up to ~3 km, illustrating the potential of the method for plot- to landscape-scale studies. The level of visual detail in the close-up photographs of canopy crowns was sufficient to support expert identification in a majority of cases in our tropical forest study sites despite their high taxonomic diversity. Although developed for tropical trees and lianas, the workflow is applicable to other forest and vegetation types for botanical, phenological and ecological applications. We outline strengths and limitations of the workflow to guide use and also provide harpia , an open-source Python library to program automatic close-up missions with the M3E (code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22116831). Resumen El dosel de los bosques tropicales alberga diversas comunidades de árboles y lianas. Sin embargo, las características foliares y reproductivas clave necesarias para la identificación taxonómica de las especies del dosel suelen ser difíciles de observar desde el suelo del bosque, lo que limita el progreso en los inventarios. Presentamos un flujo de trabajo basado en drones que adquiere automáticamente cientos de fotografías de primer plano de ultra alta resolución (~0,4 mm píxel−1) de copas de árboles seleccionadas por día, agilizando los estudios botánicos y ecológicos de las especies del dosel (demostración: https://youtu.be/80goMEifpc4). Utilizamos un dron DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise (M3E) compacto, equipado con cámaras gran angular y teleobjetivo, para (i) generar un modelo digital de superficie y un ortomosaico de alta resolución mediante fotogrametría de estructura a partir del movimiento (structure-from-motion) y (ii) capturar fotografías de primer plano desde ~6 m sobre el dosel en ubicaciones planificadas previamente. Las fotografías se georreferencian con precisión (error <13 cm) mediante un sistema global de navegación por satélite (GNSS) con posicionamiento cinemático en tiempo real (RTK), facilitando su corregistro espacial con los productos fotogramétricos. En campañas de campo, adquirimos fotografías de primer plano de hasta ~300 árboles de dosel diarios y mantuvimos correcciones RTK a distancias operativas de hasta ~3 km, lo que evidencia el potencial del método para estudios desde nivel de parcela hasta paisaje. La alta resolución de las fotografías permitió la identificación taxonómica por expertos en la mayoría de los casos, aun en ecosistemas de bosque tropical con elevada diversidad taxonómica. Aunque se desarrolló para árboles y lianas tropicales, el flujo de trabajo es aplicable a otros tipos de bosques y vegetación con fines botánicos, fenológicos y ecológicos.…

articles.title: TreeSegAgent: Agentic tree instance segmentation via a multi‐anchor pipeline
articles.abstract: Individual‐tree segmentation from three‐dimensional forest point clouds underpins forest inventory, biomass estimation and ecosystem monitoring, but remains challenging in structurally complex stands, where vertical heterogeneity and point‐density degradation weaken the robustness of centre‐offset‐based instance grouping. We present TreeSegAgent, an extensible framework for forest point‐cloud analysis, whose core segmentation component is a multi‐anchor framework for tree segmentation (MA‐TreeSeg). MA‐TreeSeg stabilizes instance formation through two modules. First, a multi‐anchor (three‐vertical‐anchor) structural grouping module within an enhanced PointGroup‐style instance segmentation network, explicitly encoding tree vertical structure to improve grouping stability under sparse canopy conditions and to better recover low‐stature and understory trees. Second, we incorporate segment anything model (SAM)‐driven trunk constraint module. SAM is applied on two‐dimensional projections to identify trunk regions and generate trunk candidates, which are then employed as spatial hard constraints to regularize centre‐offset predictions and suppress clustering drift under canopy overlap. To support reproducible ecological workflow, TreeSegAgent further provides a task‐driven agent for automated, specification‐driven orchestration of common point‐cloud operations (e.g. instance segmentation, DEM generation and height‐based filtering) across datasets. Across multiple forest point‐cloud benchmarks, our method yields more spatially coherent individual‐tree instances and improved robustness to density variation, offering an extensible solution for large‐scale forest point‐cloud analysis.

articles.title: Turning Red to Green Repeatedly: Ancestral LWS Duplications Drive Convergent Visual Tuning in Teleost Fishes
articles.abstract: Photopigments, formed by an opsin protein bound to a light‐sensitive chromophore, underlie vertebrate vision. Long‐wavelength–sensitive (LWS) opsins mediate red‐light detection, and most teleosts retain a single functional LWS1. A shorter‐shifted green‐sensitive paralog (LWS2) is found only in a few lineages. By mining teleost genomes and sequencing retinal transcriptomes, we identify elopomorphs as an additional lineage retaining LWS2 (alongside characins and osteoglossomorphs). Surprisingly, we reveal a previously overlooked, shorter‐shifted paralog, LWS3, restricted to gobies (Percomorpha) and arising from an ancestral duplication either in the teleost or in the percomorph ancestor. Structural modelling of twelve LWS opsins reveals convergent evolution at four key amino acid sites (214, 259, 261, 269) in the retinal‐binding pocket, indicating convergent substitutions in human MWS (an old‐world primate‐specific duplicate of the vertebrate LWS1), teleost LWS2, and goby LWS3 relative to red‐sensitive counterparts, consistent with repeated spectral shifts towards greener wavelengths. In several lineages, including characins, mormyrids, gobies, and primates, these shorter‐shifted LWS opsins have at least partially replaced the canonical green‐sensitive RH2‐based visual pigment. Retinal transcriptomes revealed variable lws3 expression across adult gobies, either complementing lws1 in most species, or dominating the visual opsin expression profile as in the sicydiines. In situ hybridisation in the whitebarred goby (Amblygobius phalaena; Valenciennes, 1837) showed that lws1 and lws3 are expressed in separate double‐cone members, analogous to rh2 expression in other fish species. Together, these results show that repeated convergence towards shorter LWS sensitivity in vertebrate evolution involves coordinated changes at the molecular, regulatory, and functional levels, providing a striking example of multilevel sensory adaptation.

articles.abstract: Preterm birth is the leading cause of death in children globally. We determined proteome-wide autoantibody profiles for 2,195 pregnant individuals, revealing a shared humoral program of normal pregnancy and a distinct, expanded autoreactive signature that precedes preterm birth.

articles.abstract: The alarming rise in NCDs, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, is closely linked to infectious diseases. Despite growing evidence of a bidirectional, mutually reinforcing relationship, these links have received insufficient attention from researchers and healthcare stakeholders.

articles.title: Bioresorbable metal-free molecular magnets enable untethered organ monitoring
articles.abstract: A bioresorbable, metal-free molecular magnet for wireless deep-tissue sensing is reported that enables continuous cardiac monitoring and injectable organ tracking in vivo before the material safely degrades.

articles.title: Bridging microwaves and light
articles.abstract: Strong coupling between magnons and excitons in CrSBr enables microwave-to-optical transduction, offering a route towards efficient conversion between otherwise disparate frequency regimes.

articles.title: Multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM): a reconfigurable platform for high-resolution light-sheet fluorescence microscopy
articles.abstract: The multi-immersion oblique plane microscope is a flexible and versatile light-sheet microscope that allows imaging of samples ranging from cells in culture to whole organisms or cleared tissue samples.

articles.title: An amygdala-mediated simulation-to-decision cascade aligns interbrain dynamics to solve social dilemmas
articles.abstract: Using simultaneous intracranial recordings from interacting human brains, Ma et al. show that mutual cooperation emerges when amygdala activity aligns across partners and predictions about a partner guide each person’s own decisions.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal remodeling in habenula marks the onset of depression-related phenotypes
articles.abstract: Chronic stress has lasting adverse consequences that can lead, over time, to depression, yet the optimal timeframe for effective therapies remains unclear. The lateral habenula (LHb) has been implicated in stress-related behavioral repercussions, but the precise timing of its contribution is not understood. Here, using spatial transcriptomics, we generated a spatially resolved molecular atlas of the LHb of male mice, revealing a topographically organized and temporally defined remodeling of gene expression after chronic stress. Longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of individual LHb neurons revealed progressively heightened excitatory responses to aversive stimuli. These neuronal adaptations mirrored both the progression of transcriptional changes and the emergence of depression-related behavioral phenotypes and were reversed by the antidepressant ketamine. Moreover, chemogenetically limiting LHb neuronal activity or administering ketamine at the onset of these changes exerted antidepressant effects. These findings link spatiotemporal signatures of LHb neuronal ensembles and genetic landscape with the onset of stress-induced depression-related states.

articles.title: A liquid-crystal analogue of the skyrmion Hall effect
articles.abstract: Magnetic skyrmions are known to exhibit a Hall effect in the presence of an electric current. Now it is shown that liquid-crystal solitons also exhibit a Hall-like drift under shear flow.

articles.title: Evidence for spin-fluctuation-mediated superconductivity in electron-doped cuprates
articles.abstract: In conventional, phonon-mediated superconductors, the transition temperature and the linear-in-temperature normal-state scattering rate are linked through the electron–phonon coupling strength. In cuprate high-temperature superconductors, no equivalent relationship between critical temperature and electron–boson coupling has been identified. Here we highlight such a link with electrons scattering off commensurate antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations of variable strength. We use d.c. resistivity and high-field magnetoresistance to extract the scattering rate in electron-doped La 2− x Ce x CuO 4 as a function of doping. We reveal a highly anisotropic inelastic component to the scattering rate whose magnitude diminishes markedly as doping increases. The correlation we highlight between the strength of scattering and the critical temperature then identifies low-energy spin fluctuations as the primary pairing glue in electron-doped cuprates. The contrasting magnetotransport behaviour in hole-doped cuprates suggests that the higher critical temperature in those materials cannot be attributed solely to an increase in the coupling strength to the antiferromagnetic fluctuations. The success in modelling La 2− x Ce x CuO 4 reinforces the notion that resolving the origin of high-temperature superconductivity in hole-doped cuprates may require more than a simple extension of the Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer theory.

articles.title: A solution for metal–organic cages
Stepwise and chemoselective installation of carbon substituents at silicon atoms via monobromination of hydrosilanes
articles.abstract: Although organosilicon compounds containing different carbon substituents are ubiquitous in synthetic chemistry, their preparation is challenging. Laboratory synthesis commonly relies on the sequential substitution of tetrachlorosilane or tetraalkoxysilanes, producing complex mixtures that require demanding purification. This arises from limited control over nucleophilic substitution in functionalized silanes containing three or four (identical) leaving groups. Here we introduce an experimentally straightforward and reliable procedure for the preparation of both hetero- and homoleptic silanes using an overlooked monobromination of primary and secondary hydrosilanes. An equimolar amount of elemental bromine converts a Si–H bond into an Si–Br bond without ‘overbromination’. This step also shows exceptional functional-group tolerance to existing substituents at the silicon atom. Unsaturated moieties as well as heteroatom and heteroaryl groups are compatible. When performed in an iterative fashion, multihydrosilanes can be selectively converted into secondary, tertiary and quaternary silanes with two, three or four different carbon substituents in high yields. These functionalized silicon building blocks are relevant to synthetic chemistry as well as applied chemistry materials.

articles.title: Straightforward on-demand synthesis of heteroleptic silanes
articles.abstract: The stepwise installation of carbon substituents at silicon starting from tetrachlorosilane or tetraalkoxysilanes is burdened by chemoselectivity issues, typically affording product mixtures. Now, monoselective bromination of multihydrosilanes followed by nucleophilic displacement opens the door to the programmable and reliable synthesis of functionalized silicon building blocks.

articles.title: Orientation-Dependent Structural Phase Transitions and Melting in Shock-Compressed MgO
articles.abstract: Shockwave observations resolve the high pressure structural transition and melting temperature of MgO, a critical planetary building block.

articles.abstract: Protective policies, health insurance, and community are all important variables when gender-diverse scientists ask, “Where to next?”

articles.title: MAIT cells in gastrointestinal cancer: immunity to therapy
articles.abstract: Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells are emerging as important regulators of immunity in gastrointestinal (GI) cancers. Enriched in mucosal and hepatic tissues, MAIT cells recognize microbial-derived metabolites presented by MHC class I-related molecule MR1 and rapidly exert effector functions, including cytokine production and cytotoxicity. Across GI malignancies, including hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, and esophageal cancers, MAIT cells display context-dependent roles shaped by the tumor microenvironment, microbiome, and immune signaling pathways. While they can mediate antitumor immunity, they frequently exhibit functional exhaustion or adopt pro-tumorigenic phenotypes. Therapeutic strategies aim to enhance MAIT cell activity, reverse dysfunction, and integrate them into combinatorial immunotherapy approaches. Understanding MAIT cell biology may enable their exploitation as biomarkers and therapeutic targets in GI cancers.

articles.title: Advances in poly(disulfide)s: dynamic polymerization of cyclic disulfides
articles.abstract: Advances in dynamic covalent chemistry have dramatically broadened its use in polymer research. Cyclic disulfide bonds are a widely used, versatile platform for engineering dynamic polymers. The resulting polymers leverage the dynamic character of exocyclic linkages associated with cyclic disulfide bonds, along with modular, tailorable chain-end functionalities to enable self-healing and chemical recycling. This review summarizes recent advances in dynamic polymer chemistry based on cyclic disulfide bonds that have enabled new design principles for the development and innovation in advanced polymers. We highlight living/controlled polymerization strategies for cyclic disulfide monomers, covering the principal polymerization strategies and mechanisms, and discuss the future challenges and prospective directions of the field in the context of emerging societal and technological demands.

articles.title: Plant reproductive palaeobiology: a window into long-term reproductive dynamics
articles.abstract: Reproductive dynamics strongly influence genetic diversity and population structure, with important implications for ecological interactions and evolutionary trajectories. However, our understanding of plant reproductive dynamics remains limited due to the scarcity of long-term studies. Here, we propose a conceptual and methodological framework for tracking plant reproductive dynamics over long timescales using pollen, plant spore, and seed records preserved in sedimentary archives. The analysis of counts, morphology, and DNA from fossil propagules enables reconstruction of reproductive patterns over centennial to million-year timescales. When integrated with other palaeoproxies, these records provide insights into environmental drivers and eco-evolutionary consequences of reproductive dynamics. The proposed framework opens new avenues for optimising conservation strategies, safeguarding key ecological functions, and improving predictions of future biotic responses.

articles.title: Carbonate intercalation polarizes Ni and Fe centers in NiFe-LDH for ampere-level alkaline oxygen evolution
articles.abstract: Interlayer CO 3 2− polarizes the Ni–O–Fe motif in NiFe-LDH, inducing differentiated electronic responses at the Ni and Fe sites. This site-dependent electronics promote the early formation of Ni 3+ –O and *OOH, enabling ampere-level alkaline OER.

articles.title: Critical constraints to ecological buffering in a rapidly changing Arctic: A long‐term seabird study
articles.abstract: Drawing on two decades of research in East Greenland, this study shows that little auks, key seabird indicators of Arctic ecosystem health, can adapt to rapid environmental change through behavioural flexibility. However, increasing storms and mercury pollution are pushing resilience to its limits, providing an early warning of broader Arctic disruption. Abstract Long‐term ecological studies testing global change impacts are rare yet essential in the Arctic, a region warming nearly four times faster than the global average. These rapid environmental changes reshape ecosystem functioning across the pan‐Arctic and affect the livelihoods of local communities. Seabirds are widely recognised indicators of environmental change. Identifying species‐specific critical constraints is therefore essential for detecting early warning signals of population decline and ecosystem reorganisation. Little auks (Alle alle), the most abundant Arctic seabirds, are key ecosystem engineers shaping coastal environments through for example food‐web interactions and guano deposition. We present a 20‐year study (2005–2024) of an East Greenland little auk population, combining long‐term demographic monitoring with behavioural, physiological and ecotoxicological data. We quantified fitness‐related traits (adult body condition, overwinter survival and chick growth) alongside potential constraints, including parental foraging effort, trophic ecology, winter distribution, and mercury contamination in adults, eggs and chicks. Over the study period, climate‐driven ocean warming, sea‐ice decline, altered zooplankton communities, and increasing mercury exposure reshaped environmental conditions. Faced with these changes, little auks exhibited marked behavioural and dietary plasticity, allowing them to maintain relatively stable fitness metrics in most years. However, sustained monitoring revealed key constraints that undermine this apparent resilience: (a) Elevated mercury burdens may reduce aerobic diving capacity and thermal tolerance in adults and were associated with reduced reproductive performance. (b) Chick growth was strongly impaired during years with increased summer storm activity, which disrupted adult foraging trips and provisioning rates. Winter storms are also likely to negatively affect adult overwinter survival. Together, these findings show that little auks can partially buffer rapid Arctic change through behavioural flexibility, but multiple interacting climatic and contaminant stressors impose increasing, possibly cumulative constraints on performance. Identifying such critical constraints is crucial for understanding the limits of resilience in wild populations and for improving predictions of ecosystem responses to ongoing climate change.

articles.title: Impact of polyvinyl chloride on the hydrogenolysis of low-density polyethylene over supported transition metal catalysts

Insights into two modes of TdT action in human V(D)J recombination
articles.abstract: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is a DNA polymerase expressed in pre-B and pre-T cells that functions in V(D)J recombination to add random nucleotides in a template-independent (TI) mode at junctions between antigen receptor gene segments. However, cellular, biochemical, and structural studies have also revealed a significant, short-length, template-dependent (TD) mode of TdT, in which it takes instructions from a template strand across a double-strand break. Here, we propose that this can occur through an intrachain fold-back synthesis to generate the short inverted repeats at V(D)J recombination junctions observed in early human lymphoid cells and within the adult human antigen receptor repertoire. This duality is also relevant to the functional and structural flexibility observed during the DNA repair process known as nonhomologous DNA end joining (NHEJ).

articles.title: NKG2D overexpression potentiates CAR-T cells through costimulation by tumor NKG2D ligands

Overexpressing NKG2D shields endogenous ligands and harnesses tumor NKG2DLs for costimulation, thereby enhancing CAR-T cell persistence, tumor infiltration, and antitumor efficacy across multiple models.

Vascularization enhances β cell maturation in vitro and survival under hypoxia. Following transplantation into diabetic mice, VPIOs establish functional connections with the host vasculature and effectively restore normoglycemia.

articles.title: Bacterial Surfaces and Barriers: Biogenesis and Pathogen–Host Interactions
articles.abstract: The bacterial surface represents the primary interface between pathogens and hosts, yet its chemical and architectural complexity challenges conventional classification. This Review examines structural organization, molecular composition, and biogenesis of bacterial surface components across the Gracilicutes and Terrabacteria clades, linking mechanistic detail to pathogenic function. We describe lipid diversity, integral membrane protein biogenesis, and lipoprotein processing at the inner membrane and how these components support surface remodeling, secretion, and virulence. We then examine the peptidoglycan layer and its role in immune recognition and surface protein display, teichoic acids and their contributions to antimicrobial resistance and immune evasion, and S layers, whose crystalline arrays mediate adhesion and immune modulation. The outer membrane section covers lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, outer membrane protein biogenesis and folding, lipoprotein trafficking, and contributions to pathogenicity, while the mycobacterial section addresses the mycolyl-arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan complex and virulence factors. We discuss bacterial capsule diversity, biosynthesis, and use as vaccine antigens, along with adhesive surface structures such as fimbriae, pili, and curli fibers and their roles in colonization and biofilm formation, before covering secretion systems types I through XI and their contributions to virulence. This Review provides a framework for understanding how bacterial surface diversity shapes infection and identifies chemical vulnerabilities for therapeutics.

articles.title: Mapping Local Environments in Single-Atom Catalysts
articles.abstract: Single-atom catalysts (SACs) offer exceptional structural resolution for investigating how local environments govern catalytic behavior and, ultimately, for controlling these effects through catalyst design. Yet, atomic dispersion does not imply a single or fully defined catalytic environment. The behavior of atomically dispersed active centers is shaped by a hierarchical local environment comprising persistent and transient contributions, while also being influenced by an extended reaction environment that intersects with the local environment in controlling reactivity and can become integrated into it. Establishing these boundaries and understanding how these contributions evolve and interact are central challenges in the interpretation and design of SACs. Here, we critically examine how local environments are generated and controlled, experimentally and theoretically resolved across spatial and temporal scales, transformed from synthesis through operation and deactivation, and linked to catalytic performance through structural, energetic, and electronic descriptors. By integrating aspects that are often considered separately and highlighting those that remain insufficiently addressed, we provide a roadmap toward the predictive, environment-driven design of SACs and a deeper understanding of catalytic phenomena.

articles.title: Regenerated Cellulose for Sustainable Electronic Devices
articles.abstract: Regenerated cellulose (RC), derived from natural cellulose through dissolution and regeneration processes, has emerged as a sustainable, versatile, and cost-effective material for advanced electronic devices. With unique hierarchical structures, abundant hydroxy groups, and excellent mechanical and thermal properties, RC allows extensive customization of its characteristics, offering biocompatibility, flexibility, processability, and environmental friendliness. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in RC-based electronics, focusing on its multiscale molecular configuration, dissolution and regeneration mechanisms, and functionalization and engineering strategies. It first provides a detailed molecular-level analysis of RC structures and formation mechanisms. The principles and strategies of cellulose dissolution and regeneration are then discussed, with emphasis on solvent systems and structure-regulating mechanisms essential for processing control. Functionalization strategies are categorized into direct modification and hybridization with functional materials. Notably, the hybridization approach involves the development of conductive, semiconductive, and insulating RC composites, evaluated from the perspectives of material selection, interfacial design, and processing techniques. Subsequently, engineering approaches to enhance mechanical strength, electrical conductivity, and optical transparency are explored. Applications of RC in sensors, actuators, circuits, energy harvesting and storage devices, and electromagnetic shielding devices are highlighted, demonstrating its potential to drive sustainable innovation in electronics. Finally, future directions are proposed to address remaining challenges, paving the way for RC to contribute to eco-friendly, high-performance electronic devices.

articles.title: Hole-selective self-assembled monolayers: a molecular platform for high-performance perovskite photovoltaics
